items.title: 16.2   Contributing to the book
items.text:
Even with my best efforts, this book has its share of errors and omissions. Thank you for bearing with me. If you spot a typo, a broken link, missing material, ambiguous wording, an unclear explanation, or a passage that is hard to follow because of how it is organized, please help us fix it so readers can learn more easily.

To thank everyone who contributes their time to the open-source community, we list the GitHub username of every contributor on the repository home page, the website’s home page, and the opening page of the PDF.

The appeal of open source

Print books often go a long time between printings, which makes them difficult to update.

With this open-source book, an update can reach readers in days or even hours.

items.title: 1.   Making small edits
items.text:
Each page has an edit icon in the upper-right corner, as shown below. To edit text or code, follow these steps.

  1. Click the edit icon. If GitHub prompts you to fork the repository, accept the prompt.
  2. Edit the Markdown source file, check your changes for accuracy, and try to keep the formatting consistent.
  3. At the bottom of the page, describe your changes and click “Propose file change.” On the next page, click “Create pull request” to open a pull request.

Figure 16-3   Edit button in the upper-right corner of the page

Images cannot be edited directly. Open an issue or leave a comment describing the problem, and we will redraw and replace the image as soon as we can.

items.title: 2.   Contributing new material
items.text:
To contribute to this open-source project, for example by translating code into another programming language or expanding a section of the book, follow these steps to submit a pull request.

  1. Sign in to GitHub and fork the book’s repository to your personal account.
  2. Go to your fork on GitHub and use git clone to clone it to your computer.
  3. Create the new material locally and test the code thoroughly to verify that it works correctly.
  4. Commit your changes locally, then push them to your remote repository.
  5. Refresh the repository page and click “Create pull request” to open a pull request.

items.title: 16.1.1   Installing an IDE
items.text:
We recommend VS Code, a lightweight, open-source integrated development environment (IDE), for working on your computer. Visit the VS Code website to download and install the version for your operating system.

Figure 16-1   Downloading VS Code from the official website

VS Code has a large collection of extensions that let you run and debug code in most programming languages. For example, installing the Python Extension Pack lets you debug Python code. Figure 16-2 shows how to install the pack.

Figure 16-2   Installing an extension pack in VS Code

items.title: 1.   Python
items.text:
1. Download and install Miniconda3. You need Python 3.10 or later.
  2. Search for python in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install the Python Extension Pack.
  3. (Optional) Run pip install black at the command line to install the code formatter.

items.title: 2.   C/C++
items.text:
1. On Windows, install MinGW (see the setup guide in Chinese). On macOS, Clang is already included.
  2. Search for c++ in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install the C/C++ Extension Pack.
  3. (Optional) Open Settings, search for the Clang_format_fallback Style formatting option, and set it to { BasedOnStyle: Microsoft, BreakBeforeBraces: Attach }.

items.title: 3.   Java
items.text:
1. Download and install a version of OpenJDK newer than JDK 9.
  2. Search for java in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install the Extension Pack for Java.

items.title: 4.   C
items.text:
1. Download and install .NET 8.0.
  2. Search for C# Dev Kit in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install C# Dev Kit (see the setup guide).
  3. You can also use Visual Studio (see the installation guide).

items.title: 5.   Go
items.text:
1. Download and install Go.
  2. Search for go in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install the Go extension.
  3. Press Ctrl + Shift + P to open the Command Palette, type go, and choose Go: Install/Update Tools. Select all the tools and install them.

items.title: 6.   Swift
items.text:
1. Download and install Swift.
  2. Search for swift in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install Swift for Visual Studio Code.

items.title: 7.   JavaScript
items.text:
1. Download and install Node.js.
  2. (Optional) Search for Prettier in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install the code formatter.

items.title: 8.   TypeScript
items.text:
1. Follow the steps for setting up JavaScript.
  2. Install TypeScript Execute (tsx).
  3. Search for typescript in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install Pretty TypeScript Errors.

items.title: 9.   Dart
items.text:
1. Download and install Dart.
  2. Search for dart in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install the Dart extension.

items.title: 10.   Rust
items.text:
1. Download and install Rust.
  2. Search for rust in the VS Code Extensions Marketplace and install rust-analyzer.

items.title: Chapter 4.   Arrays and linked lists
items.text:
Abstract

Imagine the world of data structures as a solid brick wall.

The bricks of an array lie in neat rows, each pressed against the next. The bricks of a linked list are scattered, joined by vines that wind freely through the gaps.

items.title: 4.1   Arrays
items.text:
An array is a linear data structure that stores elements of the same type in contiguous memory. An element's position in the array is its index. Figure 4-1 shows how the elements are indexed and stored.

Figure 4-1   An array and its memory layout

items.title: 1.   Initializing an array
items.text:
Depending on what we need, we can create an array with or without specifying initial values. When no initial values are supplied, most programming languages initialize the elements to \(0\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array.py
# Initialize the array
arr: list[int] = [0] * 5  # [ 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 ]
nums: list[int] = [1, 3, 2, 5, 4]
array.cpp
/* Initialize the array */
// Stored on the stack
int arr[5] = {};
int nums[5] = {1, 3, 2, 5, 4};
// Stored on the heap (must be freed manually)
int *arr1 = new int[5]{};
int *nums1 = new int[5]{1, 3, 2, 5, 4};
array.java
/* Initialize the array */
int[] arr = new int[5]; // { 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 }
int[] nums = { 1, 3, 2, 5, 4 };
array.cs
// Initialize the array
int[] arr = new int[5]; // [ 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 ]
int[] nums = [1, 3, 2, 5, 4];
array.go
/* Initialize the array */
var arr [5]int
// In Go, specifying the length ([5]int) gives an array, while omitting it ([]int) gives a slice
// Go fixes array lengths at compile time, so the length must be a constant
// To simplify the extend() function for extending an array, we use a slice as the array below
nums := []int{1, 3, 2, 5, 4}

/* Initialize the array */
let arr = Array(repeating: 0, count: 5) // [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
var nums = [1, 3, 2, 5, 4]

const arr = new Array(5).fill(0);
let nums = [1, 3, 2, 5, 4];

// Rust fixes array lengths at compile time, so the length must be a constant
// A vector is the usual dynamic array type in Rust

items.title: 2.   Accessing an element
items.text:
Because array elements occupy contiguous memory, their addresses are easy to calculate. Given the base address of the array (the address of its first element) and the index of an element, we can use the formula below to calculate that element's address and access it directly.

Figure 4-2   Calculating the memory address of an array element

In the figure, the first element has index \(0\). That may seem surprising if counting from \(1\) feels more natural. The address formula explains why: an index is essentially an offset from the base address, measured in elements. The first element's offset is \(0\), so its index is naturally \(0\).

Array access is efficient. We can access any element at random in \(O(1)\) time.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array.py
def random_access(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    """Access a random element"""
    # Pick a random index in [0, len(nums)-1]
    random_index = random.randint(0, len(nums) - 1)
    # Get and return the element at that index
    random_num = nums[random_index]
    return random_num
array.cpp
/* Access a random element */
int randomAccess(int *nums, int size) {
    // Pick a random index in [0, size)
    int randomIndex = rand() % size;
    // Get and return the element at that index
    int randomNum = nums[randomIndex];
    return randomNum;
}
array.java
/* Access a random element */
int randomAccess(int[] nums) {
    // Pick a random index in [0, nums.length)
    int randomIndex = ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(0, nums.length);
    // Get and return the element at that index
    int randomNum = nums[randomIndex];
    return randomNum;
}
array.cs
/* Access a random element */
int RandomAccess(int[] nums) {
    Random random = new();
    // Pick a random index in [0, nums.Length)
    int randomIndex = random.Next(nums.Length);
    // Get and return the element at that index
    int randomNum = nums[randomIndex];
    return randomNum;
}

}

    let randomNum = nums[randomIndex]
    return randomNum

items.title: 3.   Inserting an element
items.text:
Array elements sit right next to one another in memory, with no room between them for additional data. To insert an element in the middle, shift the elements from the insertion point onward one position to the right, then write the new element at the desired index, as shown below.

Figure 4-3   Inserting an element into an array

Because the array has a fixed length, inserting an element this way necessarily “loses” the element previously in its last slot. We will discuss a solution in the section on lists.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array.py
def insert(nums: list[int], num: int, index: int):
    """Insert num at the specified array index"""
    # Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1, index, -1):
        nums[i] = nums[i - 1]
    # Store num at the specified index
    nums[index] = num
array.cpp
/* Insert num at the specified array index */
void insert(int *nums, int size, int num, int index) {
    // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
    for (int i = size - 1; i > index; i--) {
        nums[i] = nums[i - 1];
    }
    // Store num at the specified index
    nums[index] = num;
}
array.java
/* Insert num at the specified array index */
void insert(int[] nums, int num, int index) {
    // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
    for (int i = nums.length - 1; i > index; i--) {
        nums[i] = nums[i - 1];
    }
    // Store num at the specified index
    nums[index] = num;
}
array.cs
/* Insert num at the specified array index */
void Insert(int[] nums, int num, int index) {
    // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
    for (int i = nums.Length - 1; i > index; i--) {
        nums[i] = nums[i - 1];
    }
    // Store num at the specified index
    nums[index] = num;
}

/* Insert num at the specified array index */
func insert(nums []int, num int, index int) {
    // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
    for i := len(nums) - 1; i > index; i-- {
        nums[i] = nums[i-1]
    }
    // Store num at the specified index
    nums[index] = num
}

    }
    // Store num at the specified index

}

    // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right

}
array.dart
/* Insert _num at the specified array index */

array.rs

    // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
    for i in (index + 1..nums.len()).rev() {
        nums[i] = nums[i - 1];
    }
    // Store num at the specified index
    nums[index] = num;
}

/* Insert num at the specified array index */

    // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right

        nums[i] = nums[i - 1];

}

/* Insert num at the specified array index */

    // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
    for (i in nums.size - 1 downTo index + 1) {
        nums[i] = nums[i - 1]
    }
    // Store num at the specified index
    nums[index] = num
}

  end

  # Store num at the specified index
  nums[index] = num
end

items.title: 4.   Removing an element
items.text:
Similarly, to remove the element at index \(i\), shift every element after \(i\) one position to the left, as shown below.

Figure 4-4   Removing an element from an array

After removal, the value left in the last slot is no longer meaningful, so there is no need to change it explicitly.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array.py
def remove(nums: list[int], index: int):
    """Remove the element at the specified index"""
    # Shift all elements after index one position to the left
    for i in range(index, len(nums) - 1):
        nums[i] = nums[i + 1]
array.cpp
/* Remove the element at the specified index */
void remove(int *nums, int size, int index) {
    // Shift all elements after index one position to the left
    for (int i = index; i < size - 1; i++) {
        nums[i] = nums[i + 1];
    }
}
array.java
/* Remove the element at the specified index */
void remove(int[] nums, int index) {
    // Shift all elements after index one position to the left
    for (int i = index; i < nums.length - 1; i++) {
        nums[i] = nums[i + 1];
    }
}
array.cs
/* Remove the element at the specified index */
void Remove(int[] nums, int index) {

        nums[i] = nums[i + 1];
    }
}

}

    }
}

### Remove the element at the specified index ###
def remove(nums, index)
  # Shift all elements after index one position to the left
  for i in index...(nums.length - 1)
    nums[i] = nums[i + 1]
  end
end
Visualize execution

View full screen >

Insertion and removal in an array have the following drawbacks.

  • High time complexity. Insertion and removal both take \(O(n)\) time on average, where \(n\) is the array length.
  • Loss of elements. Because an array's length is fixed, insertion loses any element shifted beyond its bounds.
  • Wasted memory. We can allocate a longer array and use only its first few slots. Then any trailing values lost during insertion are insignificant, but the unused slots waste memory.

items.text:
Most programming languages let us traverse an array by index or iterate directly over its elements:

    # Iterate directly over the array elements
    for num in nums:
        count += num
    # Iterate over indices and elements together
    for i, num in enumerate(nums):
        count += nums[i]
        count += num

items.title: 7.   Growing an array
items.text:
In a complex system, a program can rarely guarantee that the memory immediately after an array is available, so it cannot safely extend the array in place. In most programming languages, an array has a fixed length.

To grow an array, create a larger one and copy the original elements into it in order. This takes \(O(n)\) time and can be slow for very large arrays. Here is the code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array.py
def extend(nums: list[int], enlarge: int) -> list[int]:
    """Extend the array"""
    # Initialize an array with the new length
    res = [0] * (len(nums) + enlarge)
    # Copy all elements from the original array into the new array
    for i in range(len(nums)):
        res[i] = nums[i]
    # Return the new, longer array
    return res
array.cpp
/* Extend the array */
int *extend(int *nums, int size, int enlarge) {
    // Initialize an array with the new length
    int *res = new int[size + enlarge]{};
    // Copy all elements from the original array into the new array
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        res[i] = nums[i];
    }
    // Free memory
    delete[] nums;
    // Return the new, longer array
    return res;
}

/* Extend the array */

    // Copy all elements from the original array into the new array

        res[i] = nums[i];
    }
    // Return the new, longer array
    return res;
}

}

items.title: 4.1.2   Advantages and limitations of arrays
items.text:
An array's elements occupy contiguous memory and have the same type. Knowing these properties in advance lets the system optimize operations on the data.

  • Space efficiency. An array allocates a contiguous block of memory for its data, without extra structural overhead.
  • Random access. An array provides access to any element in \(O(1)\) time.
  • Cache locality. When the computer accesses an array element, it also caches nearby data. Later operations on those elements can run faster by using the cache.

Contiguous storage also has limitations.

  • Costly insertion and removal. When an array holds many elements, inserting or removing one can require shifting many others.
  • Fixed length. An array's length is fixed at initialization. Growing it requires copying all its data into a new array, which is expensive.
  • Wasted space. If an array is larger than needed, the extra space goes unused.

items.title: 4.1.3   Common uses of arrays
items.text:
Arrays are a fundamental, widely used data structure. Many algorithms operate on them, and many more complex data structures are built from them.

  • Random access. To draw random samples, store the data in an array and generate a sequence of random indices to select the samples.
  • Sorting and searching. Arrays are the most common data structure for sorting and searching. Quicksort, merge sort, and binary search, for example, operate primarily on arrays.
  • Lookup tables. An array can serve as a lookup table when we need to find an element or its associated value quickly. For example, to map characters to ASCII codes, use the character's ASCII value as the index and store the associated element at that position.
  • Machine learning. Neural networks rely heavily on linear algebra operations involving vectors, matrices, and tensors, all of which are represented as arrays. Arrays are the most widely used data structure in neural network programming.
  • Implementing data structures. Arrays can implement stacks, queues, hash tables, heaps, graphs, and more. For example, the adjacency matrix of a graph is a two-dimensional array.

items.title: 1.   How do arrays and linked lists locate elements?
items.text:
An array and a singly linked list each store [A, B, C, D, E] in that order. You want to read the fourth element, D.

  1. Which index can you use to read the element directly from the array?
  2. Starting at the head node A, which nodes do you visit in order as you follow next in the singly linked list?
  3. How does the number of steps change in each structure as the desired position moves farther from the start? Which structure is better suited to repeated reads by position, and why?
Sample answer

  1. With indexing from 0, the fourth element has index 3, so you can read arr[3] directly.

  2. In the singly linked list, you must start at the head. The path is A → B → C → D, which requires following next three times.

  3. An array can locate an element directly from the base address and index, so access by position takes \(O(1)\) time. To reach the \(k\)-th node in a singly linked list, start at the head and follow next a total of \(k-1\) times. In the worst case this takes \(O(n)\) time.

    This comparison applies only to reading by position. A linked list need not be slower for every operation.

items.title: 2.   How do arrays and linked lists insert elements?
items.text:
An array and a singly linked list each contain A, B, C, D. You want to insert X after B.

  • The array has capacity 5 and currently contains [A, B, C, D, _].
  • The linked list is A → B → C → D, and you already have a reference to node B.
  1. Which array elements must move? Write out the array after insertion.
  2. In what order should you update X.next and B.next? Write out the linked list after insertion.
  3. Why does it matter for the efficiency comparison that you already have a reference to node B?
Sample answer

  1. First move D one place to the right, then move C one place to the right, and finally put X at index 2. The resulting array is [A, B, X, C, D].

  2. Initially, B.next points to C. First set X.next = B.next so that X points to C. Then set B.next = X. The result is A → B → X → C → D. If you overwrite B.next first without saving the original link, you may lose track of C.

  3. Once you have located B, insertion in the linked list changes just two links and takes \(O(1)\) time. If you have to find B by searching from the head, the search itself can take \(O(n)\) time.

items.title: 3.   How does list capacity grow?
items.text:
An array-backed list contains [A, B, C], with size = 3 and capacity = 4. When there is no room for another element, the new array has twice the capacity of the old one.

  1. After you append D, what are the length and capacity of the list? Does the capacity need to grow?
  2. When you then append E, what is the new capacity? How many existing elements must you copy?
  3. The underlying array has a fixed length. Why, then, does the capacity of the list appear to grow?
Sample answer

  1. D fits in the last available slot. The list now contains [A, B, C, D], with size = 4 and capacity = 4. No increase in capacity is needed.

  2. When you append E next, there are no slots left. Create a new array with capacity 8, copy all four existing elements (A, B, C, D) into it, and then append E. The list now has size = 5 and capacity = 8.

  3. The original array keeps its length. The list creates a larger array, copies the existing elements into it, and uses it as the new underlying storage. From the user's perspective, the capacity has grown.

items.title: 1.   Add one to a large integer represented by an array
items.text:
The array digits stores the digits of a nonnegative integer from left to right. For example, [3, 0, 8] represents 308. Zero is represented by [0]. Every other input starts with a nonzero digit.

Add 1 to the integer as you would by hand in base ten. Return the result in the same array format. You may modify digits directly. If there is a carry past the first digit, you may return a longer array.

Hints
  1. Start at the last digit, just as you would when adding by hand.
  2. If the current digit is less than 9, increment it and return immediately.
  3. If the current digit is 9, change it to 0. If every digit is 9, insert a 1 at the front.

items.title: 4.2   Linked lists
items.text:
Programs share memory, and in a complex system, free space may be scattered throughout it. An array needs contiguous storage, and a sufficiently large contiguous block may be unavailable for a very large array. This is where the flexibility of a linked list pays off.

A linked list is a linear data structure in which each element is a node object. References connect the nodes. A reference records the address of the next node, letting us reach it from the current one.

With this design, nodes can be scattered throughout memory. Their addresses do not need to be contiguous.

Figure 4-5   A linked list and its memory layout

As the figure shows, a linked list is made up of node objects. Each node contains two pieces of data: its value and a reference to the next node.

  • The first node is called the head, and the last node is called the tail.
  • The tail points to nothing, represented by null in Java, nullptr in C++, and None in Python.
  • In languages that support pointers, such as C, C++, Go, and Rust, the links described above as references can be expressed as pointers.

As the following code shows, a ListNode node stores an extra reference (pointer) alongside its value. For the same amount of data, a linked list therefore occupies more memory than an array.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby 
class ListNode:
    """Linked list node class"""

    def __init__(self, val: int):
        self.val: int = val  # Node value
        self.next: ListNode | None = None  # Reference to the next node

/* Linked list node */
struct ListNode {
    int val;        // Node value
    ListNode *next; // Pointer to the next node
    ListNode(int x) : val(x), next(nullptr) {
    }
};

    public int val;       // Node value
    public ListNode next; // Reference to the next node

    public ListNode(int x) {

}

    public int val = x;    // Node value
    public ListNode? next; // Reference to the next node
}

    Next *ListNode // Pointer to the next node
}

    return &ListNode{
        Val:  v,
        Next: nil,
    }
}

items.title: 1.   Initializing a linked list
items.text:
Building a linked list takes two steps. First initialize the individual nodes, then set up the references between them. Once the list is initialized, we can visit every node in order by starting at the head and following the next references.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linked_list.py
# Initialize the linked list 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 5 -> 4
# Initialize the nodes
n0 = ListNode(1)
n1 = ListNode(3)
n2 = ListNode(2)

A single variable represents an entire array. For example, the array nums contains elements such as nums[0] and nums[1]. A linked list, however, consists of independent node objects. We usually refer to the whole list by its head node. For example, we can call the list in the preceding code the list n0.

items.title: 2.   Inserting a node
items.text:
Inserting a node into a linked list is straightforward. To insert a new node P between adjacent nodes n0 and n1 as shown below, change just two node references (pointers). This takes \(O(1)\) time.

In comparison, inserting an element into an array takes \(O(n)\) time and is less efficient for large amounts of data.

Figure 4-6   Inserting a node into a linked list

def insert(n0: ListNode, P: ListNode):
    """Insert node P after node n0 in the linked list"""
    n1 = n0.next
    P.next = n1
    n0.next = P

items.title: 3.   Removing a node
items.text:
Removing a node is straightforward as well. As the figure shows, only one node reference (pointer) needs to change.

After removal, node P still points to n1. However, traversing the list can no longer reach P, so P no longer belongs to the list.

Figure 4-7   Removing a node from a linked list

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linked_list.py

    """Remove the node immediately after n0 in the linked list"""
    if not n0.next:
        return
    # n0 -> P -> n1
    P = n0.next
    n1 = P.next
    n0.next = n1

}

items.title: 4.   Accessing a node
items.text:
Accessing a node by position in a linked list is relatively slow. As we saw in the previous section, any array element can be accessed in \(O(1)\) time. In a linked list, the program must start at the head and visit nodes one by one until it reaches the desired node. Reaching the \(i\)-th node thus takes \(i - 1\) iterations, for a time complexity of \(O(n)\).

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linked_list.py
def access(head: ListNode, index: int) -> ListNode | None:
    """Access the linked list node at the specified index"""
    for _ in range(index):
        if not head:
            return None
        head = head.next
    return head

Traverse the list to find a node whose value is target and report its index. This is another linear search. Here is the code:

        head = head.next
        index += 1
    return -1

items.title: 4.2.2   Arrays vs. linked lists
items.text:
The table below compares the properties of arrays and linked lists and the efficiency of their operations. Their contrasting storage strategies lead to different strengths and weaknesses.

Table   Comparing the efficiency of arrays and linked lists Arrays Linked lists Storage layout Contiguous memory Noncontiguous memory Capacity growth Fixed length Can grow as needed Memory efficiency Less memory per element, but unused slots can waste space More memory per element Accessing an element \(O(1)\) \(O(n)\) Adding an element \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Removing an element \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\)

items.title: 4.2.3   Common types of linked lists
items.text:
Figure 4-8 shows three common types of linked lists.

  • Singly linked list. This is the list introduced above. Each node contains a value and a reference to the next node. The first node is the head, and the last node is the tail. The tail points to None.
  • Circular linked list. Point the tail of a singly linked list back to its head to form a circular linked list. Any node in the circle can serve as the head.
  • Doubly linked list. Unlike a singly linked list, a doubly linked list records references in both directions. Each node holds a reference (pointer) to its successor (the next node) and to its predecessor (the previous node). This allows more flexible traversal in either direction, at the cost of additional memory.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby 
class ListNode:
    """Doubly linked list node"""

    def __init__(self, val: int):
        """Constructor"""
        self.val: int = val  # Node value
        self.next: ListNode | None = None  # Reference to the next node
        self.prev: ListNode | None = None  # Reference to the previous node

/* Doubly linked list node */
struct DoublyListNode {
    int val;              // Node value
    DoublyListNode *next; // Pointer to the next node
    DoublyListNode *prev; // Pointer to the previous node
    DoublyListNode(int val) : val(val), prev(nullptr), next(nullptr) {
    }
};

/* Doubly linked list node */
class ListNode {
    int val;       // Node value
    ListNode next; // Reference to the next node
    ListNode prev; // Reference to the previous node

    ListNode(int val) {
        this.val = val;
        prev = next = null;
    }
}

/* Doubly linked list node */
public class ListNode(int val) {
    public int val = val;         // Node value
    public ListNode? next = null; // Reference to the next node
    public ListNode? prev = null; // Reference to the previous node
}

/* Doubly linked list node structure */
type DoublyListNode struct {
    Val  int             // Node value
    Next *DoublyListNode // Pointer to the next node
    Prev *DoublyListNode // Pointer to the previous node
}

// NewDoublyListNode initializes a node
func NewDoublyListNode(val int) *DoublyListNode {
    return &DoublyListNode{
        Val:  val,
        Next: nil,
        Prev: nil,
    }

items.title: 4.2.4   Common uses of linked lists
items.text:
Singly linked lists are often used to implement stacks, queues, hash tables, and graphs.

  • Stacks and queues. Inserting and removing at the same end of a linked list gives last-in, first-out behavior, as in a stack. Inserting at one end and removing at the other gives first-in, first-out behavior, as in a queue.
  • Hash tables. Separate chaining is a common way to resolve hash collisions. It stores all elements that collide in the same linked list.
  • Graphs. An adjacency list is a common representation of a graph. Each vertex has an associated list whose elements represent the other vertices connected to it.

Doubly linked lists are useful when we need quick access to both the previous and the next element.

  • Advanced data structures. In red-black trees and B-trees, for example, we need to access a node's parent. A node can store a reference back to its parent, much like a backward link in a doubly linked list.
  • Browser history. When a user clicks Forward or Back, the browser needs to know which page comes next or came before in the browsing history. A doubly linked list makes these operations straightforward.
  • LRU cache eviction. A least recently used (LRU) eviction algorithm needs to locate the least recently used data quickly and to add and remove nodes efficiently. A doubly linked list is well suited to these operations.

Circular linked lists are useful when operations repeat in cycles, as in operating system resource scheduling.

  • Round-robin scheduling. In this common CPU scheduling algorithm, the operating system cycles through a set of processes. Each process gets a time slice. When it expires, the CPU switches to the next process. A circular linked list can implement this rotation.
  • Data buffers. Some buffers use circular linked lists. For instance, an audio or video player might divide its data stream into buffer blocks and place them in a circular linked list for seamless playback.

items.title: 4.3   Lists
items.text:
A list is an abstract data structure representing an ordered collection of elements. It supports access, updates, insertion, removal, and traversal without requiring the user to manage capacity limits. A list can be implemented with a linked list or an array.

  • A linked list naturally serves as a list: we can insert, remove, find, and update elements, and it can grow dynamically as needed.
  • An array also supports insertion, removal, lookup, and updates. Its fixed length, however, makes it a list with a length limit.

When a list is backed by an array, the array's fixed length makes the list less practical. We usually do not know in advance how much data we will store, so choosing a suitable length is difficult. Too short, and the list may not meet our needs. Too long, and it wastes memory.

We can solve this problem by implementing the list with a dynamic array. It preserves the advantages of an array and can grow while the program is running.

In fact, many programming languages provide lists backed by dynamic arrays in their standard libraries. Examples include Python's list, Java's ArrayList, C++'s vector, and C#'s List. In the discussion that follows, we use “list” and “dynamic array” interchangeably.

items.title: 4.3.2   Implementing a list
items.text:
Many languages, including Java, C++, and Python, provide lists. Their implementations are complex and their parameters, such as initial capacity and growth factor, are carefully chosen. You can explore these choices in the source code.

To see how a list works, let's implement a simple one. The design has three main parts.

  • Initial capacity. Choose a reasonable initial capacity for the array. In this example, we use 10.
  • Element count. Declare a variable size to track the current number of elements and update it whenever an element is inserted or removed. It tells us where the list ends and whether the array needs to grow.
  • Capacity growth. If the list is full when we insert an element, it needs more space. Create a larger array using the growth factor and move all current elements into it in order. In this example, we double the capacity each time.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby my_list.py
class MyList:
    """List class"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self._capacity: int = 10  # List capacity
        self._arr: list[int] = [0] * self._capacity  # Array that stores the list elements
        self._size: int = 0  # List length (current number of elements)
        self._extend_ratio: int = 2  # Factor by which the list capacity grows

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the list length (current number of elements)"""
        return self._size

    def capacity(self) -> int:
        """Get the list capacity"""
        return self._capacity

    def get(self, index: int) -> int:
        """Access an element"""
        # Throw an exception if the index is out of bounds, here and below
        if index < 0 or index >= self._size:
            raise IndexError("Index out of bounds")
        return self._arr[index]

    def set(self, num: int, index: int):
        """Update an element"""
        if index < 0 or index >= self._size:
            raise IndexError("Index out of bounds")
        self._arr[index] = num

    def add(self, num: int):
        """Append an element"""
        # Increase capacity when the elements would no longer fit
        if self.size() == self.capacity():
            self.extend_capacity()
        self._arr[self._size] = num
        self._size += 1

    def insert(self, num: int, index: int):
        """Insert an element in the middle"""
        if index < 0 or index >= self._size:
            raise IndexError("Index out of bounds")
        # Increase capacity when the elements would no longer fit
        if self._size == self.capacity():
            self.extend_capacity()
        # Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
        for j in range(self._size - 1, index - 1, -1):
            self._arr[j + 1] = self._arr[j]
        self._arr[index] = num
        # Update the element count
        self._size += 1

    def remove(self, index: int) -> int:
        """Remove an element"""
        if index < 0 or index >= self._size:
            raise IndexError("Index out of bounds")
        num = self._arr[index]
        # Shift the elements after index one position to the left
        for j in range(index, self._size - 1):
            self._arr[j] = self._arr[j + 1]
        # Update the element count
        self._size -= 1
        # Return the removed element
        return num

    def extend_capacity(self):
        """Increase the list capacity"""
        # Create an array _extend_ratio times as long and copy the original array into it
        self._arr = self._arr + [0] * self.capacity() * (self._extend_ratio - 1)

        self.size -= 1;
        // Return the removed element
        return num;
    }

    /* Increase the list capacity */
    pub fn extend_capacity(&mut self) {
        // Create an array extend_ratio times as long and copy the original array into it
        let new_capacity = self.capacity * self.extend_ratio;
        self.arr.resize(new_capacity, 0);
        // Update the list capacity
        self.capacity = new_capacity;
    }

    /* Convert the list to an array */
    pub fn to_array(&self) -> Vec<i32> {
        // Convert only the elements within the current list length
        let mut arr = Vec::new();
        for i in 0..self.size {
            arr.push(self.get(i));
        }
        arr
    }
}

/* List class */
typedef struct {
    int *arr;        // Array that stores the list elements
    int capacity;    // List capacity
    int size;        // List size
    int extendRatio; // Factor by which the list capacity grows
} MyList;

/* Constructor */
MyList *newMyList() {
    MyList *nums = malloc(sizeof(MyList));
    nums->capacity = 10;
    nums->arr = malloc(sizeof(int) * nums->capacity);
    nums->size = 0;
    nums->extendRatio = 2;
    return nums;
}

/* Destructor */
void delMyList(MyList *nums) {
    free(nums->arr);
    free(nums);
}

/* Get the list length */
int size(MyList *nums) {
    return nums->size;
}

/* Get the list capacity */
int capacity(MyList *nums) {
    return nums->capacity;
}

/* Access an element */
int get(MyList *nums, int index) {
    assert(index >= 0 && index < nums->size);
    return nums->arr[index];
}

/* Update an element */
void set(MyList *nums, int index, int num) {
    assert(index >= 0 && index < nums->size);
    nums->arr[index] = num;
}

/* Append an element */
void add(MyList *nums, int num) {
    if (size(nums) == capacity(nums)) {
        extendCapacity(nums); // Increase capacity
    }
    nums->arr[size(nums)] = num;
    nums->size++;
}

/* Insert an element in the middle */
void insert(MyList *nums, int index, int num) {
    assert(index >= 0 && index < size(nums));
    // Increase capacity when the elements would no longer fit
    if (size(nums) == capacity(nums)) {
        extendCapacity(nums); // Increase capacity
    }
    for (int i = size(nums); i > index; --i) {
        nums->arr[i] = nums->arr[i - 1];
    }
    nums->arr[index] = num;
    nums->size++;
}

/* Remove an element */
// Note: stdio.h already uses the name remove
int removeItem(MyList *nums, int index) {
    assert(index >= 0 && index < size(nums));
    int num = nums->arr[index];
    for (int i = index; i < size(nums) - 1; i++) {
        nums->arr[i] = nums->arr[i + 1];
    }
    nums->size--;
    return num;
}

/* Increase the list capacity */
void extendCapacity(MyList *nums) {
    // Allocate space first
    int newCapacity = capacity(nums) * nums->extendRatio;
    int *extend = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int) * newCapacity);
    int *temp = nums->arr;

    // Copy the old data into the new space
    for (int i = 0; i < size(nums); i++)
        extend[i] = nums->arr[i];

    // Free the old storage
    free(temp);

    // Use the new storage
    nums->arr = extend;
    nums->capacity = newCapacity;
}

/* Convert the list to an array for printing */
int *toArray(MyList *nums) {
    return nums->arr;
}

/* List class */
class MyList {
    private var arr: IntArray = intArrayOf() // Array that stores the list elements
    private var capacity: Int = 10 // List capacity
    private var size: Int = 0 // List length (current number of elements)
    private var extendRatio: Int = 2 // Factor by which the list capacity grows

    /* Constructor */
    init {
        arr = IntArray(capacity)
    }

    /* Get the list length (current number of elements) */
    fun size(): Int {
        return size
    }

    /* Get the list capacity */
    fun capacity(): Int {
        return capacity
    }

    /* Access an element */
    fun get(index: Int): Int {
        // Throw an exception if the index is out of bounds, here and below
        if (index < 0 || index >= size)
            throw IndexOutOfBoundsException("Index out of bounds")
        return arr[index]
    }

    /* Update an element */
    fun set(index: Int, num: Int) {
        if (index < 0 || index >= size)
            throw IndexOutOfBoundsException("Index out of bounds")
        arr[index] = num
    }

    /* Append an element */
    fun add(num: Int) {
        // Increase capacity when the elements would no longer fit
        if (size == capacity())
            extendCapacity()
        arr[size] = num
        // Update the element count
        size++
    }

    /* Insert an element in the middle */
    fun insert(index: Int, num: Int) {
        if (index < 0 || index >= size)
            throw IndexOutOfBoundsException("Index out of bounds")
        // Increase capacity when the elements would no longer fit
        if (size == capacity())
            extendCapacity()
        // Shift the elements from index onward one position to the right
        for (j in size - 1 downTo index)
            arr[j + 1] = arr[j]
        arr[index] = num
        // Update the element count
        size++
    }

    /* Remove an element */
    fun remove(index: Int): Int {
        if (index < 0 || index >= size)
            throw IndexOutOfBoundsException("Index out of bounds")
        val num = arr[index]
        // Shift the elements after index one position to the left
        for (j in index..<size - 1)
            arr[j] = arr[j + 1]
        // Update the element count
        size--
        // Return the removed element
        return num
    }

    /* Increase the list capacity */
    fun extendCapacity() {
        // Create an array extendRatio times as long and copy the original array into it
        arr = arr.copyOf(capacity() * extendRatio)
        // Update the list capacity
        capacity = arr.size
    }

    /* Convert the list to an array */
    fun toArray(): IntArray {
        val size = size()
        // Convert only the elements within the current list length
        val arr = IntArray(size)
        for (i in 0..<size) {
            arr[i] = get(i)
        }
        return arr
    }
}

items.title: 4.4   Memory and cache *
items.text:
In the first two sections of this chapter, we explored two fundamental data structures, arrays and linked lists. They illustrate two physical layouts: contiguous and noncontiguous storage.

In fact, the physical layout largely determines how efficiently a program uses memory and cache, which in turn affects the overall performance of an algorithm's implementation.

items.title: 4.4.1   Computer memory and storage devices
items.text:
A computer has three types of storage: disk, main memory (random-access memory, RAM), and cache memory. The table compares their roles and performance characteristics.

Table   Computer memory and storage devices Disk Main memory Cache Purpose Long-term storage for data, including the operating system, programs, and files Temporary storage for running programs and the data being processed Stores frequently accessed data and instructions to reduce CPU accesses to main memory Volatility Retains data when power is lost Loses data when power is lost Loses data when power is lost Capacity Large, on the order of terabytes Smaller, on the order of gigabytes Very small, on the order of megabytes Speed Slower, hundreds to thousands of MB/s Faster, tens of GB/s Very fast, tens to hundreds of GB/s Price (Chinese yuan) Relatively inexpensive, a fraction of a yuan to a few yuan per GB More expensive, tens to hundreds of yuan per GB Very expensive, priced as part of the CPU

Picture the computer's memory and storage system as the pyramid below. The closer a device is to the top, the faster, smaller, and more expensive it is. Computer scientists and engineers designed this hierarchy deliberately.

  • Main memory is unlikely to replace disks. First, main memory loses its data when power is lost, making it unsuitable for long-term storage. Second, it costs tens of times as much as disk storage, which makes it difficult to adopt widely as a replacement in the consumer market.
  • Large capacity and high speed are difficult to achieve in the same cache. From L1 to L2 to L3, caches increase in capacity and physical size and sit farther from the CPU core. Data takes longer to travel, increasing access latency. With current technology, a hierarchy of caches offers the best balance of capacity, speed, and cost.

Figure 4-9   Computer memory and storage hierarchy

Tip

The computer memory hierarchy strikes a careful balance among speed, capacity, and cost. Designers face similar trade-offs across industries, where they must weigh competing advantages and limitations.

In short, disks store large amounts of data for the long term, main memory temporarily holds data that running programs are processing, and cache holds frequently accessed data and instructions to speed up execution. The three work together to keep the system running efficiently.

As the figure shows, when a program runs, data is read from disk into main memory for the CPU to process. The cache can be viewed as part of the CPU. By selectively loading data from main memory, it gives the CPU fast access to that data, significantly improving program performance and reducing reliance on slower main memory.

Figure 4-10   Data flow between disk, main memory, and cache

items.title: 4.4.2   Memory efficiency of data structures
items.text:
Arrays and linked lists each have advantages and limitations in how they use memory.

First, memory is limited, and a block allocated for one program's private use is unavailable to others, so we want our data structures to use space efficiently. Array elements are packed together without the extra references (pointers) that link list nodes, making arrays more space-efficient. However, an array needs a sufficiently large contiguous block all at once. Some of it may go unused, and growing the array costs extra time and space. A linked list offers more flexibility by allocating and reclaiming memory one node at a time.

Second, repeatedly allocating and freeing memory as a program runs leaves free memory increasingly fragmented, reducing how efficiently it can be used. Arrays occupy contiguous storage and are relatively unlikely to cause fragmentation. Linked list elements are scattered, making fragmentation more likely when insertions and removals are frequent.

items.title: 4.4.3   Cache efficiency of data structures
items.text:
A cache holds far less data than main memory but is much faster, so it plays a crucial role in execution speed. Its limited capacity holds only a small portion of frequently used data. When the CPU requests data that is absent from the cache, a cache miss occurs, and the CPU must load it from slower main memory.

Fewer cache misses mean more efficient CPU reads and writes and better program performance. The fraction of accesses for which the CPU successfully obtains the data from cache is the cache hit rate, a common measure of cache efficiency.

To work as efficiently as possible, caches use the following mechanisms when loading data.

  • Cache lines. A cache stores and loads data a line at a time. Transferring a whole cache line is more efficient than transferring individual bytes.
  • Prefetching. The processor tries to predict access patterns, such as sequential access or jumps at a fixed stride. It loads data into the cache based on these patterns to increase the hit rate.
  • Spatial locality. When a program accesses an item, it may soon access nearby data. Loading the neighboring data along with the requested item improves the hit rate.
  • Temporal locality. A program that accesses an item is likely to access it again soon. The cache takes advantage of this by retaining recently accessed data to improve the hit rate.

Arrays and linked lists use the cache with different degrees of efficiency for several reasons.

  • Space requirements. Linked list elements occupy more space than array elements, leaving room for less useful data in the cache.
  • Cache lines. Linked list nodes are scattered throughout memory. Because the cache loads whole lines, a higher proportion of the data it loads goes unused.
  • Prefetching. An array's access pattern is more predictable than a linked list's, so the system can more easily anticipate which data it will need next.
  • Spatial locality. An array occupies a contiguous block of memory, making it more likely that data near a loaded element will be accessed soon.

Overall, arrays have higher cache hit rates, so operations on them are usually more efficient than operations on linked lists. This helps explain why array-backed data structures are often preferred for algorithm problems.

Still, high cache efficiency does not make arrays better than linked lists in every situation. The choice depends on the requirements. For example, both can implement a stack (covered in the next chapter), but the two implementations suit different situations.

  • For algorithm problems, we tend to choose an array-backed stack because it offers efficient operations and random access. The trade-off is that some memory must be allocated for the array in advance.
  • A linked-list stack is a better fit when the data volume is very large, changes greatly, and the expected stack size is hard to estimate. The nodes can occupy different parts of memory, avoiding the extra overhead of growing an array.

items.title: 1.   Chapter review
items.text:
• Arrays and linked lists are two fundamental data structures. They represent two ways to store data in memory, contiguous and noncontiguous storage, and their strengths complement each other.
  • Arrays support random access and use relatively little memory, but insertion and removal are inefficient, and the length is fixed after initialization.
  • A linked list supports efficient insertion and removal by changing references (pointers), and its length is flexible. However, accessing nodes by position is inefficient, and nodes use more memory. Common types include singly linked, circular, and doubly linked lists.
  • A list is an ordered collection that supports insertion, removal, lookup, and updates. It is usually backed by a dynamic array, preserving the advantages of an array while allowing its length to change.
  • Lists make arrays much more practical but can leave some memory unused.
  • While a program is running, its data is stored mainly in main memory. Arrays can use memory more efficiently, while linked lists offer greater flexibility in how memory is allocated.
  • Cache lines, prefetching, and the use of spatial and temporal locality give the CPU fast access to data and significantly improve execution speed.
  • Arrays generally have higher cache hit rates and are therefore usually more efficient than linked lists. Choose the structure that fits the particular requirements and situation.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: Does storing an array on the stack or on the heap affect its time or space efficiency?

Arrays occupy contiguous memory on both the stack and the heap, so operations on their data have essentially the same efficiency. The stack and heap differ in other respects, however.

  1. Allocation and deallocation: The stack is a relatively small region of memory where the compiler manages allocation automatically. The heap is larger, supports dynamic allocation in code, and is more prone to fragmentation. Allocating and freeing heap memory are therefore usually slower than the corresponding stack operations.
  2. Size limits: Stack space is relatively small, while heap size is generally limited by available memory. The heap is therefore better suited to large arrays.
  3. Flexibility: The size of a stack array must be determined at compile time, while a heap array's size can be determined dynamically at runtime.

Q: Why do we say array elements must have the same type without imposing the same requirement on linked lists?

A linked list consists of nodes connected by references (pointers). Individual nodes can store different types of data, such as int, double, string, or object.

Array elements, on the other hand, must have the same type so we can locate an element by calculating its offset. Suppose an array contained both int and long elements, occupying 4 and 8 bytes, respectively. With two different element sizes, the following formula would no longer give the correct offset.

# Element address = array address (address of the first element) + element size * element index

Q: After removing node P, do we need to set P.next to None?

You can leave P.next as it is. Traversing the list from head to tail will no longer encounter P. Node P has therefore been removed, and where P points no longer affects this list.

For an algorithm exercise, leaving the link intact is fine as long as the program's logic is correct. In a standard library, severing it is safer and makes the intent clearer. If a removed node is not reclaimed properly, its outgoing link can interfere with reclaiming its successor.

Q: Inserting or removing a node in a linked list takes \(O(1)\) time. If finding the element first takes \(O(n)\) time, why isn't the complexity \(O(n)\)?

If you first search for an element and then remove it, the time is indeed \(O(n)\). The advantage of \(O(1)\) insertion and removal shows up in other uses. A linked list is a good fit for a deque, for example: keep pointers to the head and tail, and each insertion or removal takes \(O(1)\) time.

Q: In “A linked list and its memory layout,” does the light blue cell for the node pointer take up one memory location, or do the pointer and value each occupy half of the node?

The diagram is qualitative. The actual sizes depend on the circumstances.

  • Node values occupy different amounts of space depending on their type, such as int, long, double, or a class instance.
  • The space occupied by a pointer depends on the operating system and compilation environment. It is typically 8 or 4 bytes.

Q: Does appending an element to a list always take \(O(1)\) time?

If the new element will not fit, the list must grow before the element can be added. The system allocates a new block of memory and moves all existing elements into it. In this case the operation takes \(O(n)\) time.

Q: When we say “Lists make arrays much more practical but can leave some memory unused,” does the wasted space refer to variables added for capacity, length, and growth factor?

The unused space comes mainly from two sources. First, a list has an initial allocation that we may not need in full. Second, to avoid frequent resizing, the capacity usually grows by a factor such as \(\times 1.5\). This can leave many empty slots that we typically do not fill.

Q: After I initialize n = [1, 2, 3] in Python, the three elements appear to have consecutive addresses. But after I initialize m = [2, 1, 3], their IDs are no longer consecutive and instead match the corresponding IDs in n. If the elements have nonconsecutive addresses, is m still an array?

Consider a list of linked list nodes, n = [n1, n2, n3, n4, n5]. The five node objects will usually be scattered throughout memory. Yet given a list index, we can still retrieve the address of the corresponding node in \(O(1)\) time and access it. The array stores references to the nodes rather than the nodes themselves.

Unlike many languages, Python represents numbers as objects too. A list stores references to those objects rather than the numbers themselves. This explains why the same numbers in these two arrays have the same IDs and why the number objects need not occupy consecutive addresses.

Q: The C++ STL provides a doubly linked list, std::list. Why do some algorithm books rarely use it directly? Does it have limitations?

For one thing, we usually prefer to implement algorithms with arrays and use linked lists only when needed, for two main reasons.

  • Space overhead: Each element needs two extra pointers, one to the previous element and one to the next, so std::list usually takes up more space than std::vector.
  • Poor cache locality: Because the data is not contiguous, std::list makes less efficient use of the cache. In general, std::vector performs better.

For another, the main uses that call for linked nodes are binary trees and graphs. For stacks and queues, programmers often use the language's stack and queue types instead of a linked list.

Q: When res = [[0]] * n creates a two-dimensional list, is each [0] independent?

No. Every [0] in this two-dimensional list refers to the same object. If you change one element, you will see all the corresponding elements change along with it.

To give each [0] its own object, use res = [[0] for _ in range(n)]. This initializes \(n\) independent [0] list objects.

Q: When res = [0] * n creates a list, is each integer 0 independent?

All the zeros in this list refer to the same object. Python caches small integers (typically −5 through 256) so that objects can be reused as much as possible, improving performance.

Although the elements refer to the same object, we can still update each list entry independently because Python integers are immutable. Assigning a new value to an entry redirects its reference to another object and leaves the original object unchanged.

When the elements refer to a mutable object, such as a list, dictionary, or class instance, modifying the object through one entry changes the object itself. Every entry referring to it then reflects the same change.

items.title: Chapter 13.   Backtracking
items.text:
Abstract

Like explorers in a maze, we may meet obstacles along the way.

Backtracking lets us retrace our steps and try again until we find the way out into the light.

items.title: 13.1   Backtracking
items.text:
A backtracking algorithm solves a problem by exhaustive search. Starting from an initial state, it explores possible solutions and records each valid solution it finds. The search can stop when it finds the solution it needs or when it has tried every choice without success.

Backtracking usually explores the solution space using depth-first search. In the chapter on binary trees, we saw three forms of depth-first search: preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal. Let’s build a backtracking problem around preorder traversal to see how the algorithm works.

Example 1

Given a binary tree, find every node with value \(7\) and return the list of matching nodes.

Traverse the tree in preorder and check whether the current node’s value is \(7\). If it is, add the node’s value to the result list res. The figure and code below show the process:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby preorder_traversal_i_compact.py
def pre_order(root: TreeNode):
    """Preorder traversal: example 1"""
    if root is None:
        return
    if root.val == 7:
        # Record the solution
        res.append(root)
    pre_order(root.left)
    pre_order(root.right)

items.title: 13.1.1   Trying a choice and backtracking
items.text:
Backtracking gets its name from the way it tries choices and then retraces its steps as it explores the solution space. Whenever the search reaches a state from which it cannot proceed or produce a valid solution, it undoes the last choice, returns to the previous state, and tries another choice.

In example 1, each node visit is an attempt. A return after stepping past a leaf or when going back to a parent is a backtracking step.

However, backtracking can involve more than returning from a function. A small extension of example 1 illustrates this point.

Example 2

Find all nodes with value \(7\) in a binary tree and return the paths from the root to those nodes.

Extend the code from example 1 with a list path that tracks the nodes along the current path. When a node has value \(7\), copy path and append the copy to the result list res. Once traversal ends, res holds all solutions. Here is the code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby preorder_traversal_ii_compact.py
def pre_order(root: TreeNode):
    """Preorder traversal: example 2"""
    if root is None:
        return
    # Try a choice
    path.append(root)
    if root.val == 7:
        # Record the solution
        res.append(list(path))
    pre_order(root.left)
    pre_order(root.right)
    # Backtrack
    path.pop()

        res.push_back(path);
    }

    preOrder(root->right);
    // Backtrack
    path.pop_back();
}

fn pre_order(
    res: &mut Vec<Vec<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>>,
    path: &mut Vec<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
    root: Option<&Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,
) {
    if root.is_none() {
        return;
    }
    if let Some(node) = root {
        // Try a choice
        path.push(node.clone());
        if node.borrow().val == 7 {
            // Record the solution
            res.push(path.clone());
        }
        pre_order(res, path, node.borrow().left.as_ref());
        pre_order(res, path, node.borrow().right.as_ref());
        // Backtrack
        path.pop();
    }
}

When trying a choice, append the current node to path to record the path. Before returning, pop that node from path to restore the state from before the attempt.

In Figure 13-2, trying a choice is a step forward and backtracking undoes that step. The two operations are inverses.

items.title: 13.1.2   Pruning
items.text:
More complex backtracking problems typically have one or more constraints. These constraints often let us prune the search.

Example 3

Find all nodes with value \(7\) in a binary tree and return the paths from the root to those nodes, excluding any path that contains a node with value \(3\).

To enforce this constraint, add a pruning step. When the search encounters a node with value \(3\), return immediately and stop exploring that branch. Here is the code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby preorder_traversal_iii_compact.py
def pre_order(root: TreeNode):
    """Preorder traversal: example 3"""
    # Prune
    if root is None or root.val == 3:
        return
    # Try a choice
    path.append(root)
    if root.val == 7:
        # Record the solution
        res.append(list(path))
    pre_order(root.left)
    pre_order(root.right)
    # Backtrack
    path.pop()

items.title: 13.1.3   A backtracking framework
items.text:
We can make the code more widely applicable by extracting the steps that backtracking problems share: try a choice, undo it, and prune invalid branches.

In the framework below, state describes the current state of the problem, and choices contains the choices available in that state:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby 
def backtrack(state: State, choices: list[Choice], res: list[State]):
    """Backtracking framework"""
    # Check for a solution
    if is_solution(state):
        # Record the solution
        record_solution(state, res)
        # Stop searching
        return
    # Try each choice
    for choice in choices:
        # Prune: check whether the choice is valid
        if is_valid(state, choice):
            # Make a choice and update the state
            make_choice(state, choice)
            backtrack(state, choices, res)
            # Backtrack: undo the choice to restore the previous state
            undo_choice(state, choice)

/* Backtracking framework */
void backtrack(State *state, vector<Choice *> &choices, vector<State *> &res) {
    // Check for a solution
    if (isSolution(state)) {
        // Record the solution
        recordSolution(state, res);
        // Stop searching
        return;
    }
    // Try each choice
    for (Choice *choice : choices) {
        // Prune: check whether the choice is valid
        if (isValid(state, choice)) {
            // Make a choice and update the state
            makeChoice(state, choice);
            backtrack(state, choices, res);
            // Backtrack: undo the choice to restore the previous state
            undoChoice(state, choice);
        }
    }
}

        # Prune: check whether the choice is valid

            undo_choice(state, choice)

We can now use this framework to solve example 3. The state state is the current path of nodes, the choices choices are the current node’s left and right children, and the result res is a list of paths:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby preorder_traversal_iii_template.py
def is_solution(state: list[TreeNode]) -> bool:
    """Check whether the current state is a solution"""
    return state and state[-1].val == 7

def record_solution(state: list[TreeNode], res: list[list[TreeNode]]):
    """Record the solution"""
    res.append(list(state))

def is_valid(state: list[TreeNode], choice: TreeNode) -> bool:
    """Check whether this choice is valid in the current state"""
    return choice is not None and choice.val != 3

def make_choice(state: list[TreeNode], choice: TreeNode):
    """Update the state"""
    state.append(choice)

def undo_choice(state: list[TreeNode], choice: TreeNode):
    """Restore the state"""
    state.pop()

def backtrack(
    state: list[TreeNode], choices: list[TreeNode], res: list[list[TreeNode]]
):
    """Backtracking: example 3"""
    # Check for a solution
    if is_solution(state):
        # Record the solution
        record_solution(state, res)
    # Try each choice
    for choice in choices:
        # Prune: check whether the choice is valid
        if is_valid(state, choice):
            # Make a choice and update the state
            make_choice(state, choice)
            # Make the next choice
            backtrack(state, [choice.left, choice.right], res)
            # Backtrack: undo the choice to restore the previous state
            undo_choice(state, choice)

items.title: 13.1.4   Common terms
items.text:
The table summarizes common backtracking terms and illustrates each one using example 3. These terms will help us describe algorithms more precisely.

Table 13-1   Common backtracking terms

Term Definition Example 3 Solution An answer that satisfies the problem’s conditions. A problem may have one or more solutions. All paths from the root to a node with value \(7\) that satisfy the constraint Constraint A condition that limits which solutions are valid. Constraints often help prune the search. The path must contain no node with value \(3\) State The situation at a particular point in the search, including choices already made The current path of visited nodes, stored in the list path Attempt Exploring the solution space by making an available choice, updating the state, and checking for a solution Recursively visit the left or right child, add it to path, and check whether its value is \(7\) Backtracking Undoing a previous choice and returning to the preceding state when the current state violates a constraint Stop searching and return when the traversal passes a leaf, finishes visiting a node, or encounters a node with value \(3\) Pruning Using the problem’s properties and constraints to skip unproductive search paths and improve efficiency Stop exploring a branch upon reaching a node with value \(3\)

Tip

Concepts such as problems, solutions, and states also appear in divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms.

items.title: 13.1.5   Advantages and limitations
items.text:
Backtracking is essentially a depth-first search. It tries possible solutions until it finds one that meets the requirements. It can find every solution and can be highly efficient with well-chosen pruning rules.

For large or complex problems, however, backtracking may be prohibitively expensive.

  • Time: Backtracking often has to explore every possibility in the state space. Its time complexity can be exponential or even factorial.
  • Space: Recursive calls must preserve the current state, such as the path and auxiliary variables used for pruning. Deep recursion can require considerable space.

Even so, backtracking remains the best approach for some search and constraint satisfaction problems. When we cannot predict which choices will lead to a valid solution, we must explore every possibility. The question then becomes how to make the search more efficient. Two common approaches follow.

  • Pruning: Skip paths that cannot produce a solution to save time and space.
  • Heuristic search: Use a strategy or estimate to explore the most promising paths first.

items.title: 13.1.6   Typical backtracking problems
items.text:
Backtracking can solve many search, constraint satisfaction, and combinatorial optimization problems.

Search problems ask for solutions that meet specified conditions.

  • Permutations: Given a set, find every possible ordering of its elements.
  • Subset sum: Given a set and a target sum, find all subsets whose elements add up to the target.
  • Tower of Hanoi: Given three pegs and disks of different sizes, move all disks from one peg to another. Move only one disk at a time and never place a larger disk on a smaller one.

Constraint satisfaction problems ask for solutions that satisfy every constraint.

  • \(n\)-queens: On an \(n \times n\) board, place \(n\) queens so that no two attack each other.
  • Sudoku: Fill a \(9 \times 9\) grid with the digits \(1\) through \(9\) so that no digit repeats in any row, column, or \(3 \times 3\) box.
  • Graph coloring: Given an undirected graph, color its vertices using as few colors as possible while giving adjacent vertices different colors.

Combinatorial optimization problems ask for the best combination that satisfies specified conditions.

  • 0-1 knapsack: Given items with specified values and weights, choose the items of greatest total value that fit within a knapsack’s weight capacity.
  • Traveling salesperson: Find the shortest route in a graph that starts at one vertex, visits every other vertex exactly once, and returns to the start.
  • Maximum clique: Given an undirected graph, find its largest complete subgraph, one in which every pair of vertices is connected by an edge.

For many combinatorial optimization problems, other approaches are preferable to backtracking.

  • Dynamic programming usually solves the 0-1 knapsack problem more efficiently.
  • The traveling salesperson problem is a well-known NP-hard problem. Common approaches include genetic algorithms and ant colony optimization.
  • The maximum clique problem is a classic problem in graph theory. Heuristics such as greedy algorithms can be used to tackle it.

items.title: 1.   Will this permutation algorithm miss any results?
items.text:
A backtracking algorithm tries the numbers 1, 2, 3 in that order to generate all permutations. Each time it chooses a number x, it takes these steps:

  1. Append x to the current path.
  2. Mark x as used.
  3. Recursively fill the next position.

When the recursive call returns, a student removes x from the end of the path and goes straight on to try the next number.

  1. Which permutation does the algorithm produce first? Can it still produce all six?
  2. Before returning to the previous level, is it enough to remove the last number from the path? If not, what else must you do, and why?
Sample answer

  1. The first permutation is [1, 2, 3], but the algorithm misses the rest. Although the path gets shorter as the calls return, the numbers 1, 2, and 3 are all still marked as used, leaving no choices for later branches.

  2. No. After removing x from the end of the path, you must also mark x as unused. The path and the usage flags together describe the search state. A choice changes both, so backtracking must restore both to let other branches choose x again.

items.title: 2.   Does the order of the choices matter?
items.text:
Given the sorted array [2, 3, 5] and a target of 5, you may choose each number more than once. The algorithm requires the numbers on each search path to appear in nondecreasing order.

  1. Which distinct combinations can you obtain?
  2. Why is there no need to search for the same combination in different orders? What does the ordering constraint accomplish?
  3. Suppose the current path is [3], you still need 2, and the next candidate is 3. Why can you stop checking candidates at this level?
Sample answer

  1. The distinct combinations are [2, 3] and [5].

  2. The problem treats [2, 3] and [3, 2] as the same combination. The order of selection does not count. Keeping the path in nondecreasing order lets the search skip duplicates such as [3, 2].

  3. You still need 2, and the candidate 3 already exceeds 2. Because the array is sorted, every candidate after 3 is even larger. None can join the current combination, so you can stop checking at this level.

items.title: 3.   Where can the next queen go?
items.text:
Place queens one row at a time on a 4 × 4 board, with row and column indices starting at 0. Queens already occupy (0, 1) and (1, 3). The next queen goes in row 2.

  1. Which columns already contain a queen and can be ruled out?
  2. Of the remaining squares, which can you rule out because they share a diagonal with a queen?
  3. Which squares in row 2 can you still try?
Sample answer

  1. Columns 1 and 3 already contain queens, ruling out (2, 1) and (2, 3).

  2. Among the remaining squares, (2, 2) shares a diagonal with (1, 3), so you can rule it out as well. Square (2, 0) shares neither a column nor a diagonal with either queen.

  3. The only square you can try in row 2 is (2, 0).

    This placement is valid so far. If you cannot complete the board later, you must still backtrack and try a different earlier choice.

items.title: 1.   Permutations of distinct elements
items.text:
The integer array nums contains at least one element, and all its elements are distinct. Return every possible ordering as an array, using each element exactly once in each ordering. The permutations may appear in any order in the result. Use backtracking and a Boolean array to track whether the element at each index is already in the current permutation.

Hints
  1. The recursion depth tells you which position to fill
  2. At each level, try only unused elements
  3. When the path is as long as nums, add a copy to the result

items.title: 13.4   The n-queens problem
items.text:
Question

In chess, a queen can attack a piece in the same row, column, or diagonal. Given \(n\) queens and an \(n \times n\) board, find the arrangements in which no two queens attack each other.

As the figure shows, there are two solutions when \(n = 4\). In a backtracking search, the \(n^2\) squares of the \(n \times n\) board constitute the possible choices choices. As we place one queen after another, the board changes. Its arrangement at any point is the current state state.

Figure 13-15   Solutions to the 4-queens problem

The figure illustrates three constraints: no two queens may share a row, a column, or a diagonal. Diagonals run in two directions: main diagonals \ and secondary diagonals /.

Figure 13-16   Constraints in the n-queens problem

items.title: 1.   Placing queens row by row
items.text:
Both the number of queens and the number of rows equal \(n\). It follows that each row must contain exactly one queen.

We can therefore place queens row by row, starting at the first row and placing one queen in each row through the last.

The figure shows row-by-row placement for four queens. To save space, it expands just one branch from the first row. Branches that violate a column or diagonal constraint have been pruned.

Figure 13-17   Placing queens row by row

In effect, placing queens row by row prunes the search by excluding every branch that would place multiple queens in one row.

items.title: 2.   Pruning by column and diagonal
items.text:
To enforce the column constraint, use a Boolean array cols of length \(n\) to track which columns already contain queens. Before placing a queen, consult cols to skip occupied columns. Update cols as the search proceeds and backtracks.

Tip

The matrix starts in the upper-left corner. Row indices increase downward and column indices increase to the right.

How can we enforce the diagonal constraints? Let \((row, col)\) be the row and column indices of a square. Along any main diagonal, subtracting the column index from the row index always gives the same result: the value of \(row - col\) is constant along a main diagonal.

Thus, if two squares satisfy \(row_1 - col_1 = row_2 - col_2\), they lie on the same main diagonal. We can use this property to track which main diagonals contain queens in the array diags1, as shown below.

Similarly, the value of \(row + col\) is constant along a secondary diagonal. The array diags2 lets us enforce this constraint as well.

Figure 13-18   Checking column and diagonal constraints

items.title: 3.   Implementation
items.text:
In a square matrix with \(n\) rows, \(row - col\) ranges over \([-n + 1, n - 1]\), and \(row + col\) ranges over \([0, 2n - 2]\). There are therefore \(2n - 1\) diagonals in each direction, so diags1 and diags2 each have length \(2n - 1\).

def backtrack(
    row: int,
    n: int,
    state: list[list[str]],
    res: list[list[list[str]]],
    cols: list[bool],
    diags1: list[bool],
    diags2: list[bool],
):
    """Backtracking: n-queens"""
    # Record the solution once every row has a queen
    if row == n:
        res.append([list(row) for row in state])
        return
    # Try each column
    for col in range(n):
        # Find the two diagonals through this square
        diag1 = row - col + n - 1
        diag2 = row + col
        # Prune if the column or either diagonal already has a queen
        if not cols[col] and not diags1[diag1] and not diags2[diag2]:
            # Try placing a queen on this square
            state[row][col] = "Q"
            cols[col] = diags1[diag1] = diags2[diag2] = True
            # Place a queen in the next row
            backtrack(row + 1, n, state, res, cols, diags1, diags2)
            # Backtrack: clear this square
            state[row][col] = "#"
            cols[col] = diags1[diag1] = diags2[diag2] = False

def n_queens(n: int) -> list[list[list[str]]]:
    """Solve the n-queens problem"""
    # Set up an n-by-n board with 'Q' for a queen and '#' for an empty square
    state = [["#" for _ in range(n)] for _ in range(n)]
    cols = [False] * n  # Track occupied columns
    diags1 = [False] * (2 * n - 1)  # Track occupied main diagonals
    diags2 = [False] * (2 * n - 1)  # Track occupied secondary diagonals
    res = []
    backtrack(0, n, state, res, cols, diags1, diags2)

    return res

            // Place a queen in the next row
