items.title: 3.2   Basic data types
items.text:
Computer data takes many forms, including text, images, video, speech, and 3D models. Although these forms organize data differently, they are all built from basic data types.

Basic data types are types the CPU can operate on directly. Algorithms use them directly as well. The main kinds are:

  • Integer types: byte, short, int, and long.
  • Floating-point types: float and double, used to represent numbers with fractional parts.
  • Character type: char, used to represent letters in various languages, punctuation, and even emoji.
  • Boolean type: bool, used to represent yes-or-no decisions.

Computers store values of basic data types in binary. A binary digit is \(1\) bit. On the vast majority of modern operating systems, \(1\) byte consists of \(8\) bits.

The range of a basic data type depends on how much space it occupies. Consider Java as an example.

  • The integer type byte occupies \(1\) byte = \(8\) bits and can represent \(2^{8}\) distinct values.
  • The integer type int occupies \(4\) bytes = \(32\) bits and can represent \(2^{32}\) distinct values.

The table lists the storage requirements, ranges, and default values of Java's basic data types. There is no need to memorize it. Get a general sense of the types and consult the table when you need a detail.

Table   Storage requirements and ranges of basic data types Type Type name Storage Minimum Maximum Default Integer byte 1 byte \(-2^7\) (\(-128\)) \(2^7 - 1\) (\(127\)) \(0\) short 2 bytes \(-2^{15}\) \(2^{15} - 1\) \(0\) int 4 bytes \(-2^{31}\) \(2^{31} - 1\) \(0\) long 8 bytes \(-2^{63}\) \(2^{63} - 1\) \(0\) Floating-point float 4 bytes \(1.175 \times 10^{-38}\) \(3.403 \times 10^{38}\) \(0.0\text{f}\) double 8 bytes \(2.225 \times 10^{-308}\) \(1.798 \times 10^{308}\) \(0.0\) Character char 2 bytes \(0\) \(2^{16} - 1\) \(0\) Boolean bool 1 byte \(\text{false}\) \(\text{true}\) \(\text{false}\)

The table describes Java's basic data types. Each programming language defines its own types, which may differ in size, range, and default value.

  • In Python, an int can grow as large as available memory allows, and a float is a 64-bit double-precision number. Python has no char type: a single character is a str of length 1.
  • C and C++ leave the exact sizes of basic types to the implementation and platform. The table follows the LP64 data model used by 64-bit Unix platforms, including Linux and macOS.
  • In C and C++, a char occupies 1 byte. In most programming languages, character size depends on the encoding, as discussed in “Character encoding.”
  • Although a Boolean value needs only 1 bit (\(0\) or \(1\)), it is usually stored in 1 byte of memory. Modern CPUs typically use 1 byte as the smallest addressable unit of memory.

How do basic data types relate to data structures? A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data in a computer. The focus of this definition is the structure of the data.

To represent a row of numbers, we naturally think of an array. Its linear structure captures which numbers are adjacent and in what order. Whether the contents are integers (int), floating-point numbers (float), or characters (char) is a separate matter.

In other words, a basic data type describes what is stored, while a data structure describes how it is organized. In the following code, the same structure, an array, stores and represents different basic types including int, float, char, and bool.

items.title: 3.4   Character encoding *
items.text: Computers store all data as binary numbers, including characters of type char. To represent characters, we need a character set that assigns each character a distinct number. With that mapping, a computer can look up a binary number to recover the character it represents.

items.title: 3.4.1   The ASCII character set
items.text:
ASCII, the American Standard Code for Information Interchange, was the earliest character set. It uses 7 bits (the low seven bits of a byte) for each character, allowing up to 128 distinct characters. As the figure shows, these include uppercase and lowercase English letters, the digits 0–9, punctuation marks, and control characters such as line feed and tab.

Figure 3-6   ASCII codes

However, ASCII supports only English. As computers spread around the world, extended ASCII (EASCII) character sets emerged to support additional languages. They extend ASCII from 7 to 8 bits and can represent 256 distinct characters.

Different regions developed their own extended ASCII character sets. All use ASCII for the first 128 characters, but the remaining 128 differ to meet the needs of different languages.

items.title: 3.4.2   The GBK character set
items.text:
It soon became clear that even extended ASCII had too few codes for many languages. For instance, there are nearly 100,000 Chinese characters, with thousands in everyday use. In 1980, China's national standards authority released the GB2312 character set. It included 6,763 Chinese characters and met most needs for processing Chinese text on computers.

GB2312 still could not handle some rare and traditional characters. The GBK character set extended GB2312 to include a total of 21,886 Chinese characters. GBK encodes ASCII characters in one byte and Chinese characters in two.

items.title: 3.4.3   The Unicode character set
items.text:
As computing developed rapidly, many character sets and encoding standards emerged, creating two problems. Most character sets defined characters for specific languages and could not handle multilingual text properly. Even a single language could have several standards: if two computers used different encodings, text sent between them could appear garbled.

Researchers asked: Could a character set comprehensive enough to include the world's languages and symbols solve both the multilingual text problem and the problem of garbled text? This idea led to a single, comprehensive character set: Unicode.

Unicode, whose Chinese name means “unified code,” has room for more than a million characters in principle. It aims to bring the world's characters into a common set for processing and displaying text across languages, reducing garbled text caused by incompatible standards. Unicode has added languages and characters steadily since its release in 1991. By September 2022, it contained 149,186 characters, including characters from many languages, symbols, and emoji.

As a universal character set, Unicode assigns each character a unique number called a code point. Its code space runs from U+0000 to U+10FFFF. However, assigning code points does not specify how those values are stored in a computer. If a text contains code points of different lengths, how can the system identify each character? Given two bytes, for example, how can it tell one two-byte character from two one-byte characters?

One straightforward solution is to store every character in an encoding of the same width. In Figure 3-7, each character in “Hello” fits in 1 byte, and each character in “算法” fits in 2 bytes. Padding the high bits with zeros lets us encode every character of “Hello 算法” in 2 bytes. The system can then recover the phrase by reading one character every 2 bytes.

Figure 3-7   Unicode encoding example

ASCII has already shown us that English letters need only 1 byte. With the scheme above, English text takes up twice as much space as in ASCII, wasting memory. We need a more space-efficient way to encode Unicode.

items.title: 3.4.4   UTF-8 encoding
items.text:
UTF-8 is now the most widely used Unicode encoding worldwide. It is a variable-length encoding that uses 1 to 4 bytes per character, depending on the character. ASCII characters take 1 byte, Latin letters outside ASCII and Greek letters can take 2, common Chinese characters take 3, and some rarer characters take 4.

UTF-8 has two straightforward encoding rules.

  • For a one-byte character, set the highest bit to \(0\) and put the Unicode code point in the remaining seven bits. ASCII characters occupy the first 128 Unicode code points, so UTF-8 is backward compatible with ASCII. Even old ASCII text can be read as UTF-8.
  • For a character encoded in \(n\) bytes, where \(n > 1\), set the first byte's high \(n\) bits to \(1\) and its next bit (bit \(n + 1\) counting from the left) to \(0\). Starting with the second byte, set the high two bits of each byte to \(10\). Fill the remaining bits with the character's Unicode code point.

The figure shows the UTF-8 encoding of “Hello算法.” Since the leading \(n\) bits of a multibyte character are all \(1\), the system can count the leading \(1\) bits to determine the character's length, \(n\) bytes.

Why set the high two bits of every remaining byte to \(10\)? The \(10\) prefix serves as a check. If the system starts decoding at the wrong byte, the leading \(10\) helps it detect the problem quickly.

We can use \(10\) as a check because under UTF-8, no character can begin with \(10\). To see why, suppose a character began with \(10\). The single leading one would imply a length of \(1\) byte, corresponding to ASCII. But the high bit of an ASCII character must be \(0\), a contradiction.

Figure 3-8   UTF-8 encoding example

Two other common Unicode encodings are:

  • UTF-16. Each character takes 2 or 4 bytes. All ASCII characters and commonly used non-English characters take 2 bytes, while a smaller set of characters requires 4. For a two-byte character, the UTF-16 code unit equals the Unicode code point.
  • UTF-32. Every character takes 4 bytes, so UTF-32 uses more space than UTF-8 and UTF-16, particularly for text with a large proportion of ASCII characters.

In terms of storage, UTF-8 is efficient for English letters, using only 1 byte each. UTF-16 can be more efficient for certain non-English characters, such as Chinese characters, which take only 2 bytes in UTF-16 but may need 3 in UTF-8.

In terms of compatibility, UTF-8 is the most widely supported, and many tools and libraries support it first.

items.title: 3.4.5   Character encodings in programming languages
items.text:
Historically, most programming languages used encodings such as UTF-16 or UTF-32 for strings at runtime, relying on fixed-width units. With a fixed-width encoding, we can treat a string as an array. This offers the following advantages.

  • Random access. UTF-16 makes random access to code units straightforward. With variable-width UTF-8, reaching character \(i\) requires traversing from the beginning of the string to character \(i\), which takes \(O(n)\) time.
  • Character counting. As with random access, obtaining a UTF-16 string’s length in code units is an \(O(1)\) operation. Counting the characters in a UTF-8 string, however, requires traversing the entire string.
  • String operations. Many operations, such as splitting, concatenating, inserting, and deleting, are easier on UTF-16 strings. With UTF-8, they usually require additional computation to ensure the resulting encoding is valid.

The choice of a string encoding for a programming language is an interesting design problem with many factors to consider.

  • Java's String type uses UTF-16, with 2 bytes per code unit. When Java was designed, 16 bits were thought sufficient for every possible character. That assumption proved wrong: Unicode later grew beyond 16 bits, so a character in Java may now be represented by two 16-bit values called a surrogate pair.
  • JavaScript and TypeScript use UTF-16 for strings for reasons similar to Java's. In 1995, when Netscape introduced JavaScript, Unicode was still young and 16 bits were enough to represent every Unicode character at the time.
  • C# uses UTF-16 primarily because Microsoft designed the .NET platform, and many Microsoft technologies, including Windows, use UTF-16 extensively.

Having underestimated the number of characters, these languages had to adopt surrogate pairs to represent Unicode characters beyond the 16-bit range. This was a compromise. In a string with surrogate pairs, a character can occupy 2 or 4 bytes, losing the advantage of fixed-width encoding. Handling surrogate pairs also takes extra code, making programs more complex and harder to debug.

For these reasons, some languages have adopted other representations.

  • Python's str represents Unicode text using a flexible layout whose character width depends on the largest code point in the string. If the string contains only ASCII, each character takes 1 byte. If some characters fall outside ASCII but all are in the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), each takes 2 bytes. If any character lies outside the BMP, each takes 4 bytes.
  • Go's string type uses UTF-8 internally. Go also provides the rune type for a single Unicode code point.
  • Rust's str and String types use UTF-8 internally. Rust also provides char to represent a single Unicode code point.

This discussion concerns how programming languages store strings internally. Storing text in files or transmitting it over a network is a separate question. For files and network transmission, we usually encode strings as UTF-8 for compatibility and space efficiency.

items.title: 3.1   Classifying data structures
items.text: Common data structures include arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, and graphs. We can classify them from two perspectives: logical structure and physical structure.

items.title: 3.1.1   Logical structure: linear and nonlinear
items.text:
Logical structure describes the relationships between data elements. In arrays and linked lists, elements follow a sequence, a linear relationship. A tree arranges elements in levels from top to bottom, forming ancestor-descendant relationships. A graph consists of nodes and edges that can express complex networks of relationships.

As the figure shows, logical structures fall into two broad categories: linear and nonlinear. A linear structure arranges elements logically along a single sequence. A nonlinear structure arranges them in some other way.

  • Linear data structures include arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues. Successive elements have a one-to-one relationship.
  • Nonlinear data structures include trees, heaps, and graphs.

Trees and networks are two common forms of nonlinear structure.

  • Tree structures, including trees and heaps, express one-to-many relationships between elements.
  • Network structures, such as graphs, express many-to-many relationships between elements.

A hash table looks up values by key. The figure shows this mapping separately.

Figure 3-1   Linear and nonlinear data structures

items.title: 3.1.2   Physical structure: contiguous and noncontiguous
items.text:
When an algorithm runs, the data it is processing is stored mainly in memory. Each black chip on the memory module below contains a region of memory. Imagine memory as a huge Excel spreadsheet, with each cell able to hold a fixed amount of data.

The system uses a memory address to access the data at a particular location. As shown below, the computer assigns numbers to the cells according to a set of rules so that each location has a unique address. A program uses these addresses to access the data in memory.

Figure 3-2   Memory module, memory space, and memory addresses

Tip

The spreadsheet is a simplified analogy. Actual memory systems are more complex, involving address spaces, memory management, caching, and both virtual and physical memory.

Memory is a resource shared by all programs. A block in use by one program is usually unavailable to other programs at the same time. Memory is therefore an important consideration when designing data structures and algorithms. For example, an algorithm's peak memory use should not exceed the system's remaining free memory. If no large contiguous block is available, the chosen structure must be able to use scattered memory.

As shown below, physical structure describes how data is stored in computer memory. Storage may be contiguous, as in an array, or noncontiguous, as in a linked list. The underlying layout determines how data is accessed, updated, inserted, and removed. The two layouts have complementary strengths in time and space efficiency.

Figure 3-3   Contiguous and noncontiguous storage

All data structures are implemented using arrays, linked lists, or a combination of the two. For example, either an array or a linked list can implement a stack or queue, while a hash table may combine both.

  • Arrays can implement stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, graphs, matrices, tensors (arrays of dimension \(\geq 3\)), and more.
  • Linked lists can implement stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, graphs, and more.

A linked list can still change length at runtime after initialization, so it is called a dynamic data structure. An array has a fixed length after initialization, so it is called a static data structure. Reallocating memory can nevertheless give an array some flexibility in length.

Tip

If you find physical structure difficult to visualize, try reading the next chapter and then returning to this section.

items.title: 1.   Data relationships in everyday situations
items.text:
For each scenario, examine the relationships between elements. Choose a linear, tree, or network structure and explain your reasoning.

  1. Students stand in a single line. Each student cares only about the people immediately in front of and behind them.
  2. A school is organized into levels: school → grade → class.
  3. City streets connect intersections. One intersection can lead to several others, and routes may form cycles.
Sample answer

  1. The line is a linear structure. Except at the two ends, each student has one neighbor in front and one behind, so the relationships form a single sequence.

  2. The school has a tree structure. Each class belongs to one grade, and each grade belongs to the school, forming a hierarchy from top to bottom.

  3. The streets form a network. An intersection can connect to several others, and routes can form cycles, so the relationships do not fit a single sequence or a strict hierarchy.

    To identify a structure, first examine how the elements relate to one another. How much memory they occupy is a separate question.

items.title: 2.   How is logical order represented in memory?
items.text:
Consider two simplified memory layouts that represent the logical order A → B → C.

  • Layout A stores A, B, C in memory cells 20, 21, 22, respectively.
  • Layout B stores A, B, C in memory cells 20, 7, 31, respectively. In addition, A records the location of B, and B records the location of C.
  1. Which layout uses contiguous storage? Which uses noncontiguous storage?
  2. Which layout more closely resembles an array, and which a linked list?
  3. The memory cell numbers in layout B are out of order. How can they still represent the logical order A → B → C?
Sample answer

  1. Layout A uses consecutive memory cells, so its storage is contiguous. The nodes in layout B occupy scattered locations, so its storage is noncontiguous.

  2. Layout A more closely resembles an array, and layout B a linked list.

  3. The links recorded between nodes determine their logical order, regardless of the numerical order of the memory cells. The location stored in A leads to B, and the location stored in B leads to C. You can therefore still visit A, B, C in order.

    Logical and physical structure thus describe two different aspects of the same data.

items.title: 3.   Data types and structures in a homework record
items.text:
A study group records whether four students turned in their homework, in seating order, and obtains the following:

[true, false, true, true]

  1. Which basic data type suits each element?
  2. What logical structure do the four elements form when arranged in seating order?
  3. Suppose the group switches to recording each student's homework score, [90, 0, 85, 100]. Does this change the type of data or the way it is organized? Explain.
Sample answer

  1. Each element represents only yes or no, so the Boolean type bool is a good fit.

  2. The elements form a linear structure in seating order and can be stored in an array.

  3. The type of data changes from Boolean values to integers. The organization stays the same: the values still form a sequence in seating order, so an array is still a suitable linear structure.

    A basic data type describes what is stored. A data structure describes how the data is organized.

items.title: 1.   Count the ones in a binary representation
items.text:
Given a nonnegative integer n, count the ones in its binary representation.

Use bitwise operations. Do not convert the number to a binary string or use a built-in function that counts ones directly.

Hints
  1. Use n & 1 to extract the rightmost bit of n and check whether it is 1.
  2. Shifting right by one discards the current rightmost bit. Most languages use the >> operator.
  3. After implementing the method that checks each bit and shifts right, observe what n & (n - 1) does: it clears the rightmost 1 in n.

LeetCode

items.title: 3.3   Number representations *
items.text:
Tip

In this book, an asterisk (*) marks an optional section. If you have limited time or find one difficult, you can skip it for now and return after finishing the required sections.

items.title: 3.3.1   Sign and magnitude, ones' complement, and two's complement
items.text:
The table in the previous section shows that each signed integer type represents one more negative number than positive numbers. For example, the range of byte is \([-128, 127]\). To understand this surprising asymmetry, we need to look at sign and magnitude, ones' complement, and two's complement.

First, computers store signed integers in two's complement form. Before exploring why, let's define the three representations.

  • Sign and magnitude. The highest bit is the sign bit: \(0\) indicates a positive sign and \(1\) a negative sign. The remaining bits give the magnitude.
  • Ones' complement. For a positive number, this is the same as sign and magnitude. For a negative number, start with sign and magnitude and invert all bits except the sign bit.
  • Two's complement. For a positive number, this is again the same as sign and magnitude. For a negative number, add \(1\) to its ones' complement representation.

The figure shows how to convert between sign and magnitude, ones' complement, and two's complement.

Figure 3-4   Converting between sign and magnitude, ones' complement, and two's complement

Sign and magnitude is the most intuitive representation, but it has limitations. For one, the sign-and-magnitude bit pattern of a negative number cannot be used directly in ordinary binary arithmetic. For example, adding the sign-and-magnitude bit patterns for \(1 + (-2)\) gives \(-3\), which is clearly incorrect.

\[ egin{aligned} & 1 + (-2) ewline & ightarrow 0000 \; 0001 + 1000 \; 0010 ewline & = 1000 \; 0011 ewline & ightarrow -3 \end{aligned} \]

To address this, computers introduced ones' complement. Convert the operands from sign and magnitude to ones' complement, compute \(1 + (-2)\) in ones' complement, and convert the result back to sign and magnitude. This gives the correct result, \(-1\).

\[ egin{aligned} & 1 + (-2) ewline & ightarrow 0000 \; 0001 \; ext{(sign and magnitude)} + 1000 \; 0010 \; ext{(sign and magnitude)} ewline & = 0000 \; 0001 \; ext{(ones' complement)} + 1111 \; 1101 \; ext{(ones' complement)} ewline & = 1111 \; 1110 \; ext{(ones' complement)} ewline & = 1000 \; 0001 \; ext{(sign and magnitude)} ewline & ightarrow -1 \end{aligned} \]

Another limitation is that sign and magnitude has two representations of zero, \(+0\) and \(-0\). Two different bit patterns for zero can introduce ambiguity. For example, a conditional test may give the wrong result if it does not account for positive and negative zero. Adding special checks to handle both representations can reduce computational efficiency.

\[ egin{aligned} +0 & ightarrow 0000 \; 0000 ewline -0 & ightarrow 1000 \; 0000 \end{aligned} \]

Ones' complement shares this ambiguity, which is why computers went on to adopt two's complement. Consider the conversion of negative zero from sign and magnitude to ones' complement and then to two's complement:

\[ egin{aligned} -0 ightarrow \; & 1000 \; 0000 \; ext{(sign and magnitude)} ewline = \; & 1111 \; 1111 \; ext{(ones' complement)} ewline = 1 \; & 0000 \; 0000 \; ext{(two's complement)} ewline \end{aligned} \]

Adding \(1\) to negative zero in ones' complement produces a carry. Since a byte is only 8 bits wide, the \(1\) that spills into the ninth bit is discarded. Thus the two's complement representation of negative zero is \(0000 \; 0000\), the same as for positive zero. Two's complement has only one zero, resolving the ambiguity.

One question remains. The range of byte is \([-128, 127]\), so where does the extra negative number \(-128\) come from? Every integer in the closed interval \([-127, +127]\) has a sign-and-magnitude, ones' complement, and two's complement representation, and we can convert between sign and magnitude and two's complement.

However, the two's complement bit pattern \(1000 \; 0000\) has no sign-and-magnitude counterpart. Applying the conversion procedure would give the sign-and-magnitude pattern \(0000 \; 0000\). This is a contradiction: that pattern represents \(0\), whose two's complement representation should be identical to itself. Computers assign the special two's complement pattern \(1000 \; 0000\) to \(-128\). In fact, adding \((-1) + (-127)\) in two's complement gives exactly \(-128\).

\[ egin{aligned} & (-127) + (-1) ewline & ightarrow 1111 \; 1111 \; ext{(sign and magnitude)} + 1000 \; 0001 \; ext{(sign and magnitude)} ewline & = 1000 \; 0000 \; ext{(ones' complement)} + 1111 \; 1110 \; ext{(ones' complement)} ewline & = 1000 \; 0001 \; ext{(two's complement)} + 1111 \; 1111 \; ext{(two's complement)} ewline & = 1000 \; 0000 \; ext{(two's complement)} ewline & ightarrow -128 \end{aligned} \]

Notice that every calculation above is an addition. This points to an important fact: addition is central to the design of computer arithmetic circuits. Compared with multiplication, division, or subtraction, addition is simpler to implement in hardware, easier to parallelize, and faster to execute.

Computers can, of course, do more than add. Combining addition with basic logical operations lets them perform many other mathematical operations. For example, subtraction \(a - b\) can be rewritten as addition \(a + (-b)\), and multiplication and division can be expressed as repeated addition or subtraction.

We can now see why computers use two's complement. The same circuitry and operations can add positive and negative numbers, with no need for special subtraction circuitry or special handling of positive and negative zero. This greatly simplifies hardware design and improves computational efficiency.

There is more to the design of two's complement than we have room to explore here. Interested readers can investigate it further.

items.title: 3.3.2   Floating-point representation
items.text:
Both int and float occupy 4 bytes, so why is the range of float so much larger than that of int? At first glance, having to represent fractions as well might seem to give float a smaller range.

The difference lies in how a float represents numbers. Write a 32-bit binary number as follows:

\[ b_{31} b_{30} b_{29} \ldots b_2 b_1 b_0 \]

Under IEEE 754, a 32-bit float consists of three fields.

  • Sign \(\mathrm{S}\): 1 bit, \(b_{31}\).
  • Exponent \(\mathrm{E}\): 8 bits, \(b_{30} b_{29} \ldots b_{23}\).
  • Fraction \(\mathrm{N}\): 23 bits, \(b_{22} b_{21} \ldots b_0\).

The binary representation of a float gives its value as follows:

\[ \text {val} = (-1)^{b_{31}} \times 2^{\left(b_{30} b_{29} \ldots b_{23}\right)_2-127} \times\left(1 . b_{22} b_{21} \ldots b_0\right)_2 \]

Expressed in decimal terms, the formula becomes:

\[ \text {val}=(-1)^{\mathrm{S}} \times 2^{\mathrm{E} -127} \times (1 + \mathrm{N}) \]

The terms have the following ranges:

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{S} \in & \{ 0, 1\}, \quad \mathrm{E} \in \{ 1, 2, \dots, 254 \} \newline (1 + \mathrm{N}) = & (1 + \sum_{i=1}^{23} b_{23-i} 2^{-i}) \subset [1, 2 - 2^{-23}] \end{aligned} \]

Figure 3-5   Calculating the value of an IEEE 754 float

In the example shown above, \(\mathrm{S} = 0\), \(\mathrm{E} = 124\), and \(\mathrm{N} = 2^{-2} + 2^{-3} = 0.375\). Substituting gives:

\[ \text { val } = (-1)^0 \times 2^{124 - 127} \times (1 + 0.375) = 0.171875 \]

We can now answer the original question: the exponent field gives float a far greater range than int. From the calculation above, the largest positive value of float is \(2^{254 - 127} \times (2 - 2^{-23}) \approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}\). Flipping the sign bit gives the most negative value.

The greater range of float comes at the cost of precision. The integer type int uses all 32 bits to represent evenly spaced numbers. With float, the exponent means that as the magnitude grows, the spacing between adjacent representable numbers generally increases.

As the table shows, exponent values \(\mathrm{E} = 0\) and \(\mathrm{E} = 255\) have special meanings, allowing representations of zero, infinity, \(\mathrm{NaN}\), and other cases.

Table   Meanings of exponent field values Exponent field E Fraction field \(\mathrm{N} = 0\) Fraction field \(\mathrm{N} \ne 0\) Formula \(0\) \(\pm 0\) Subnormal number \((-1)^{\mathrm{S}} \times 2^{-126} \times (0.\mathrm{N})\) \(1, 2, \dots, 254\) Normal number Normal number \((-1)^{\mathrm{S}} \times 2^{(\mathrm{E} -127)} \times (1.\mathrm{N})\) \(255\) \(\pm \infty\) \(\mathrm{NaN}\)

Subnormal numbers provide much finer resolution near zero. The smallest positive normal number is \(2^{-126}\), while the smallest positive subnormal number is \(2^{-126} \times 2^{-23}\).

Double precision (double) uses a representation similar to float, so we will omit the details.

items.title: 1.   Chapter review
items.text:
• Data structures can be classified by logical or physical structure. Logical structure describes the relationships among data elements. Physical structure describes how the data is stored in computer memory.
  • Common logical structures include sequences, trees, and networks. We usually group them into linear structures (arrays, linked lists, stacks, and queues) and nonlinear structures (trees, graphs, and heaps). A hash table implementation can combine linear and nonlinear structures.
  • While a program runs, its data is stored in memory. Each memory location has an address, which the program uses to access the data there.
  • The two main physical layouts are contiguous storage (arrays) and noncontiguous storage (linked lists). All data structures are implemented with arrays, linked lists, or both.
  • Basic data types include the integer types byte, short, int, and long, the floating-point types float and double, the character type char, and the Boolean type bool. Their ranges depend on their sizes and representations.
  • Sign and magnitude, ones' complement, and two's complement are three ways of encoding numbers, with rules for converting between them. In the sign-and-magnitude representation of an integer, the highest bit is the sign and the remaining bits give the magnitude.
  • Computers store signed integers in two's complement form. This lets the same circuitry add positive and negative numbers without dedicated subtraction hardware or ambiguity between positive and negative zero.
  • A single-precision floating-point encoding has a 1-bit sign, an 8-bit exponent, and a 23-bit fraction. The exponent gives it a far wider range than an integer of the same size, at the cost of precision.
  • ASCII, the earliest English character set, contains 128 characters stored in 1 byte each. GBK is a common Chinese character set containing over 20,000 Chinese characters. Unicode aims to provide a comprehensive standard covering characters from languages around the world and to resolve garbled text caused by incompatible character encodings.
  • UTF-8 is the most popular Unicode encoding and enjoys broad support. Its variable width makes it flexible and space-efficient. UTF-16 and UTF-32 use fixed-width code units. For Chinese text, UTF-16 can take less space than UTF-8. Languages such as Java and C# use UTF-16 by default.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: Why might a hash table use both linear and nonlinear data structures?

An array underlies a hash table. To resolve collisions, we can use separate chaining, described later in “Hash collisions.” Each array bucket points to a linked list. If the list grows beyond a threshold, it may be converted to a tree, usually a red-black tree.

In terms of storage, each bucket in the underlying array might hold a single value, a linked list, or a tree. Thus a hash table can combine linear data structures (arrays and linked lists) and nonlinear ones (trees).

Q: Is a char always 1 byte long?

The size of char depends on the encoding used by the language. Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, and C#, for example, use UTF-16 to represent Unicode code points, with a 2-byte unit for a char value.

Q: Isn't it ambiguous to call an array-backed structure “static”? A stack supports dynamic operations such as push and pop.

A stack does support dynamic operations on its data, but the underlying array is static in the sense that its length is fixed. An array-backed structure can add and remove elements dynamically within a fixed capacity. If the data outgrows the allocation, a larger array must be created and the original contents copied into it.

Q: If I don't specify a size when creating a stack or queue, why is it called a static data structure?

In high-level languages, you need not manually specify the initial capacity of a stack or queue. The class handles that internally. For example, Java's ArrayList typically starts with capacity 10. Growth is automatic as well, as discussed later in “Lists.”

Q: To convert sign and magnitude to two's complement, we invert bits and add 1. The inverse should be to subtract 1 and then invert. Why can we also convert back by inverting and adding 1 again?

The conversion works in both directions because it calculates a complement. Suppose \(a + b = c\). Then \(a\) is the complement of \(b\) with respect to \(c\). Conversely, \(b\) is the complement of \(a\) with respect to \(c\).

Take the \(n = 4\)-bit binary number \(0010\). Treat it as the original magnitude, disregarding the sign bit. To find its two's complement, invert the bits and add 1:

\[ 0010 \rightarrow 1101 \rightarrow 1110 \]

The original number and its two's complement add up as follows: \(0010 + 1110 = 10000\). Thus \(1110\) is the complement of \(0010\) with respect to \(10000\). Inverting and adding 1 therefore computes the complement with respect to \(10000\).

What, then, is the complement of \(1110\) with respect to \(10000\)? Again, inverting and adding 1 gives the answer:

\[ 1110 \rightarrow 0001 \rightarrow 0010 \]

In other words, the original number and its two's complement are each other's complements with respect to \(10000\). This is why both conversions can use the same operation: invert the bits and add 1.

Of course, the inverse operation also recovers the original number from its two's complement \(1110\): first subtract 1, then invert the bits.

\[ 1110 \rightarrow 1101 \rightarrow 0010 \]

Both procedures, “invert and add 1” and “subtract 1 and invert,” compute the complement with respect to \(10000\) and are therefore equivalent.

Inverting the bits by itself gives the complement with respect to \(1111\), because original + ones' complement = 1111 always holds. Adding 1 to this bitwise complement then gives the complement with respect to \(10000\).

The example uses \(n = 4\), but the same reasoning applies to binary numbers of any width.

items.title: Chapter 12.   Divide and conquer
items.text:
Abstract

A hard problem grows simpler each time we break it down.

Divide and conquer shows us why: start with the simple pieces, and even a complex problem becomes manageable.

items.title: 12.2   Divide-and-conquer search
items.text:
As we have seen, search algorithms fall into two broad categories.

  • Brute-force search traverses the data structure and takes \(O(n)\) time.
  • Adaptive search exploits the way the data is organized or uses prior information. It can take as little as \(O(\log n)\) or even \(O(1)\) time.

In fact, search algorithms that run in \(O(\log n)\) time commonly use divide and conquer. Examples include binary search and searches in trees.

  • At each step, binary search reduces the problem of searching an array to that of searching one half of it. This continues until the search interval is empty or the target is found.
  • Trees illustrate divide and conquer. In data structures such as binary search trees, AVL trees, and heaps, the various operations all take \(O(\log n)\) time.

Here is how binary search uses divide and conquer.

  • The problem can be divided. Comparing the middle element with the target recursively reduces a search of the whole array to a search of one half.
  • The subproblems are independent. Each round of binary search handles just one subproblem, independently of the others.
  • There are no subproblem results to combine. Binary search looks for a single element. Solving the remaining subproblem also solves the original problem.

Divide and conquer speeds up search because a brute-force scan rules out only one candidate per step, whereas divide-and-conquer search can rule out half the candidates at once.

items.title: 1.   Implementing binary search with divide and conquer
items.text:
In an earlier chapter, we implemented binary search iteratively. Now we will implement it recursively using divide and conquer.

Question

Given a sorted array nums of length \(n\) with distinct elements, find target.

Let \(f(i, j)\) denote the subproblem of searching the closed interval \([i, j]\).

Start with the original problem \(f(0, n-1)\) and perform binary search as follows.

  1. Compute the midpoint \(m\) of the search interval \([i, j]\) and use it to rule out half the interval.
  2. Recursively solve the subproblem on the remaining half, either \(f(i, m-1)\) or \(f(m+1, j)\).
  3. Repeat steps 1. and 2. until you find target or the interval is empty, then return.

The figure traces this divide-and-conquer search for \(6\) in an array.

Figure 12-4   Divide and conquer in binary search

The implementation defines a recursive function dfs() to solve \(f(i, j)\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_search_recur.py
def dfs(nums: list[int], target: int, i: int, j: int) -> int:
    """Binary search: problem f(i, j)"""
    # An empty interval contains no target, so return -1
    if i > j:
        return -1
    # Compute the middle index m
    m = (i + j) // 2
    if nums[m] < target:
        # Recursively solve f(m+1, j)
        return dfs(nums, target, m + 1, j)
    elif nums[m] > target:
        # Recursively solve f(i, m-1)
        return dfs(nums, target, i, m - 1)
    else:
        # Target found: return its index
        return m

def binary_search(nums: list[int], target: int) -> int:
    """Binary search"""
    n = len(nums)
    # Solve f(0, n-1)
    return dfs(nums, target, 0, n - 1)

items.title: 12.3   Reconstructing a binary tree
items.text:
Question

Given a binary tree’s preorder traversal preorder and inorder traversal inorder, reconstruct the tree and return its root. Assume all nodes have distinct values, as in Figure 12-5.

Figure 12-5   Example data for reconstructing a binary tree

items.title: 1.   Does the problem suit divide and conquer?
items.text:
Reconstructing a binary tree from preorder and inorder is a classic divide-and-conquer problem.

  • The problem can be divided. Initialize the root and split the remaining work into two subproblems: building the left and right subtrees. Apply the same split recursively to each subtree until the subproblem is an empty subtree.
  • The subproblems are independent. The left and right subtrees share no nodes. Building the left subtree requires only its segments of the inorder and preorder traversals. The same holds for the right subtree.
  • The subproblem solutions can be combined. Once we have built the left and right subtrees, attach them to the root to obtain the solution to the original problem.

items.title: 2.   Separating the subtrees
items.text:
We know that divide and conquer applies, but how can we identify the left and right subtrees in the preorder traversal preorder and inorder traversal inorder?

By definition, both preorder and inorder consist of three parts.

  • Preorder: [ root | left subtree | right subtree ]. For the tree above, this gives [ 3 | 9 | 2 1 7 ].
  • Inorder: [ left subtree | root | right subtree ]. For the tree above, this gives [ 9 | 3 | 1 2 7 ].

Using the data above, follow the steps in the next figure to split the traversals.

  1. The first element of the preorder traversal, 3, is the root value.
  2. Find the index of root 3 in inorder. Use this index to split inorder into [ 9 | 3 | 1 2 7 ].
  3. The split in inorder tells us that the left subtree has one node and the right subtree has three. We can therefore split preorder into [ 3 | 9 | 2 1 7 ].

Figure 12-6   Separating subtrees in preorder and inorder traversals

items.title: 3.   Representing subtree ranges with variables
items.text:
The split gives us the index ranges for the root and both subtrees in preorder and inorder. A few index variables are enough to describe those ranges.

  • Let \(i\) be the index of the current tree’s root in preorder.
  • Let \(m\) be the index of the current tree’s root in inorder.
  • Let \([l, r]\) be the index range of the current tree in inorder.

As the table shows, these variables identify the root’s index in preorder and each subtree’s index range in inorder.

Table 12-1   Root and subtree indices in preorder and inorder traversals

Root index in preorder Subtree index range in inorder Current tree \(i\) \([l, r]\) Left subtree \(i + 1\) \([l, m-1]\) Right subtree \(i + 1 + (m - l)\) \([m+1, r]\)

In the index for the root of the right subtree, \((m-l)\) is the number of nodes in the left subtree. The figure illustrates this offset.

Figure 12-7   Index ranges for the root and its left and right subtrees

items.title: 4.   Implementation
items.text:
To look up \(m\) efficiently, use a hash table hmap that maps each element of inorder to its index:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby build_tree.py
def dfs(
    preorder: list[int],
    inorder_map: dict[int, int],
    i: int,
    l: int,
    r: int,
) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Build a binary tree using divide and conquer"""
    # Stop when the subtree interval is empty
    if r - l < 0:
        return None
    # Initialize the root
    root = TreeNode(preorder[i])
    # Look up m to separate the left and right subtrees
    m = inorder_map[preorder[i]]
    # Subproblem: build the left subtree
    root.left = dfs(preorder, inorder_map, i + 1, l, m - 1)
    # Subproblem: build the right subtree
    root.right = dfs(preorder, inorder_map, i + 1 + m - l, m + 1, r)
    # Return the root
    return root

items.title: 12.1   Divide-and-conquer algorithms
items.text:
Divide and conquer is an important and widely used algorithmic strategy. It is usually implemented recursively and has two stages: divide and conquer.

  1. Divide (split): Recursively break the problem into two or more subproblems until you reach the smallest subproblems.
  2. Conquer (combine): Start with the known solutions of the smallest subproblems and combine them from the bottom up to solve the original problem.

Merge sort is a classic example of divide and conquer, as the figure shows.

  1. Divide: Recursively split the original array (the problem) into two subarrays (subproblems) until each subarray has just one element (the smallest subproblem).
  2. Conquer: Merge the sorted subarrays (subproblem solutions) from the bottom up to obtain the sorted version of the original array (the solution).

Figure 12-1   Divide and conquer in merge sort

items.title: 12.1.1   Recognizing a divide-and-conquer problem
items.text:
The following criteria can help you decide whether divide and conquer suits a problem.

  1. The problem can be divided. The original problem splits into smaller problems of the same kind, which can be divided recursively in the same way.
  2. The subproblems are independent. They do not overlap or depend on each other, so they can be solved separately.
  3. The subproblem solutions can be combined. Combining them gives a solution to the original problem.

Merge sort meets all three criteria.

  1. The problem can be divided. Recursively split the array (the original problem) into two subarrays (subproblems).
  2. The subproblems are independent. Each subarray can be sorted on its own, so each subproblem can be solved independently.
  3. The subproblem solutions can be combined. Merge the two sorted subarrays (the subproblem solutions) into one sorted array (the solution to the original problem).

items.title: 12.1.2   Improving efficiency with divide and conquer
items.text:
Divide and conquer can both solve a problem and make the algorithm more efficient. Quicksort, merge sort, and heapsort use divide and conquer, which helps explain why they are faster than selection sort, bubble sort, and insertion sort.

Why can divide and conquer improve efficiency? Why should splitting a problem, solving the pieces, and combining their results take less work than solving it directly? We can look at this from two angles: operation counts and parallel computation.

items.title: 1.   Reducing the number of operations
items.text:
Bubble sort takes \(O(n^2)\) time on an array of length \(n\). Suppose we split the array at its midpoint, as shown below. Splitting takes \(O(n)\) time, sorting each half takes \(O((n / 2)^2)\) time, and merging the two halves takes \(O(n)\) time. The overall time complexity is:

\[ O(n + (\frac{n}{2})^2 \times 2 + n) = O(\frac{n^2}{2} + 2n) \]

Figure 12-2   Bubble sort before and after splitting the array

Now solve the following inequality. The left side counts operations before the split, and the right side counts them after the split:

\[ \begin{aligned} n^2 & > \frac{n^2}{2} + 2n \newline n^2 - \frac{n^2}{2} - 2n & > 0 \newline n(n - 4) & > 0 \end{aligned} \]

When \(n > 4\), splitting reduces the operation count and should make the sort faster. Its time complexity is still quadratic, \(O(n^2)\), but the constant factor is smaller.

What if we keep splitting each subarray in half until every subarray contains just one element? This gives us merge sort, with time complexity \(O(n \log n)\).

What if we use more split points and divide the array evenly into \(k\) subarrays? This resembles bucket sort, which is well suited to large datasets and can achieve \(O(n + k)\) time in theory.

items.title: 2.   Speeding up computation with parallelism
items.text:
Divide and conquer produces independent subproblems, so we can usually solve them in parallel. Besides reducing time complexity, divide and conquer gives the operating system opportunities to parallelize the work.

Parallelism is especially effective on multicore or multiprocessor systems. Processing several subproblems at once makes fuller use of computing resources and can substantially reduce total running time.

For example, the bucket sort below distributes a large dataset evenly among buckets. We can assign different buckets to different processing units for sorting and merge the results afterward.

Figure 12-3   Parallel computation in bucket sort

items.title: 12.1.3   Common applications of divide and conquer
items.text:
Divide and conquer solves many classic algorithmic problems.

  • Closest pair of points: Split the points into two sets, find the closest pair within each, and then find the closest pair that spans the split.
  • Large integer multiplication: The Karatsuba algorithm, for example, breaks multiplication of large integers into multiplications and additions of smaller integers.
  • Matrix multiplication: Strassen’s algorithm, for example, breaks multiplication of large matrices into multiplications and additions of smaller matrices.
  • Tower of Hanoi: The puzzle has a recursive solution that illustrates divide and conquer.
  • Finding inversions: Two values form an inversion if the earlier value in a sequence is greater than the later one. Merge sort gives us a divide-and-conquer approach to finding inversions.

Divide and conquer also appears throughout the design of algorithms and data structures.

  • Binary search: Split a sorted array at the middle index. Compare the target with the middle element to decide which half to discard, then repeat the operation on the remaining interval.
  • Merge sort: We saw how this works at the beginning of the section.
  • Quicksort: Choose a pivot and partition the array into two subarrays, one containing values smaller than the pivot and the other values larger than the pivot. Repeat the partitioning until only one element remains in each subarray.
  • Bucket sort: Distribute the data among several buckets, sort each bucket, and take the elements out in bucket order to obtain a sorted array.
  • Trees: Search, insertion, and deletion in binary search trees, AVL trees, red-black trees, B-trees, and B+ trees can all be viewed as applications of divide and conquer.
  • Heaps: A heap is a special kind of complete binary tree. Operations such as insertion, deletion, and heapification also implicitly use divide and conquer.
  • Hash tables: Some collision-resolution schemes use divide and conquer indirectly. For example, a hash table that uses chaining may turn a long chain into a red-black tree to speed up lookups.

As these examples show, divide and conquer often works quietly in the background of algorithms and data structures.

items.title: 1.   Which tasks suit divide and conquer?
items.text:
A student wants to split each of the following tasks in half, solve the halves separately, and combine their results. Classify each task as “well suited to divide and conquer,” “can be divided without reducing the total work,” or “the halves cannot be solved independently.” Explain your reasoning.

  1. Sort an unsorted array.
  2. Find the maximum value in an array.
  3. Perform a sequence of stack operations push(x) and pop() in order, and output the element returned by each pop().
Sample answer
  1. Well suited. Split the array in half, sort the halves independently, and merge them in \(O(n)\) time. This is merge sort.
  2. The task can be divided, but the total work stays the same. Together, the two halves still require examining all \(n\) elements, which takes \(O(n)\) time, just like a direct scan.
  3. The halves cannot be solved independently. The contents of the stack at the start of the second half depend on the result of the first, so the two halves cannot run independently without knowing each other’s results.

items.title: 2.   How does exponentiation by squaring save work?
items.text:
The following recursive function uses divide and conquer to compute \(x^n\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby fast_power.py
def fast_pow(x: int, n: int) -> int:
    """Exponentiation by squaring"""
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    half = fast_pow(x, n // 2)
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return half * half
    return half * half * x

  half = fast_pow(x, n / 2)
  return half * half if n.even?

  half * half * x
end

Let x = 3 and n = 5. Trace the function:

  1. What values does the argument n take in successive recursive calls?
  2. As the calls return, starting with the deepest one, what value does each return?
  3. Why store the recursive result in half instead of calling the same subproblem once for each factor?
Sample answer

  1. The argument takes the values 5 → 2 → 1 → 0. Each call halves the exponent until it reaches the base case.

  2. For n = 0, the function returns 1. For n = 1, it returns \(1×1×3=3\). For n = 2, it returns \(3×3=9\). For n = 5, it returns \(9×9×3=243\).

  3. Calling the same subproblem for each factor would perform exactly the same calculation twice. Saving the result in half means each level makes just one recursive call, and the recursion depth is about \(\log n\). Making both calls would repeat a great deal of work.

items.title: 3.   Separating the left and right subtrees in traversal sequences
items.text:
A binary tree with distinct node values has the following preorder and inorder traversals:

  • Preorder: [A, B, D, E, C]
  • Inorder: [D, B, E, A, C]

Split the sequences only at the root. You do not need to recurse further or draw the whole tree.

  1. Which node is the root?
  2. Which segments of the inorder traversal represent the left and right subtrees?
  3. Which segments of the preorder traversal represent the left and right subtrees? Which nodes are the root’s immediate children?
Sample answer

  1. The first node in preorder is the root, so the root is A.

  2. A splits the inorder traversal into two parts: [D, B, E] for the left subtree and [C] for the right.

  3. The left subtree contains three nodes, so the three preorder elements after the root A belong to the left subtree, giving [B, D, E]. The remaining segment, [C], belongs to the right subtree. The root’s left child is therefore B and its right child is C.

items.title: 1.   Exponentiation by squaring
items.text:
Given a real number x and an integer n, compute \(x^n\) without calling the language’s built-in power function. Use recursive divide and conquer. Halve the exponent at each step and reuse the result of the subproblem. For this problem, \(x^0=1\) even when x = 0. When n < 0, you may assume x != 0 and compute the answer as \((1/x)^{-n}\).

Hints
  1. When n is 0, the answer is 1
  2. Save x raised to the power n // 2 as half to avoid a second recursive call
  3. If n < 0, first set x to 1 / x and n to -n. In C++ or Java, you can first promote n to a 64-bit integer to avoid overflow when negating the smallest 32-bit integer

LeetCode

items.title: 12.4   The Tower of Hanoi
items.text:
In merge sort and binary tree construction, we divided the original problem into two subproblems half its size. The Tower of Hanoi uses a different way to divide the problem.

Question

Consider three pegs labeled A, B, and C. Initially, peg A holds \(n\) disks, arranged from smallest on top to largest on the bottom. Move all \(n\) disks to peg C in their original order, as shown below. Each move must follow these rules.

  1. Take a disk only from the top of one peg and place it on top of another.
  2. Move only one disk at a time.
  3. A smaller disk must always sit above a larger one on the same peg.

Figure 12-10   Tower of Hanoi example

Let \(f(i)\) denote the Tower of Hanoi problem of size \(i\). For example, \(f(3)\) denotes the problem of moving \(3\) disks from A to C.

items.title: 1.   The base cases
items.text:
For \(f(1)\), there is just one disk. Move it directly from A to C, as shown below.

<1><2>

Figure 12-11   Solution for one disk

For \(f(2)\), there are two disks, as shown below. Because the smaller disk must stay above the larger one, we need peg B to complete the transfer.

  1. First, move the smaller disk on top from A to B.
  2. Next, move the larger disk from A to C.
  3. Finally, move the smaller disk from B to C.
<1><2><3><4>

Figure 12-12   Solution for two disks

We can summarize \(f(2)\) as follows: move two disks from A to C using B. Peg C is the destination, and peg B is the auxiliary peg.

items.title: 2.   Dividing the problem
items.text:
For \(f(3)\), with three disks, the situation is a little more involved.

We already know how to solve \(f(1)\) and \(f(2)\). Using divide and conquer, treat the two disks on top of A as a unit and follow the steps below. This moves all three disks from A to C.

  1. Use B as the destination and C as the auxiliary peg to move two disks from A to B.
  2. One disk remains on A. Move it directly from A to C.
  3. Use C as the destination and A as the auxiliary peg to move two disks from B to C.
<1><2><3><4>

Figure 12-13   Solution for three disks

In effect, we have split \(f(3)\) into two instances of \(f(2)\) and one instance of \(f(1)\). Solving the three subproblems in order solves the original problem. Thus, the subproblems can be solved independently and their solutions combined.

This gives us the divide-and-conquer strategy shown below: split \(f(n)\) into two instances of \(f(n-1)\) and one instance of \(f(1)\), then solve the three subproblems in this order.

  1. Move \(n-1\) disks from A to B using C.
  2. Move the remaining \(1\) disk directly from A to C.
  3. Move \(n-1\) disks from B to C using A.

Both instances of \(f(n-1)\) can be divided recursively in the same way until we reach the smallest subproblem, \(f(1)\). We already know how to solve \(f(1)\): it takes just one move.

Figure 12-14   A divide-and-conquer strategy for the Tower of Hanoi

items.title: 3.   Implementation
items.text:
The recursive function dfs(i, src, buf, tar) moves the top \(i\) disks from peg src to the destination tar using auxiliary peg buf:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby hanota.py
def move(src: list[int], tar: list[int]):
    """Move one disk"""
    # Take a disk from the top of src
    pan = src.pop()
    # Place the disk on top of tar
    tar.append(pan)

def dfs(i: int, src: list[int], buf: list[int], tar: list[int]):
    """Solve Tower of Hanoi subproblem f(i)"""
    # If only one disk remains on src, move it directly to tar
    if i == 1:
        move(src, tar)
        return
    # Subproblem f(i-1): move the top i-1 disks from src to buf using tar
    dfs(i - 1, src, tar, buf)
    # Subproblem f(1): move the remaining disk from src to tar
    move(src, tar)
    # Subproblem f(i-1): move the top i-1 disks from buf to tar using src
    dfs(i - 1, buf, src, tar)

def solve_hanota(A: list[int], B: list[int], C: list[int]):
    """Solve the Tower of Hanoi"""
    n = len(A)
    # Move the top n disks from A to C using B
    dfs(n, A, B, C)

Quote

The Tower of Hanoi comes from an old legend. In a temple in ancient India, monks had three tall diamond pegs and \(64\) gold disks of different sizes. They kept moving the disks, believing the world would end the moment they placed the last disk correctly.

Even at one move per second, the monks would need about \(2^{64} \approx 1.84×10^{19}\) seconds to finish. items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• Divide and conquer is a common algorithm design strategy with two stages: divide (split) and conquer (combine). It is usually implemented recursively.
  • To recognize a divide-and-conquer problem, ask whether it can be divided, whether the subproblems are independent, and whether their solutions can be combined.
  • Merge sort is a classic example. It recursively splits an array into two halves until only single elements remain, then merges them level by level to produce a sorted array.
  • Divide and conquer often improves efficiency in two ways: it reduces the number of operations, and it creates opportunities for parallel processing.
  • Divide and conquer solves many algorithmic problems and appears throughout the design of algorithms and data structures.
  • Adaptive search is more efficient than brute-force search. Algorithms that search in \(O(\log n)\) time commonly use divide and conquer.
  • Binary search is another classic example. It needs no step to combine subproblem solutions and can be implemented recursively using divide and conquer.
  • To reconstruct a binary tree, split the original problem into building its left and right subtrees. Split the index ranges of the preorder and inorder traversals to identify those subproblems.
  • In the Tower of Hanoi, a problem of size \(n\) splits into two subproblems of size \(n-1\) and one of size \(1\). Solving the three in order solves the original problem.

items.title: Chapter 14.   Dynamic programming
items.text:
Abstract

Streams flow into rivers, and rivers flow into the sea.

Dynamic programming brings the solutions to small problems together, carrying us step by step toward the answer to a larger one.

items.title: 14.2   Properties of dynamic programming problems
items.text:
In the previous section, we saw how dynamic programming solves a problem by breaking it into subproblems. This is a general algorithmic technique. Divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and backtracking each use it differently.

  • Divide and conquer recursively splits a problem into independent subproblems until it reaches the smallest ones. As the recursion unwinds, it combines their solutions to solve the original problem.
  • Dynamic programming also breaks problems down recursively. The main difference from divide and conquer is that its subproblems depend on one another, so many of them overlap.
  • Backtracking enumerates all possible solutions by trying choices and undoing them. Pruning avoids unnecessary search branches. A solution consists of a series of decisions, and we can treat the sequence leading up to each decision as a subproblem.

Dynamic programming is often used for optimization problems. Along with overlapping subproblems, these problems have two other important properties: optimal substructure and the no-aftereffect property.

items.title: 14.2.1   Optimal substructure
items.text:
Let's modify the stair-climbing problem slightly to illustrate optimal substructure.

Minimum cost to climb stairs

On a staircase, each move takes you up \(1\) or \(2\) stairs. Each stair is labeled with a nonnegative integer, the cost of landing on it. Given a nonnegative integer array \(cost\), where \(cost[i]\) is the cost of stair \(i\) and \(cost[0]\) corresponds to the ground (the starting point), find the minimum total cost to reach the top.

In Figure 14-6, stairs \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\) cost \(1\), \(10\), and \(1\), respectively. The minimum cost to climb from the ground to stair \(3\) is \(2\).

Figure 14-6   Minimum cost to reach stair 3

Let \(dp[i]\) be the cumulative cost to reach stair \(i\). We can reach stair \(i\) only from stair \(i - 1\) or \(i - 2\), so \(dp[i]\) must be either \(dp[i - 1] + cost[i]\) or \(dp[i - 2] + cost[i]\). To minimize the cost, we take the smaller value:

\[ dp[i] = \min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]) + cost[i] \]

This illustrates optimal substructure: an optimal solution to the original problem is built from optimal solutions to its subproblems.

Our problem has optimal substructure: we choose the better of the two optimal subproblem solutions, \(dp[i-1]\) and \(dp[i-2]\), and use it to construct the optimal solution to \(dp[i]\).

Does the stair-climbing problem in the previous section also have optimal substructure? Finding the number of ways seems like a counting problem. But try asking for the “maximum number of ways.” Now the question is equivalent, yet the optimal substructure becomes apparent: the maximum number of ways to reach stair \(n\) equals the sum of the maximum numbers of ways to reach stairs \(n-1\) and \(n-2\). The interpretation of optimal substructure can vary with the problem.

With the recurrence and the initial states \(dp[1] = cost[1]\) and \(dp[2] = cost[2]\), we can write the dynamic programming solution:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_cost_climbing_stairs_dp.py
def min_cost_climbing_stairs_dp(cost: list[int]) -> int:
    """Minimum cost to climb stairs with dynamic programming"""
    n = len(cost) - 1
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return cost[n]
    # Initialize the dp table to store subproblem solutions

items.title: 14.2.2   The no-aftereffect property
items.text:
An important reason dynamic programming works is the no-aftereffect property: given a state, what happens next depends only on that state, regardless of the states visited on the way there.

In stair climbing, state \(i\) can lead to \(i+1\) or \(i+2\) by climbing \(1\) or \(2\) stairs, respectively. Neither choice requires us to consider any state before \(i\). Those states have no effect on what we can do from \(i\).

Adding a constraint to the stair-climbing problem changes the picture.

Climbing stairs with a constraint

A staircase has \(n\) stairs. Each move climbs \(1\) or \(2\) stairs, but you cannot climb \(1\) stair twice in a row. How many ways can you reach the top?

As the figure shows, only \(2\) ways to reach stair \(3\) remain. Climbing \(1\) stair three times in a row violates the constraint and is ruled out.

Figure 14-8   Number of ways to reach stair 3 with the constraint

If the previous move climbed \(1\) stair, the next move must climb \(2\) stairs. Thus the current state (the stair we are on) no longer determines the next choice by itself. The choice also depends on the previous state (the stair we came from).

With the state defined this way, the no-aftereffect property no longer holds and the recurrence \(dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]\) breaks down. The term \(dp[i-1]\) counts ways to make a final move of \(1\) stair, including many where the preceding move also climbed \(1\) stair. To respect the constraint, we cannot add all of \(dp[i-1]\) to \(dp[i]\).

We therefore extend the state definition: state \([i, j]\) means we are on stair \(i\) and the last move climbed \(j\) stairs, where \(j \in \{1, 2\}\). Distinguishing a final move of \(1\) stair from one of \(2\) stairs lets us identify the possible predecessors.

  • If the last move climbed \(1\) stair, the preceding move must have climbed \(2\) stairs. Thus \(dp[i, 1]\) can come only from \(dp[i-1, 2]\).
  • If the last move climbed \(2\) stairs, the preceding move could have climbed \(1\) or \(2\) stairs. Thus \(dp[i, 2]\) can come from \(dp[i-2, 1]\) or \(dp[i-2, 2]\).

With this definition, \(dp[i, j]\) counts the ways to reach state \([i, j]\), as shown below. The recurrence becomes:

\[ \begin{cases} dp[i, 1] = dp[i-1, 2] \\ dp[i, 2] = dp[i-2, 1] + dp[i-2, 2] \end{cases} \]

Figure 14-9   Recurrence with the stair-climbing constraint

Finally, return \(dp[n, 1] + dp[n, 2]\). The sum counts all ways to reach stair \(n\):

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_constraint_dp.py
def climbing_stairs_constraint_dp(n: int) -> int:
    """Constrained stair climbing with dynamic programming"""
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return 1
    # Initialize the dp table to store subproblem solutions
    dp = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # Base cases: set the solutions to the smallest subproblems
    dp[1][1], dp[1][2] = 1, 0
    dp[2][1], dp[2][2] = 0, 1
    # State transition: solve larger subproblems using smaller ones
    for i in range(3, n + 1):
        dp[i][1] = dp[i - 1][2]
        dp[i][2] = dp[i - 2][1] + dp[i - 2][2]
    return dp[n][1] + dp[n][2]

fn climbing_stairs_constraint_dp(n: usize) -> i32 {
    if n == 1 || n == 2 {
        return 1;
    };
    // Initialize the dp table to store subproblem solutions
    let mut dp = vec![vec![-1; 3]; n + 1];
    // Base cases: set the solutions to the smallest subproblems
    dp[1][1] = 1;
    dp[1][2] = 0;
    dp[2][1] = 0;
    dp[2][2] = 1;
    // State transition: solve larger subproblems using smaller ones
    for i in 3..=n {
        dp[i][1] = dp[i - 1][2];
        dp[i][2] = dp[i - 2][1] + dp[i - 2][2];
    }
    dp[n][1] + dp[n][2]
}

/* Constrained stair climbing with dynamic programming */
int climbingStairsConstraintDP(int n) {
    if (n == 1 || n == 2) {
        return 1;
    }
    // Initialize the dp table to store subproblem solutions
    int **dp = malloc((n + 1) * sizeof(int *));
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        dp[i] = calloc(3, sizeof(int));
    }
    // Base cases: set the solutions to the smallest subproblems
    dp[1][1] = 1;
    dp[1][2] = 0;
    dp[2][1] = 0;
    dp[2][2] = 1;
    // State transition: solve larger subproblems using smaller ones
    for (int i = 3; i <= n; i++) {
        dp[i][1] = dp[i - 1][2];
        dp[i][2] = dp[i - 2][1] + dp[i - 2][2];
    }
    int res = dp[n][1] + dp[n][2];
    // Free the memory
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        free(dp[i]);
    }
    free(dp);
    return res;
}

Here we needed information from just one earlier state. Extending the state definition restored the no-aftereffect property. In some problems, however, the influence of earlier states is much harder to capture.

Climbing stairs with obstacles that appear along the way

A staircase has \(n\) stairs, and each move climbs \(1\) or \(2\) stairs. Whenever you land on stair \(i\), the system places an obstacle on stair \(2i\). You cannot land on stair \(2i\) on any later move. For example, if your first two moves land on stairs \(2\) and \(3\), then stairs \(4\) and \(6\) are off-limits thereafter. How many ways can you reach the top?

The next move depends on all previous states. Each move places an obstacle farther up the staircase and affects future moves. Dynamic programming often struggles with such problems.

Many complex combinatorial optimization problems, such as the traveling salesperson problem, exhibit this dependence on the past. For such problems, we often turn to methods such as heuristic search, genetic algorithms, or reinforcement learning to find a usable local optimum within a limited time.

items.title: 14.3   Solving problems with dynamic programming
items.text:
The previous two sections introduced the main properties of dynamic programming problems. Let's now consider two practical questions.

  1. How can we recognize a dynamic programming problem?
  2. Where should we start, and what steps should we follow to solve it?

items.title: 14.3.1   Recognizing a dynamic programming problem
items.text:
Problems with overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, and the no-aftereffect property are usually good candidates for dynamic programming. These properties can be hard to spot in the problem statement. We often start with a simpler test: could backtracking (exhaustive search) solve the problem?

Problems suited to backtracking usually fit a decision tree model. Each node in the tree represents a decision, and each path represents a sequence of decisions.

In other words, when there are clearly defined choices and a solution results from a sequence of choices, the problem fits a decision tree and can usually be solved by backtracking.

Several additional clues favor dynamic programming.

  • The problem asks for an optimum, such as the largest or smallest value or the greatest or least number of items.
  • A list, multidimensional array, or tree can represent the states, and a recurrence relates a state to neighboring states.

Other clues make dynamic programming less likely to be suitable.

  • The goal is to find every possible solution rather than an optimum.
  • The problem clearly involves permutations or combinations and asks you to return multiple specific arrangements.

If a problem fits a decision tree and shows clear signs favoring dynamic programming, we can try that approach and test our assumption as we work.

items.title: 14.3.2   Steps for solving the problem
items.text:
The details depend on the nature and difficulty of the problem. Typically, we describe the decisions, define the states, set up a \(dp\) table, derive a recurrence, and establish the boundary conditions.

Let's work through a classic example, the minimum path sum.

Question

An \(n \times m\) grid grid contains a nonnegative integer in each cell representing its cost. A robot starts at the top left and moves one cell down or right at each step until it reaches the bottom right. Return the minimum path sum from the top left to the bottom right.

In the example below, the minimum path sum is \(13\).

Figure 14-10   Example input for minimum path sum

Step 1: Identify the decision at each step and define the state and \(dp\) table

At each step we decide whether to move down or right from the current cell. If its row and column indices are \([i, j]\), the next cell is \([i+1, j]\) or \([i, j+1]\). The state therefore needs two variables, the row and column, written \([i, j]\).

The subproblem for state \([i, j]\) asks for the minimum path sum from the starting cell \([0, 0]\) to \([i, j]\). Denote its solution by \(dp[i, j]\).

This gives us the two-dimensional \(dp\) matrix below, with the same dimensions as the input grid \(grid\).

Figure 14-11   State definition and dp table

Note

Both dynamic programming and backtracking can be described as sequences of decisions. A state consists of the decision variables. It should include every variable needed to describe our progress and enough information to determine the next state.

Each state corresponds to a subproblem. We use a \(dp\) table to store their solutions, with one dimension of the \(dp\) table for each independent state variable. In essence, the \(dp\) table maps each state to the solution of its subproblem.

Step 2: Identify optimal substructure and derive the recurrence

State \([i, j]\) can be reached only from the cell above, \([i-1, j]\), or the cell to the left, \([i, j-1]\). This gives the optimal substructure: the minimum path sum to \([i, j]\) depends on the smaller of the minimum path sums to \([i, j-1]\) and \([i-1, j]\).

This gives the recurrence shown below:

\[ dp[i, j] = \min(dp[i-1, j], dp[i, j-1]) + grid[i, j] \]

Figure 14-12   Optimal substructure and the recurrence

Note

Using the \(dp\) table definition, examine how the original problem relates to its subproblems. Look for a way to construct an optimal solution from optimal subproblem solutions. That is the optimal substructure.

Once we identify the optimal substructure, we can use it to write the recurrence.

Step 3: Determine the boundary conditions and the order of computation

A state in the first row can only be reached from its left, and a state in the first column only from above. The first row \(i = 0\) and first column \(j = 0\) therefore give the boundary conditions.

As shown below, each cell depends on the cells to its left and above it. We traverse the matrix with nested loops: the outer loop visits the rows and the inner loop the columns.

Figure 14-13   Boundary conditions and order of computation

Note

Boundary conditions initialize the \(dp\) table in dynamic programming and prune branches in search.

Choose an order that ensures every smaller subproblem a state depends on has already been solved correctly when we calculate that state.

We now have enough information to write the dynamic programming code directly. Since breaking a problem down is a top-down process, however, it is often more natural to implement the approaches in this order: brute-force search \(\rightarrow\) memoized search \(\rightarrow\) dynamic programming.

items.title: 1.   Method 1: Brute-force search
items.text:
Start the search at state \([i, j]\) and recursively break it down into smaller states \([i-1, j]\) and \([i, j-1]\). The recursive function has the following parts.

  • Recursive parameters: the state \([i, j]\).
  • Return value: the minimum path sum \(dp[i, j]\) from \([0, 0]\) to \([i, j]\).
  • Base case: when \(i = 0\) and \(j = 0\), return the cost \(grid[0, 0]\).
  • Pruning: if \(i < 0\) or \(j < 0\), an index is out of bounds. Return cost \(+\infty\) to indicate an infeasible path.

Here is the implementation:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_path_sum.py
def min_path_sum_dfs(grid: list[list[int]], i: int, j: int) -> int:
    """Minimum path sum with brute-force search"""
    # Stop searching at the top-left cell
    if i == 0 and j == 0:
        return grid[0][0]
    # Return a cost of +∞ if either index is out of bounds
    if i < 0 or j < 0:
        return inf
    # Find the minimum path costs from the top left to (i-1, j) and (i, j-1)
    up = min_path_sum_dfs(grid, i - 1, j)
    left = min_path_sum_dfs(grid, i, j - 1)
    # Return the minimum path cost from the top left to (i, j)
    return min(left, up) + grid[i][j]

/* Minimum path sum with brute-force search */
int minPathSumDFS(vector<vector<int>> &grid, int i, int j) {
    // Stop searching at the top-left cell
    if (i == 0 && j == 0) {
        return grid[0][0];
    }
    // Return a cost of +∞ if either index is out of bounds
    if (i < 0 || j < 0) {

    int up = minPathSumDFS(grid, i - 1, j);
    int left = minPathSumDFS(grid, i, j - 1);

    return min(left, up) != INT_MAX ? min(left, up) + grid[i][j] : INT_MAX;
}

The recursion tree rooted at \(dp[2, 1]\) below contains overlapping subproblems. Their number grows rapidly with the size of the grid grid.

Subproblems overlap because multiple paths can lead from the top left to the same cell.

Figure 14-14   Recursion tree for brute-force search

Each state offers two moves, down and right. Reaching the bottom right from the top left takes \(m + n - 2\) moves, so the worst-case time complexity is \(O(2^{m + n})\), where \(n\) and \(m\) are the numbers of rows and columns. This estimate ignores the restriction at the grid boundary, where just one move remains, so the actual number of paths is smaller.

items.title: 2.   Method 2: Memoized search
items.text:
Create a cache mem the same size as the grid grid. Store each subproblem's solution in it so we can prune repeated searches:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_path_sum.py
def min_path_sum_dfs_mem(
    grid: list[list[int]], mem: list[list[int]], i: int, j: int
) -> int:
    """Minimum path sum with memoized search"""
    # Stop searching at the top-left cell
    if i == 0 and j == 0:
        return grid[0][0]
    # Return a cost of +∞ if either index is out of bounds
    if i < 0 or j < 0:
        return inf
    # Return the cached result if available
    if mem[i][j] != -1:
        return mem[i][j]
    # Minimum path costs for the cells to the left and above
    up = min_path_sum_dfs_mem(grid, mem, i - 1, j)
    left = min_path_sum_dfs_mem(grid, mem, i, j - 1)
    # Cache and return the minimum path cost from the top left to (i, j)
    mem[i][j] = min(left, up) + grid[i][j]
    return mem[i][j]

    if (i < 0 || j < 0) {
        return Infinity;
    }
    // Return the cached result if available
    if (mem[i][j] !== -1) {
        return mem[i][j];
    }
    // Minimum path costs for the cells to the left and above
    const up = minPathSumDFSMem(grid, mem, i - 1, j);
    const left = minPathSumDFSMem(grid, mem, i, j - 1);
    // Cache and return the minimum path cost from the top left to (i, j)
    mem[i][j] = Math.min(left, up) + grid[i][j];
    return mem[i][j];
}

items.text:
Here is the iterative dynamic programming solution:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_path_sum.py
def min_path_sum_dp(grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    """Minimum path sum with dynamic programming"""
    n, m = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [[0] * m for _ in range(n)]
    dp[0][0] = grid[0][0]
    # State transitions for the first row
    for j in range(1, m):
        dp[0][j] = dp[0][j - 1] + grid[0][j]
    # State transitions for the first column
    for i in range(1, n):
        dp[i][0] = dp[i - 1][0] + grid[i][0]
    # State transitions for the remaining rows and columns
    for i in range(1, n):
        for j in range(1, m):
            dp[i][j] = min(dp[i][j - 1], dp[i - 1][j]) + grid[i][j]
    return dp[n - 1][m - 1]
