items.title: 4.   Space optimization
items.text:
Each cell depends only on the cells to its left and above it, so a single row of storage suffices for the \(dp\) table.

Because the dp array holds only one row of states, we cannot initialize the entire first column in advance. Instead, we update its entry as we visit each row:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby min_path_sum.py
def min_path_sum_dp_comp(grid: list[list[int]]) -> int:
    """Minimum path sum with space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n, m = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [0] * m
    # State transitions for the first row
    dp[0] = grid[0][0]
    for j in range(1, m):
        dp[j] = dp[j - 1] + grid[0][j]
    # State transitions for the remaining rows
    for i in range(1, n):
        # State transitions for the first column
        dp[0] = dp[0] + grid[i][0]
        # State transitions for the remaining columns
        for j in range(1, m):
            dp[j] = min(dp[j - 1], dp[j]) + grid[i][j]
    return dp[m - 1]

items.title: 14.6   The edit distance problem
items.text:
Edit distance, also called Levenshtein distance, is the fewest edits needed to transform one string into another. It is commonly used in information retrieval and natural language processing to measure the similarity of two sequences.

Question

Given two strings \(s\) and \(t\), return the minimum number of edits needed to transform \(s\) into \(t\).

You may insert one character, delete one character, or replace one character with any character.

As shown below, changing kitten to sitting takes 3 edits: 2 replacements and 1 insertion. Changing hello to algo also takes 3 edits: 2 replacements and 1 deletion.

Figure 14-27   Edit distance examples

A decision tree provides a natural model for edit distance. Each node is a string, and each edge represents a decision to make one edit.

As the figure shows, without restrictions each node can have many outgoing edges, one for each possible edit. There are therefore many paths from hello to algo.

In the decision tree, our goal is the shortest path from node hello to node algo.

Figure 14-28   Modeling edit distance with a decision tree

items.title: 1.   A dynamic programming approach
items.text:
Step 1: Identify the decision at each step and define the state and \(dp\) table

At each step, we choose an edit to apply to string \(s\).

To form subproblems, we want each editing decision to reduce the size of the remaining problem. Let \(s\) and \(t\) have lengths \(n\) and \(m\), respectively. Consider their final characters \(s[n-1]\) and \(t[m-1]\).

  • If \(s[n-1]\) and \(t[m-1]\) match, skip both and move on to \(s[n-2]\) and \(t[m-2]\).
  • If \(s[n-1]\) and \(t[m-1]\) differ, we need to edit \(s\) (insert, delete, or replace a character) to resolve the mismatch at the end. We can then skip the resolved characters and work on a smaller problem.

Each editing decision on \(s\) changes which characters in \(s\) and \(t\) remain to be matched. The state therefore identifies the characters currently under consideration in \(s\) and \(t\) by their positions \(i\) and \(j\). Write the state as \([i, j]\).

The subproblem for state \([i, j]\) is the minimum number of edits to change the first \(i\) characters of \(s\) into the first \(j\) characters of \(t\).

This gives us a two-dimensional \(dp\) table of size \((n+1) \times (m+1)\).

Step 2: Identify optimal substructure and derive the recurrence

For subproblem \(dp[i, j]\), the two prefixes end in \(s[i-1]\) and \(t[j-1]\). The three possible edits give the cases shown below.

  1. Insert \(t[j-1]\) after \(s[i-1]\). The remaining subproblem is \(dp[i, j-1]\).
  2. Delete \(s[i-1]\). The remaining subproblem is \(dp[i-1, j]\).
  3. Replace \(s[i-1]\) with \(t[j-1]\). The remaining subproblem is \(dp[i-1, j-1]\).

Figure 14-29   State transitions for edit distance

The optimal substructure now follows: the minimum edit count \(dp[i, j]\) is the smallest of \(dp[i, j-1]\), \(dp[i-1, j]\), and \(dp[i-1, j-1]\), plus \(1\) for the current edit. The recurrence is:

\[ dp[i, j] = \min(dp[i, j-1], dp[i-1, j], dp[i-1, j-1]) + 1 \]

When \(s[i-1]\) and \(t[j-1]\) match, the current character needs no edit. In that case the recurrence is:

\[ dp[i, j] = dp[i-1, j-1] \]

Step 3: Determine the boundary conditions and the order of computation

When both strings are empty, the edit count is \(0\), so \(dp[0, 0] = 0\). When \(s\) is empty and \(t\) is not, the minimum edit count is the length of \(t\), giving the first row \(dp[0, j] = j\). When \(s\) is nonempty and \(t\) is empty, the minimum count is the length of \(s\), giving the first column \(dp[i, 0] = i\).

The recurrence for \(dp[i, j]\) depends on the cells to the left, above, and diagonally above to the left. Two forward loops can therefore fill the entire \(dp\) table.

items.title: 2.   Implementation
3.   Space optimization
items.text:
State \(dp[i,j]\) depends on \(dp[i-1, j]\) above, \(dp[i, j-1]\) to the left, and \(dp[i-1, j-1]\) at the upper left. With one row of storage, forward traversal loses the upper-left value \(dp[i-1, j-1]\), while reverse traversal cannot compute \(dp[i, j-1]\) in time. Neither order works on its own.

Save the upper-left value \(dp[i-1, j-1]\) in a variable leftup. That leaves only the left and upper entries to track in the row, just as in unbounded knapsack, so we can traverse forward:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby edit_distance.py
def edit_distance_dp_comp(s: str, t: str) -> int:
    """Edit distance with space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n, m = len(s), len(t)
    dp = [0] * (m + 1)
    # State transitions for the first row
    for j in range(1, m + 1):
        dp[j] = j
    # State transitions for the remaining rows
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # State transitions for the first column
        leftup = dp[0]  # Save dp[i-1, j-1] temporarily
        dp[0] += 1
        # State transitions for the remaining columns
        for j in range(1, m + 1):
            temp = dp[j]
            if s[i - 1] == t[j - 1]:
                # Skip both characters if they match
                dp[j] = leftup
            else:
                # Minimum edits = 1 + the smallest remaining edit count after an insertion, deletion, or replacement
                dp[j] = min(dp[j - 1], dp[j], leftup) + 1
            leftup = temp  # Update the saved value to hold dp[i-1, j-1] for the next iteration
    return dp[m]

items.title: 1.   When should you use dynamic programming?
items.text:
A student says, “Whenever you can write a recurrence, you should use dynamic programming.” For each task below, decide whether to use dynamic programming, backtracking, or a loop or mathematical formula without a dp table. Give one key reason for each choice.

  1. Find the fewest coins needed to make 6 using denominations [1, 3, 4]. You can reuse each denomination.
  2. List all permutations of [1, 2, 3].

  3. Calculate \(1 + 2 + \dots + n\).

    For any task where you chose dynamic programming, also explain what dp[i] represents.

Sample answer

  1. Use dynamic programming. Let dp[i] be the fewest coins needed to make amount i. For each coin of value c no greater than i, consider dp[i-c] + 1 as a candidate, then take the minimum of these candidates. Different choices lead back to the same amounts, and an optimal solution for a larger amount can be built from optimal solutions for smaller amounts. For amount 6, the answer is 2 coins: 3 + 3.

  2. Use backtracking. The task asks for all 6 permutations, one by one. Backtracking systematically makes a choice, continues the search, then undoes the choice and explores another branch. Any method that outputs the permutations has to enumerate them.

  3. Use a loop or the arithmetic series formula. Although we can write S(i) = S(i-1) + i, the calculation of S(i) depends on just one smaller sum, S(i-1). Each partial sum is computed only once. There are no overlapping subproblems, so we do not need a dp table. A recurrence alone does not mean dynamic programming is necessary.

items.title: 2.   How do you calculate one cell in the knapsack table?
items.text:
In a 0-1 knapsack problem, the item weights are wgt = [1, 2, 3], their values are val = [5, 11, 15], and the knapsack capacity is 4. dp[i][c] denotes the maximum value achievable using only the first \(i\) items with a capacity limit of \(c\). You do not need to fill the knapsack exactly.

Calculate just the state dp[3][4]. You know that dp[2][4] = 16 and dp[2][1] = 5.

  1. If you skip item 3, what value do you get?
  2. If you take item 3, how much capacity remains, and what value do you get?
  3. What should dp[3][4] be? Which items give that value?
Sample answer

  1. If you skip item 3, keep the result for the first two items. The candidate value is dp[2][4] = 16.

  2. Item 3 weighs 3. Taking it leaves capacity \(4-3=1\), so the candidate value is dp[2][1] + 15 = 5 + 15 = 20.

  3. Comparing 16 and 20 gives dp[3][4] = 20. This corresponds to taking items 1 and 3, with total weight \(1+3=4\) and total value \(5+15=20\).

    Calculating this state illustrates one take-or-skip decision in the 0-1 knapsack problem.

items.title: 3.   In what order should you update knapsack capacities?
items.text:
A 0-1 knapsack problem has just one item, with weight 2 and value 5. The knapsack capacity is 4. You can take each item at most once. The one-dimensional array starts at dp = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0].

A student processes this item by updating capacities from 2 to 4 in order:

  • Updating dp[2] gives 5.
  • Updating dp[3] also gives 5.
  • To update dp[4], the student uses the newly computed dp[2], giving dp[4] = 10.
  1. Is dp[4] = 10 correct? Why or why not?
  2. Given that you can take each item at most once, what should dp[4] be?
  3. When processing each item, should you update capacities in descending or ascending order? What problem does that prevent?
Sample answer

  1. The result is incorrect. A value of 10 means taking the item worth 5 twice, which violates the rule that each item can be taken at most once.

  2. The knapsack can hold at most the one available item, so the correct value of dp[4] is 5.

  3. Update capacities in descending order: 4, then 3, then 2. That way, when calculating dp[c], you read the value of dp[c-2] from before you processed the current item, so you cannot reuse that item in the same round.

items.title: 1.   Counting ways to climb stairs
items.text:
A staircase has n stairs. Each move takes you up either 1 or 2 stairs, and you must land exactly on stair n. How many different ways can you climb the staircase? Assume n >= 1. Two ways differ only in their sequence of one- and two-stair moves. Use a one-dimensional dynamic programming array. For this exercise, keep the full array before trying the space optimization that retains just two states.

Hints
  1. The last move to stair i must cover either 1 or 2 stairs
  2. This gives dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]
  3. Handle n = 1 and n = 2 first, then fill the table starting at stair 3

items.title: 2.   0-1 knapsack
items.text:
Given arrays wgt and val of equal length, item i has positive integer weight wgt[i] and nonnegative integer value val[i]. The knapsack capacity cap is a nonnegative integer. You can take each item at most once. With the total weight limited to cap, find the maximum total value you can pack. Use one-dimensional dynamic programming.

Hints
  1. Initialize an array dp of length cap + 1, where dp[c] is the maximum value for a capacity limit of c
  2. When processing item i, compare dp[c] for skipping it with dp[c-wgt[i]] + val[i] for taking it
  3. Update capacities from largest to smallest to avoid taking the current item repeatedly in the same round

items.title: 14.1   Introduction to dynamic programming
items.text:
Dynamic programming is an important algorithmic paradigm. It breaks a problem into smaller subproblems and stores their solutions to avoid repeated work, often saving a great deal of time.

We'll start with a classic example, solve it by brute-force backtracking, identify the overlapping subproblems, and gradually derive a more efficient dynamic programming solution.

Climbing stairs

A staircase has \(n\) stairs. Each move takes you up either \(1\) or \(2\) stairs. How many ways can you reach the top?

As Figure 14-1 shows, a staircase with \(3\) stairs has \(3\) ways to reach the top.

Figure 14-1   Number of ways to reach stair 3

We want the number of ways, so we can enumerate all possibilities by backtracking. Think of climbing as a series of choices. Start on the ground and choose to climb \(1\) or \(2\) stairs at each move. Add \(1\) to the count whenever you reach the top, and prune moves that would overshoot it. Here is the code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_backtrack.py
def backtrack(choices: list[int], state: int, n: int, res: list[int]) -> int:
    """Backtracking"""
    # Count one more way when we reach stair n
    if state == n:
        res[0] += 1
    # Iterate over all choices
    for choice in choices:
        # Prune moves that would overshoot stair n
        if state + choice > n:
            continue
        # Try a choice and update the state
        backtrack(choices, state + choice, n, res)
        # Undo the choice

def climbing_stairs_backtrack(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs with backtracking"""
    choices = [1, 2]  # Each move can climb 1 or 2 stairs
    state = 0  # Start at stair 0
    res = [0]  # Store the number of ways in res[0]
    backtrack(choices, state, n, res)
    return res[0]

items.title: 14.1.1   Method 1: Brute-force search
items.text:
Backtracking usually does not explicitly split the problem into subproblems. It treats the solution as a sequence of decisions and searches for all possible solutions by trying choices and pruning branches.

We can also view the problem in terms of subproblems. Let \(dp[i]\) be the number of ways to reach stair \(i\). Then \(dp[i]\) is the original problem, with subproblems including the following:

\[ dp[i-1], dp[i-2], \dots, dp[2], dp[1] \]

Each move climbs \(1\) or \(2\) stairs. If we are now on stair \(i\), we must previously have been on stair \(i - 1\) or \(i - 2\). In other words, only stairs \(i -1\) and \(i - 2\) can lead directly to stair \(i\).

This gives an important result: the number of ways to reach stair \(i - 1\) plus the number of ways to reach stair \(i - 2\) equals the number of ways to reach stair \(i\). In symbols:

\[ dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2] \]

The stair-climbing subproblems are related by a recurrence, and we can build the original solution from the subproblem solutions. Figure 14-2 illustrates this relationship.

Figure 14-2   Recurrence for the number of ways

The recurrence gives us a brute-force search. Start at \(dp[n]\) and recursively break each larger problem into the sum of two smaller ones until reaching the smallest subproblems \(dp[1]\) and \(dp[2]\). Their solutions are known: \(dp[1] = 1\) and \(dp[2] = 2\). There are \(1\) and \(2\) ways to reach stairs \(1\) and \(2\), respectively.

Like the standard backtracking code, the following code performs a depth-first search, but it is more concise:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_dfs.py
def dfs(i: int) -> int:
    """Search"""
    # Return the known value for dp[1] or dp[2]
    if i == 1 or i == 2:
        return i
    # dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]
    count = dfs(i - 1) + dfs(i - 2)
    return count

def climbing_stairs_dfs(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs with search"""
    return dfs(n)

Figure 14-3 shows the recursion tree for brute-force search. For \(dp[n]\), the tree has depth \(n\) and time complexity \(O(2^n)\). Exponential growth is explosive: even a moderately large \(n\) can mean a long wait.

Figure 14-3   Recursion tree for climbing stairs

In the figure, overlapping subproblems cause the exponential time complexity. For example, \(dp[9]\) splits into \(dp[8]\) and \(dp[7]\), while \(dp[8]\) splits into \(dp[7]\) and \(dp[6]\). Both include \(dp[7]\).

Those subproblems contain still smaller overlapping subproblems, and so on down the tree. These repeated calculations consume most of the computational effort.

items.title: 14.1.2   Method 2: Memoized search
items.text:
For better efficiency, we want to solve each overlapping subproblem just once. We can store each result in an array mem and prune repeated subproblems during the search.

  1. The first time we calculate \(dp[i]\), store it in mem[i] for later use.
  2. When we need \(dp[i]\) again, read the result from mem[i] and avoid solving the same subproblem again.

Here is the code:

items.title: 14.1.3   Method 3: Dynamic programming
items.text:
Memoized search works from the top down. Start with the original problem (the root) and recursively split larger subproblems into smaller ones until reaching the smallest subproblems with known answers (the leaves). As the calls return, combine their solutions level by level to solve the original problem.

Conversely, dynamic programming works from the bottom up. Start with the solutions to the smallest subproblems and iteratively build solutions to larger ones until reaching the original problem.

This dynamic programming approach requires no backtracking. A loop suffices, with no need for recursion. In the code below, an array dp stores the subproblem solutions, much as the array mem did in memoized search:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby climbing_stairs_dp.py
def climbing_stairs_dp(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs with dynamic programming"""
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return n
    # Initialize the dp table to store subproblem solutions
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    # Base cases: set the solutions to the smallest subproblems
    dp[1], dp[2] = 1, 2
    # State transition: solve larger subproblems using smaller ones
    for i in range(3, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + dp[i - 2]
    return dp[n]

Figure 14-5   Counting ways to climb stairs with dynamic programming

Like backtracking, dynamic programming uses a state to represent a particular stage of a solution. Each state corresponds to a subproblem and its local optimum. In stair climbing, for example, the state is the current stair number \(i\).

This example illustrates several common dynamic programming terms.

  • The array dp is the dp table. Its entry \(dp[i]\) holds the solution to the subproblem for state \(i\).
  • The states for the smallest subproblems (stairs \(1\) and \(2\)) are the initial states.
  • The recurrence \(dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]\) is called the state transition equation.

items.title: 14.1.4   Space optimization
items.text:
Notice that because \(dp[i]\) depends only on \(dp[i-1]\) and \(dp[i-2]\), we do not need an array dp to store all the subproblem solutions. We can carry just two variables forward, as shown here:

def climbing_stairs_dp_comp(n: int) -> int:
    """Climbing stairs with space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    if n == 1 or n == 2:
        return n
    a, b = 1, 2
    for _ in range(3, n + 1):
        a, b = b, a + b
    return b

In dynamic programming, a state often depends on only a limited number of earlier states. Keeping just those states reduces the dimension of the table and saves memory. This space optimization is called using rolling variables or a rolling array.

items.title: 14.4   The 0-1 knapsack problem
items.text:
Knapsack is a good introduction to dynamic programming and one of its most common problem types. Variants include 0-1 knapsack, unbounded knapsack, and bounded knapsack.

We'll start with the most common variant, 0-1 knapsack.

Question

Given \(n\) items, where item \(i\) weighs \(wgt[i-1]\) and has value \(val[i-1]\), and a knapsack of capacity \(cap\), find the maximum total value you can pack without exceeding capacity. Each item can be taken at most once.

In Figure 14-17, item numbers \(i\) start at \(1\), while array indices start at \(0\). Thus item \(i\) has weight \(wgt[i-1]\) and value \(val[i-1]\).

Figure 14-17   Example input for 0-1 knapsack

We can view 0-1 knapsack as \(n\) successive decisions. Each item has two choices, skip or take, so the problem fits a decision tree.

The goal is to maximize the value packed within a capacity limit, making dynamic programming a likely fit.

Step 1: Identify the decision at each step and define the state and \(dp\) table

Skipping an item leaves the available capacity unchanged. Taking it reduces that capacity. We can therefore define the state by the current item number \(i\) and available capacity \(c\), written \([i, c]\).

The subproblem for state \([i, c]\) is the maximum value obtainable from the first \(i\) items with a knapsack of capacity \(c\). Denote this value by \(dp[i, c]\).

We want \(dp[n, cap]\), so we need a two-dimensional \(dp\) table of size \((n+1) \times (cap+1)\).

Step 2: Identify optimal substructure and derive the recurrence

After deciding on item \(i\), we have a subproblem involving the first \(i-1\) items. There are two cases.

  • Skip item \(i\). Capacity stays the same, leaving state \([i-1, c]\).
  • Take item \(i\). Capacity decreases by \(wgt[i-1]\), value increases by \(val[i-1]\), and the remaining state is \([i-1, c-wgt[i-1]]\).

This gives the optimal substructure: the maximum value \(dp[i, c]\) is the larger of the values for skipping item \(i\) and taking item \(i\). The recurrence is:

\[ dp[i, c] = \max(dp[i-1, c], dp[i-1, c - wgt[i-1]] + val[i-1]) \]

If the current item's weight \(wgt[i - 1]\) exceeds the remaining capacity \(c\), we can only skip it.

Step 3: Determine the boundary conditions and the order of computation

With no items or a capacity of \(0\), the maximum value is \(0\). Thus the first column \(dp[i, 0]\) and first row \(dp[0, c]\) both contain \(0\).

The current state \([i, c]\) depends on \([i-1, c]\) directly above and \([i-1, c-wgt[i-1]]\) above and to the left. We can therefore traverse the entire \(dp\) table in increasing order with two nested loops.

We'll now implement brute-force search, memoized search, and dynamic programming in that order.

items.title: 1.   Method 1: Brute-force search
items.text:
The search has the following components.

  • Recursive parameters: the state \([i, c]\).
  • Return value: the subproblem solution \(dp[i, c]\).
  • Base case: when we run out of items (\(i = 0\)) or the remaining capacity is \(0\), stop recursing and return value \(0\).
  • Pruning: if the current item weighs more than the remaining capacity, we can only skip it.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby knapsack.py
def knapsack_dfs(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], i: int, c: int) -> int:
    """0-1 knapsack with brute-force search"""
    # Return a value of 0 if all items have been considered or no capacity remains
    if i == 0 or c == 0:
        return 0
    # If the item exceeds the remaining capacity, we can only skip it
    if wgt[i - 1] > c:
        return knapsack_dfs(wgt, val, i - 1, c)
    # Compute the maximum values for skipping and taking item i
    no = knapsack_dfs(wgt, val, i - 1, c)
    yes = knapsack_dfs(wgt, val, i - 1, c - wgt[i - 1]) + val[i - 1]
    # Return the larger of the two values
    return max(no, yes)

items.title: 2.   Method 2: Memoized search
items.text:
To solve each overlapping subproblem just once, store its solution in a cache mem, where mem[i][c] corresponds to \(dp[i, c]\).

With memoization, time complexity depends on the number of subproblems, giving \(O(n \times cap)\). Here is the implementation:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby knapsack.py
def knapsack_dfs_mem(
    wgt: list[int], val: list[int], mem: list[list[int]], i: int, c: int
) -> int:
    """0-1 knapsack with memoized search"""
    # Return a value of 0 if all items have been considered or no capacity remains
    if i == 0 or c == 0:
        return 0
    # Return the cached result if available
    if mem[i][c] != -1:
        return mem[i][c]
    # If the item exceeds the remaining capacity, we can only skip it
    if wgt[i - 1] > c:
        return knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c)
    # Compute the maximum values for skipping and taking item i
    no = knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c)
    yes = knapsack_dfs_mem(wgt, val, mem, i - 1, c - wgt[i - 1]) + val[i - 1]
    # Cache and return the larger of the two values
    mem[i][c] = max(no, yes)
    return mem[i][c]

/* 0-1 knapsack with memoized search */
fun knapsackDFSMem(
    wgt: IntArray,
    _val: IntArray,
    mem: Array<IntArray>,
    i: Int,
    c: Int
): Int {
    // Return a value of 0 if all items have been considered or no capacity remains
    if (i == 0 || c == 0) {
        return 0
    }
    // Return the cached result if available
    if (mem[i][c] != -1) {
        return mem[i][c]
    }
    // If the item exceeds the remaining capacity, we can only skip it
    if (wgt[i - 1] > c) {
        return knapsackDFSMem(wgt, _val, mem, i - 1, c)
    }
    // Compute the maximum values for skipping and taking item i
    val no = knapsackDFSMem(wgt, _val, mem, i - 1, c)
    val yes = knapsackDFSMem(wgt, _val, mem, i - 1, c - wgt[i - 1]) + _val[i - 1]
    // Cache and return the larger of the two values
    mem[i][c] = max(no, yes)
    return mem[i][c]
}

Dynamic programming fills the \(dp\) table by applying state transitions, as in the following code:

def knapsack_dp(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """0-1 knapsack with dynamic programming"""
    n = len(wgt)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [[0] * (cap + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # State transition
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for c in range(1, cap + 1):
            if wgt[i - 1] > c:
                # Skip item i if its weight exceeds the capacity
                dp[i][c] = dp[i - 1][c]
            else:
                # Take the larger value from skipping or taking item i
                dp[i][c] = max(dp[i - 1][c], dp[i - 1][c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1])
    return dp[n][cap]

items.title: 4.   Space optimization
items.text:
Each state depends only on the previous row, so we can alternate between two arrays and reduce space complexity from \(O(n \times cap)\) to \(O(cap)\).

Can we go further and use just one array? Each state comes from a cell directly above or above and to the left. With one array, when we start row \(i\), the array still holds the states from row \(i-1\).

  • When capacities are processed in increasing order, the previous-row value \(dp[i-1, c-wgt[i-1]]\) needed for \(dp[i, c]\) may already have been overwritten. This can count the same item more than once.
  • Reverse order preserves the old values until they are needed, so the transition works correctly.

The figure shows one array changing from row \(i = 1\) to row \(i = 2\). Consider how forward and reverse traversal differ.

<1><2><3><4><5><6>

Figure 14-21   Solving 0-1 knapsack with a space-optimized dp table

def knapsack_dp_comp(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """0-1 knapsack with space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n = len(wgt)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [0] * (cap + 1)
    # State transition
    for i in range(1, n + 1):

                # Skip item i if its weight exceeds the capacity
                dp[c] = dp[c]
            else:
                # Take the larger value from skipping or taking item i
                dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1])
    return dp[cap]

items.title: 1.   Key points
items.text:
• Dynamic programming breaks a problem into subproblems and stores their solutions to avoid repeated work and improve efficiency.
  • Given enough time, backtracking (brute-force search) can solve any dynamic programming problem. The many overlapping subproblems in its recursion tree make it highly inefficient. A cache stores solved subproblems so that each overlapping subproblem is calculated only once.
  • Memoized search is a top-down recursive approach. Its bottom-up dynamic programming counterpart iterates through a recurrence, much like filling a table. When a state depends only on nearby states, we can remove a dimension from the \(dp\) table to reduce space complexity.
  • Breaking a problem into subproblems is a general algorithmic technique. Divide and conquer, dynamic programming, and backtracking use it in different ways.
  • Dynamic programming problems have three main properties: overlapping subproblems, optimal substructure, and the no-aftereffect property.
  • A problem has optimal substructure if an optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions to its subproblems.
  • The no-aftereffect property means that what can happen next depends only on the current state, regardless of how we reached it. Many combinatorial optimization problems lack this property and cannot be solved quickly with dynamic programming.

Knapsack problems

  • Knapsack is a classic dynamic programming problem. Its variants include 0-1, unbounded, and bounded knapsack.
  • In 0-1 knapsack, the state value is the maximum value from the first \(i\) items with capacity \(c\). The choices of skipping or taking the current item reveal the optimal substructure and give the recurrence. When reducing space, traverse capacities in reverse because each state needs values directly above and to the upper left. This preserves the upper-left values until they are read.
  • Unbounded knapsack allows unlimited copies of each item, so taking an item leads to a different transition from 0-1 knapsack. Each state depends on the cells above and to its left, so the space-optimized version traverses forward.
  • Coin change is a variant of unbounded knapsack. We minimize the coin count instead of maximizing value, so \(\max()\) becomes \(\min()\) in the recurrence. We must make the target amount exactly rather than stay within a capacity limit, so \(amt + 1\) marks an unreachable amount.
  • Coin change II counts coin combinations rather than minimizing the number of coins. The recurrence replaces \(\min()\) with addition.

The edit distance problem

  • Edit distance (Levenshtein distance) measures string similarity. It is the fewest insertions, deletions, and replacements needed to change one string into another.
  • An edit distance state gives the minimum edits to change the first \(i\) characters of \(s\) into the first \(j\) characters of \(t\). When \(s[i-1] \ne t[j-1]\), the three choices are insertion, deletion, and replacement. Each leaves a corresponding subproblem, giving the optimal substructure and recurrence. When \(s[i-1] = t[j-1]\), the current character needs no edit.
  • An edit distance state depends on the cells immediately above, to the left, and diagonally above to the left. With one row, neither forward nor reverse traversal alone preserves all three. Saving the upper-left value in a variable leaves the same row dependencies as unbounded knapsack, allowing forward traversal.

items.title: 14.5   The unbounded knapsack problem
items.text: In this section, we'll solve another common knapsack problem, unbounded knapsack, and explore a special case: coin change.

items.title: 14.5.1   The unbounded knapsack problem
items.text:
Question

Given \(n\) item types, where type \(i\) has weight \(wgt[i-1]\) and value \(val[i-1]\), and a knapsack of capacity \(cap\), you can take multiple copies of each type. Find the maximum total value you can pack within the capacity limit. Figure 14-22 shows an example.

Figure 14-22   Example input for unbounded knapsack

items.title: 1.   A dynamic programming approach
items.text:
Unbounded knapsack closely resembles 0-1 knapsack. The only difference is that a type can be taken any number of times.

  • In 0-1 knapsack, each item is available once. After packing item \(i\), we can choose only from the first \(i-1\) items.
  • In unbounded knapsack, each type has an unlimited supply. After packing item \(i\), we can still choose from the first \(i\) types.

Under these rules, state \([i, c]\) has two possible transitions.

  • Skip item \(i\). As in 0-1 knapsack, the remaining state is \([i-1, c]\).
  • Take item \(i\). Unlike 0-1 knapsack, the remaining state is \([i, c-wgt[i-1]]\).

The recurrence therefore becomes:

\[ dp[i, c] = \max(dp[i-1, c], dp[i, c - wgt[i-1]] + val[i-1]) \]

items.title: 2.   Implementation
items.text:
Comparing the code for the two problems, just one index in the transition changes from \(i-1\) to \(i\). The rest is identical:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby unbounded_knapsack.py
def unbounded_knapsack_dp(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """Unbounded knapsack with dynamic programming"""
    n = len(wgt)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [[0] * (cap + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # State transition
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for c in range(1, cap + 1):
            if wgt[i - 1] > c:
                # Skip item i if its weight exceeds the capacity
                dp[i][c] = dp[i - 1][c]
            else:
                # Take the larger value from skipping or taking item i
                dp[i][c] = max(dp[i - 1][c], dp[i][c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1])
    return dp[n][cap]

items.title: 3.   Space optimization
items.text:
Each state depends on the cells to its left and above it. After reducing space, traverse each row of the \(dp\) table in forward order.

This is the opposite of the order for 0-1 knapsack. Figure 14-23 illustrates the difference.

<1><2><3><4><5><6>

Figure 14-23   Solving unbounded knapsack with a space-optimized dp table

To implement this, simply remove the first dimension of the array dp:

def unbounded_knapsack_dp_comp(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """Unbounded knapsack with space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n = len(wgt)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [0] * (cap + 1)
    # State transition
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # Iterate in ascending order
        for c in range(1, cap + 1):
            if wgt[i - 1] > c:
                # Skip item i if its weight exceeds the capacity
                dp[c] = dp[c]
            else:
                # Take the larger value from skipping or taking item i
                dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c - wgt[i - 1]] + val[i - 1])
    return dp[cap]

items.title: 14.5.2   The coin change problem
items.text:
Knapsack represents a large family of dynamic programming problems with many variants, including coin change.

Question

Given \(n\) coin types, where type \(i\) has denomination \(coins[i - 1]\), and a target amount \(amt\), each denomination can be used repeatedly. Find the fewest coins that make the target amount. Return \(-1\) if the amount cannot be made. Figure 14-24 shows an example.

Figure 14-24   Example input for coin change

items.title: 1.   A dynamic programming approach
items.text:
Coin change can be viewed as a special case of unbounded knapsack. The two problems correspond in the following ways and differ in their goals.

  • We can map one problem to the other: items correspond to coins, item weights to denominations, and knapsack capacity to the target amount.
  • Their objectives point in opposite directions. Unbounded knapsack maximizes item value, while coin change minimizes coin count.
  • Unbounded knapsack asks for a solution within the capacity limit. Coin change requires the target amount exactly.

Step 1: Identify the decision at each step and define the state and \(dp\) table

The subproblem for state \([i, a]\) is the fewest coins from the first \(i\) types that can make amount \(a\). Write its solution as \(dp[i, a]\).

The two-dimensional \(dp\) table has dimensions \((n+1) \times (amt+1)\).

Step 2: Identify optimal substructure and derive the recurrence

The recurrence differs from unbounded knapsack in two ways.

  • We want a minimum, so replace the operator \(\max()\) with \(\min()\).
  • We optimize the number of coins rather than item value, so taking a coin contributes \(+1\).
\[ dp[i, a] = \min(dp[i-1, a], dp[i, a - coins[i-1]] + 1) \]

Step 3: Determine the boundary conditions and the order of computation

For target amount \(0\), the minimum number of coins is \(0\). Thus all entries \(dp[i, 0]\) in the first column equal \(0\).

With no coins, no target amount \(> 0\) can be made. Such a state has no valid solution. To let \(\min()\) ignore invalid candidates, we could represent them by \(+ \infty\), setting the first-row entries \(dp[0, a]\) for positive amounts to \(+ \infty\).

items.title: 2.   Implementation
items.text:
Most programming languages do not provide an integer value for \(+ \infty\). Substituting the largest int value can cause overflow in the recurrence's \(+ 1\) operation.

Instead, use \(amt + 1\) for an invalid solution: making amount \(amt\) can require at most \(amt\) coins. Before returning, check whether \(dp[n, amt]\) equals \(amt + 1\). If it does, return \(-1\) to indicate the target is unreachable. Here is the code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby coin_change.py
def coin_change_dp(coins: list[int], amt: int) -> int:
    """Coin change with dynamic programming"""
    n = len(coins)
    MAX = amt + 1
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [[0] * (amt + 1) for _ in range(n + 1)]
    # State transitions for the first row and column
    for a in range(1, amt + 1):
        dp[0][a] = MAX
    # State transitions for the remaining rows and columns
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        for a in range(1, amt + 1):
            if coins[i - 1] > a:
                # Skip coin i if its value exceeds the target amount
                dp[i][a] = dp[i - 1][a]
            else:
                # Take the minimum of the counts for skipping and taking coin i
                dp[i][a] = min(dp[i - 1][a], dp[i][a - coins[i - 1]] + 1)
    return dp[n][amt] if dp[n][amt] != MAX else -1

    """Coin change with space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n = len(coins)

    end
  end
  dp[amt] != _MAX ? dp[amt] : -1
end

items.title: 14.5.3   Coin change II
items.text:
Question

Given \(n\) denominations, where type \(i\) has value \(coins[i - 1]\), and a target amount \(amt\), each denomination can be used repeatedly. How many coin combinations make the target amount? Figure 14-26 shows an example.

Figure 14-26   Example input for coin change II

items.title: 1.   A dynamic programming approach
items.text:
Here we count combinations, so the subproblem becomes the number of combinations of the first \(i\) denominations that make amount \(a\). The \(dp\) table is still a two-dimensional matrix of size \((n+1) \times (amt + 1)\).

The number of combinations for a state is the sum of the counts for skipping and taking the current coin. The recurrence is:

\[ dp[i, a] = dp[i-1, a] + dp[i, a - coins[i-1]] \]

When the target amount is \(0\), taking no coins makes it exactly. Initialize all entries \(dp[i, 0]\) in the first column to \(1\). With no coins, no target amount \(>0\) can be made, so all first-row entries \(dp[0, a]\) for positive amounts equal \(0\).

items.title: 2.   Implementation
3.   Space optimization
items.text:
Use the same space optimization by removing the coin dimension:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby coin_change_ii.py
def coin_change_ii_dp_comp(coins: list[int], amt: int) -> int:
    """Coin change II with space-optimized dynamic programming"""
    n = len(coins)
    # Initialize the dp table
    dp = [0] * (amt + 1)
    dp[0] = 1
    # State transition
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # Iterate in ascending order
        for a in range(1, amt + 1):
            if coins[i - 1] > a:
                # Skip coin i if its value exceeds the target amount
                dp[a] = dp[a]
            else:
                # Add the counts for skipping and taking coin i
                dp[a] = dp[a] + dp[a - coins[i - 1]]
    return dp[amt]

items.title: Chapter 9.   Graphs
items.text:
Abstract

On life's journey, each of us is a node connected to others by countless invisible edges.

Every meeting and every parting leaves its own mark on this vast network.

items.title: 1.   Two ways to represent the same graph
items.text:
An undirected graph has four vertices A, B, C, D and edges A-B, A-C, B-C, C-D.

  1. Write the adjacency list for the graph.
  2. Fill in the adjacency matrix using only 0s and 1s.
  3. Which representation lets you tell whether A and D are directly connected by checking a single entry?
  4. If the graph has many vertices but few edges, which representation usually takes up less space?
Sample answer

  1. The adjacency list is shown below.

    A: B, C
B: A, C
C: A, B, D
D: C

  2. The adjacency matrix is shown below.

    A B C D A 0 1 1 0 B 1 0 1 0 C 1 1 0 1 D 0 0 1 0

  3. In the adjacency matrix, you can look up the entry in row A and column D directly. This makes it easy to check whether any two vertices share an edge.

  4. When a graph has many vertices but few edges, an adjacency list usually takes up less space. It stores only the edges that exist, while an adjacency matrix reserves an entry for every pair of vertices.

items.title: 2.   Vertex order in breadth-first and depth-first traversal
items.text:
An undirected graph has vertices A, B, C, D, E and edges A-B, A-C, B-D, C-D, D-E.

Start at A. Whenever there is more than one unvisited neighbor to choose from, choose in alphabetical order.

  1. List the vertices in the order a breadth-first search (BFS) visits them.
  2. List the vertices in the order a recursive depth-first search (DFS) visits them.
  3. Why do both traversals need to keep track of the vertices they have already visited?
Sample answer

  1. BFS visits the vertices in the order A, B, C, D, E. It visits B and C, which are one edge away from A, before visiting D and E, which are farther away.

  2. DFS visits the vertices in the order A, B, D, C, E. At each vertex, it explores one unvisited neighbor at a time, so it first follows A → B → D → C. When C has no unvisited neighbors left, the search returns to D and then visits E.

  3. The graph contains a cycle, such as A-B-D-C-A. Without a record of visited vertices, a traversal could keep following the cycle and visiting the same vertices indefinitely.

items.title: 3.   Can a single BFS visit the entire graph?
items.text:
An undirected graph has vertices A, B, C, D, E, F. Its only edges are A-B, B-C, D-E.

  1. Which vertices can a single BFS visit if it starts at A?
  2. Based on your answer to question 1, does this BFS visit every vertex in the graph? Why or why not?
  3. Suppose you scan all the vertices in alphabetical order and start a new BFS whenever you encounter an unvisited vertex. Where does each BFS start? How many separate parts (connected components) does the graph have?
Sample answer

  1. Starting at A, BFS can visit only the vertices A, B, C.

  2. No. The vertices D, E form a separate connected component, and F is an isolated vertex. There is no path from A to any of these three vertices, so a search starting at A cannot reach them.

  3. The three searches start at A, D, F in that order. The sets of vertices they visit are {A, B, C}, {D, E}, and {F}, respectively. The graph therefore has three connected components.

items.title: 1.   Determine whether a path exists in an undirected graph
items.text:
An undirected graph has \(n\) vertices numbered from \(0\) to \(n-1\). Each entry [u, v] in the array edges represents an undirected edge between vertices u and v.

You are also given a start vertex source and an end vertex destination. First build an adjacency list from edges, then use BFS or DFS to determine whether a path leads from source to destination. Return true if a path exists and false otherwise. The graph may contain cycles and may be disconnected.

Hints
  1. Add each undirected edge in both directions.
  2. The graph may contain cycles, so keep track of the vertices you have visited.
  3. Start at source. Return true if you reach destination, or false if the traversal ends before you reach it.

items.title: 9.1   Graph
items.text:
A graph is a nonlinear data structure made up of vertices and edges. We can describe a graph \(G\) in terms of a set of vertices \(V\) and a set of edges \(E\). The following example shows a graph with five vertices and seven edges.

\[ egin{aligned} V & = \{ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 \} ewline E & = \{ (1,2), (1,3), (1,5), (2,3), (2,4), (2,5), (4,5) \} ewline G & = \{ V, E \} ewline \end{aligned} \]

If we think of vertices as nodes and edges as references (pointers) connecting them, we can view a graph as an extension of a linked list. As Figure 9-1 shows, a network (graph) allows more flexible connections than a linear structure (linked list) or a branching, divide-and-conquer structure (tree), making it more complex.

Figure 9-1   Relationships among linked lists, trees, and graphs

items.title: 9.1.1   Common graph types and terminology
items.text:
We distinguish between undirected graphs and directed graphs according to whether their edges have a direction, as shown below.

  • In an undirected graph, each edge represents a two-way connection between two vertices, such as a friendship on WeChat or QQ.
  • In a directed graph, each edge has a direction. An edge \(A \rightarrow B\) is independent of an edge \(A \leftarrow B\), just as following someone on Weibo or Douyin is independent of being followed by them.

Figure 9-2   Directed and undirected graphs

Depending on whether all vertices are mutually reachable, a graph is either a connected graph or a disconnected graph, as shown below.

  • In a connected graph, you can start at any vertex and reach every other vertex.
  • In a disconnected graph, at least one vertex is unreachable from a given starting vertex.

Figure 9-3   Connected and disconnected graphs

We can also assign a weight to each edge to obtain a weighted graph, as shown below. For example, mobile games such as Honor of Kings calculate how close two players are based on how long they play together. A weighted graph can represent this network of relationships.

Figure 9-4   Weighted and unweighted graphs

The following terms are commonly used to describe graphs.

  • Adjacency: Two vertices are adjacent if an edge connects them. In the graph above, vertices 2, 3, and 5 are adjacent to vertex 1.
  • Path: A path from A to B is a sequence of edges that takes you from vertex A to vertex B. In the graph above, 1-5-2-4 describes a path from vertex 1 to vertex 4.
  • Degree: The number of edges incident to a vertex. In a directed graph, the in-degree counts the edges pointing into the vertex, and the out-degree counts the edges pointing out of it.

items.title: 9.1.2   Graph representations
items.text: Two common ways to represent a graph are an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list. We use undirected graphs in the following examples.

items.title: 1.   Adjacency matrix
items.text:
For a graph with \(n\) vertices, an adjacency matrix uses a matrix of size \(n \times n\). Each row and each column represents a vertex. The entries represent edges, with \(1\) or \(0\) indicating whether an edge exists between two vertices.

In Figure 9-5, \(M\) is the adjacency matrix and \(V\) is the vertex list. The entry \(M[i, j] = 1\) means there is an edge from vertex \(V[i]\) to vertex \(V[j]\), while \(M[i, j] = 0\) means there is no edge between them.

Figure 9-5   Adjacency matrix representation of a graph

An adjacency matrix has the following properties.

  • In a simple graph, vertices cannot connect to themselves, so the main diagonal carries no information about connections.
  • In an undirected graph, an edge is equivalent in either direction, so the adjacency matrix is symmetric across its main diagonal.
  • Replacing the entries \(1\) and \(0\) with weights lets the matrix represent a weighted graph.

An adjacency matrix gives direct access to the entry for an edge, so adding, removing, looking up, or updating an edge takes \(O(1)\) time. However, the matrix takes \(O(n^2)\) space, which can require substantial memory.

items.title: 2.   Adjacency list
items.text:
An adjacency list represents a graph using \(n\) linked lists whose nodes represent vertices. List \(i\) corresponds to vertex \(i\) and stores all its neighbors (vertices connected to it by an edge). Figure 9-6 shows a graph stored as an adjacency list.

Figure 9-6   Adjacency list representation of a graph

An adjacency list stores only edges that exist. Since the number of edges is usually much smaller than \(n^2\), this representation saves space. Looking up an edge, however, requires scanning a linked list, which takes longer than a lookup in an adjacency matrix.

As Figure 9-6 shows, an adjacency list resembles separate chaining in a hash table, so similar optimizations apply. For example, replacing a long linked list with an AVL tree or a red-black tree can reduce lookup time from \(O(n)\) to \(O(\log n)\). Replacing it with a hash table can reduce lookup time to \(O(1)\).

items.title: 9.1.3   Common applications of graphs
items.text:
As Table 9-1 shows, many real-world systems can be modeled as graphs, and problems involving those systems can be expressed as graph computations.

Table 9-1   Graphs in everyday life

Vertex Edge Graph problem Social network User Friendship Suggest potential friends Subway network Station Connection between stations Recommend the shortest route Solar system Celestial body Gravitational attraction between bodies Calculate planetary orbits

items.title: 9.2   Basic graph operations
items.text: Basic graph operations act on either edges or vertices. Their implementations depend on whether we use an adjacency matrix or an adjacency list.

items.title: 9.2.1   Adjacency matrix implementation
items.text:
For an undirected graph with \(n\) vertices, Figure 9-7 illustrates the following operations.

  • Add or remove an edge: Update the corresponding adjacency matrix entries directly in \(O(1)\) time. Since the graph is undirected, update the entries for both directions.
  • Add a vertex: Append a row and a column to the adjacency matrix, filling both with \(0\). This takes \(O(n)\) time.
  • Remove a vertex: Remove its row and column from the adjacency matrix. The worst case is removing the first row and column, which shifts \((n-1)^2\) elements up and to the left and takes \(O(n^2)\) time.
  • Initialize: Given \(n\) vertices, initialize the vertex list vertices of length \(n\) in \(O(n)\) time and the \(n \times n\) adjacency matrix adjMat in \(O(n^2)\) time.
<1><2><3><4><5>

Figure 9-7   Initializing an adjacency matrix and adding or removing edges and vertices

The following code implements a graph using an adjacency matrix.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby graph_adjacency_matrix.py
class GraphAdjMat:
    """Undirected graph represented by an adjacency matrix"""

    def __init__(self, vertices: list[int], edges: list[list[int]]):
        """Constructor"""
        # Vertex list: each element holds a vertex value, and its position is the vertex index
        self.vertices: list[int] = []
        # Adjacency matrix: row and column indices are vertex indices
        self.adj_mat: list[list[int]] = []
        # Add a vertex
        for val in vertices:
            self.add_vertex(val)
        # Add an edge
        # The entries in edges are vertex indices, that is, indices into vertices
        for e in edges:
            self.add_edge(e[0], e[1])

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the vertex count"""
        return len(self.vertices)

    def add_vertex(self, val: int):
        """Add a vertex"""
        n = self.size()
        # Append the new vertex value to the vertex list
        self.vertices.append(val)
        # Add a row to the adjacency matrix
        new_row = [0] * n
        self.adj_mat.append(new_row)
        # Add a column to the adjacency matrix
        for row in self.adj_mat:
            row.append(0)

    def remove_vertex(self, index: int):
        """Remove a vertex"""
        if index >= self.size():
            raise IndexError()
        # Remove the vertex at the specified index from the vertex list
        self.vertices.pop(index)
        # Remove the row at the specified index from the adjacency matrix
        self.adj_mat.pop(index)
        # Remove the column at the specified index from the adjacency matrix
        for row in self.adj_mat:
            row.pop(index)

    def add_edge(self, i: int, j: int):
        """Add an edge"""
        # Parameters i and j are indices into vertices
        # Check for out-of-bounds or equal indices
        if i < 0 or j < 0 or i >= self.size() or j >= self.size() or i == j:
            raise IndexError()
        # An undirected graph has a symmetric adjacency matrix: (i, j) == (j, i)
        self.adj_mat[i][j] = 1
        self.adj_mat[j][i] = 1

    def remove_edge(self, i: int, j: int):
        """Remove an edge"""
        # Parameters i and j are indices into vertices
        # Check for out-of-bounds or equal indices
        if i < 0 or j < 0 or i >= self.size() or j >= self.size() or i == j:
            raise IndexError()
        self.adj_mat[i][j] = 0
        self.adj_mat[j][i] = 0

    def print(self):
        """Print the adjacency matrix"""
        print("Vertex list =", self.vertices)
        print("Adjacency matrix =")
        print_matrix(self.adj_mat)

/* Undirected graph represented by an adjacency matrix */
class GraphAdjMat {
    vector<int> vertices;       // Vertex list: each element holds a vertex value, and its position is the vertex index
    vector<vector<int>> adjMat; // Adjacency matrix: row and column indices are vertex indices

  public:
    /* Constructor */
    GraphAdjMat(const vector<int> &vertices, const vector<vector<int>> &edges) {
        // Add a vertex
        for (int val : vertices) {
            addVertex(val);
        }
        // Add an edge
        // The entries in edges are vertex indices, that is, indices into vertices
        for (const vector<int> &edge : edges) {
            addEdge(edge[0], edge[1]);
        }
    }

    /* Get the vertex count */
    int size() const {
        return vertices.size();
    }

    /* Add a vertex */
    void addVertex(int val) {
        int n = size();
        // Append the new vertex value to the vertex list
        vertices.push_back(val);
        // Add a row to the adjacency matrix
        adjMat.emplace_back(vector<int>(n, 0));
        // Add a column to the adjacency matrix
        for (vector<int> &row : adjMat) {
            row.push_back(0);
        }
    }

    /* Remove a vertex */
    void removeVertex(int index) {
        if (index >= size()) {
            throw out_of_range("Vertex does not exist");
        }
        // Remove the vertex at the specified index from the vertex list
        vertices.erase(vertices.begin() + index);
        // Remove the row at the specified index from the adjacency matrix
        adjMat.erase(adjMat.begin() + index);
        // Remove the column at the specified index from the adjacency matrix
        for (vector<int> &row : adjMat) {
            row.erase(row.begin() + index);
        }
    }

    /* Add an edge */
    // Parameters i and j are indices into vertices
    void addEdge(int i, int j) {
        // Check for out-of-bounds or equal indices
        if (i < 0 || j < 0 || i >= size() || j >= size() || i == j) {
            throw out_of_range("Vertex does not exist");
        }
        // An undirected graph has a symmetric adjacency matrix: (i, j) == (j, i)
        adjMat[i][j] = 1;
        adjMat[j][i] = 1;
    }

    /* Remove an edge */
    // Parameters i and j are indices into vertices
    void removeEdge(int i, int j) {
        // Check for out-of-bounds or equal indices
        if (i < 0 || j < 0 || i >= size() || j >= size() || i == j) {
            throw out_of_range("Vertex does not exist");
        }
        adjMat[i][j] = 0;
        adjMat[j][i] = 0;
    }

    /* Print the adjacency matrix */
    void print() {

typedef struct {
    int vertices[MAX_SIZE];
    int adjMat[MAX_SIZE][MAX_SIZE];
    int size;
} GraphAdjMat;

/* Constructor */
GraphAdjMat *newGraphAdjMat() {
    GraphAdjMat *graph = (GraphAdjMat *)malloc(sizeof(GraphAdjMat));
    graph->size = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_SIZE; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < MAX_SIZE; j++) {
            graph->adjMat[i][j] = 0;
        }
    }
    return graph;
}

/* Destructor */
void delGraphAdjMat(GraphAdjMat *graph) {
    free(graph);
}

/* Add a vertex */
void addVertex(GraphAdjMat *graph, int val) {
    if (graph->size == MAX_SIZE) {
        fprintf(stderr, "The graph has reached its maximum number of vertices\n");
        return;
    }
    // Add the nth vertex and set row n and column n to zero
    int n = graph->size;
    graph->vertices[n] = val;
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
        graph->adjMat[n][i] = graph->adjMat[i][n] = 0;
    }
    graph->size++;
}

/* Remove a vertex */
void removeVertex(GraphAdjMat *graph, int index) {
    if (index < 0 || index >= graph->size) {
        fprintf(stderr, "Vertex index out of bounds\n");
        return;
    }
    // Remove the vertex at the specified index from the vertex list
    for (int i = index; i < graph->size - 1; i++) {
        graph->vertices[i] = graph->vertices[i + 1];
    }
    // Remove the row at the specified index from the adjacency matrix
    for (int i = index; i < graph->size - 1; i++) {
        for (int j = 0; j < graph->size; j++) {
            graph->adjMat[i][j] = graph->adjMat[i + 1][j];
        }
    }
    // Remove the column at the specified index from the adjacency matrix
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        for (int j = index; j < graph->size - 1; j++) {
            graph->adjMat[i][j] = graph->adjMat[i][j + 1];
        }
    }
    graph->size--;

items.title: 9.2.2   Adjacency list implementation
items.text:
For an undirected graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges, we can implement each operation as shown below.

  • Add an edge: Append the edge to the list for each endpoint in \(O(1)\) time. Since the graph is undirected, add entries in both directions.
  • Remove an edge: Find and remove the specified edge in the corresponding lists in \(O(m)\) time. In an undirected graph, remove the entries for both directions.
  • Add a vertex: Add a linked list to the adjacency list, using the new vertex as its head. This takes \(O(1)\) time.
  • Remove a vertex: Traverse the entire adjacency list and remove every edge incident to the vertex. This takes \(O(n + m)\) time.
  • Initialize: Create \(n\) vertices and \(2m\) edges in the adjacency list in \(O(n + m)\) time.
<1><2><3><4><5>

Figure 9-8   Initializing an adjacency list and adding or removing edges and vertices

The following code implements an adjacency list. It differs from Figure 9-8 in two ways.

  • To simplify the code and make vertices easy to add and remove, we use lists (dynamic arrays) in place of linked lists.
  • We store the adjacency list in a hash table. Each key is a vertex instance, and its value is the list of adjacent vertices (the linked list in the figure).

We also use the Vertex class to represent vertices in the adjacency list. Suppose we identified vertices by list index, as we did in the adjacency matrix. Removing the vertex at index \(i\) would require scanning the entire adjacency list and decreasing every index greater than \(i\) by \(1\), which is inefficient. When each vertex is a distinct Vertex instance, removing one vertex leaves the identities of all others unchanged.

class GraphAdjList:
    """Undirected graph represented by an adjacency list"""

    def __init__(self, edges: list[list[Vertex]]):
        """Constructor"""
        # Adjacency list: each vertex maps to its neighbors
        self.adj_list = dict[Vertex, list[Vertex]]()
        # Add all vertices and edges
        for edge in edges:
            self.add_vertex(edge[0])
            self.add_vertex(edge[1])
            self.add_edge(edge[0], edge[1])

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the vertex count"""
        return len(self.adj_list)

    def add_edge(self, vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex):
        """Add an edge"""
        if vet1 not in self.adj_list or vet2 not in self.adj_list or vet1 == vet2:
            raise ValueError()
        # Add the edge vet1 - vet2
        self.adj_list[vet1].append(vet2)
        self.adj_list[vet2].append(vet1)

    def remove_edge(self, vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex):
        """Remove an edge"""
        if vet1 not in self.adj_list or vet2 not in self.adj_list or vet1 == vet2:
            raise ValueError()
        # Remove the edge vet1 - vet2
        self.adj_list[vet1].remove(vet2)
        self.adj_list[vet2].remove(vet1)

    def add_vertex(self, vet: Vertex):
        """Add a vertex"""
        if vet in self.adj_list:
            return
        # Add a new linked list to the adjacency list
        self.adj_list[vet] = []

    def remove_vertex(self, vet: Vertex):
        """Remove a vertex"""
        if vet not in self.adj_list:
            raise ValueError()
        # Remove the linked list for vertex vet from the adjacency list
        self.adj_list.pop(vet)
        # Traverse the other vertices' lists and remove every edge incident to vet
        for vertex in self.adj_list:
            if vet in self.adj_list[vertex]:
                self.adj_list[vertex].remove(vet)

    def print(self):
        """Print the adjacency list"""
        print("Adjacency list =")
        for vertex in self.adj_list:
            tmp = [v.val for v in self.adj_list[vertex]]
            print(f"{vertex.val}: {tmp},")

class GraphAdjList {
  public:
    // Adjacency list: each vertex maps to its neighbors
    unordered_map<Vertex *, vector<Vertex *>> adjList;

    /* Remove the specified node from the vector */
    void remove(vector<Vertex *> &vec, Vertex *vet) {
        for (int i = 0; i < vec.size(); i++) {
            if (vec[i] == vet) {
                vec.erase(vec.begin() + i);
                break;
            }
        }
    }

    /* Constructor */
    GraphAdjList(const vector<vector<Vertex *>> &edges) {
        // Add all vertices and edges
        for (const vector<Vertex *> &edge : edges) {
            addVertex(edge[0]);
            addVertex(edge[1]);
            addEdge(edge[0], edge[1]);
        }
    }

    /* Get the vertex count */
    int size() {
        return adjList.size();
    }

    /* Add an edge */
    void addEdge(Vertex *vet1, Vertex *vet2) {
        if (!adjList.count(vet1) || !adjList.count(vet2) || vet1 == vet2)
            throw invalid_argument("Vertex does not exist");
        // Add the edge vet1 - vet2
        adjList[vet1].push_back(vet2);
        adjList[vet2].push_back(vet1);
    }

    /* Remove an edge */
    void removeEdge(Vertex *vet1, Vertex *vet2) {
        if (!adjList.count(vet1) || !adjList.count(vet2) || vet1 == vet2)
            throw invalid_argument("Vertex does not exist");
        // Remove the edge vet1 - vet2
        remove(adjList[vet1], vet2);
        remove(adjList[vet2], vet1);
    }

    /* Add a vertex */
    void addVertex(Vertex *vet) {
        if (adjList.count(vet))
            return;
        // Add a new linked list to the adjacency list
        adjList[vet] = vector<Vertex *>();
    }

    /* Remove a vertex */
    void removeVertex(Vertex *vet) {
        if (!adjList.count(vet))
            throw invalid_argument("Vertex does not exist");
        // Remove the linked list for vertex vet from the adjacency list
        adjList.erase(vet);
        // Traverse the other vertices' lists and remove every edge incident to vet
        for (auto &adj : adjList) {
            remove(adj.second, vet);
        }
    }

    /* Print the adjacency list */
    void print() {
        cout << "Adjacency list =" << endl;
        for (auto &adj : adjList) {
            const auto &key = adj.first;
            const auto &vec = adj.second;
            cout << key->val << ": ";
            printVector(vetsToVals(vec));
        }
    }
};

/* Undirected graph represented by an adjacency list */
class GraphAdjList {
    // Adjacency list: each vertex maps to its neighbors
    adjList;

    /* Constructor */
    constructor(edges) {
        this.adjList = new Map();
        // Add all vertices and edges
        for (const edge of edges) {
            this.addVertex(edge[0]);
            this.addVertex(edge[1]);
            this.addEdge(edge[0], edge[1]);
        }
    }

    /* Get the vertex count */
    size() {
        return this.adjList.size;
    }

    /* Add an edge */
    addEdge(vet1, vet2) {
        if (
            !this.adjList.has(vet1) ||
            !this.adjList.has(vet2) ||
            vet1 === vet2
        ) {
            throw new Error('Illegal Argument Exception');
        }
        // Add the edge vet1 - vet2
        this.adjList.get(vet1).push(vet2);
        this.adjList.get(vet2).push(vet1);
    }

    /* Remove an edge */
    removeEdge(vet1, vet2) {
        if (
            !this.adjList.has(vet1) ||
            !this.adjList.has(vet2) ||
            vet1 === vet2 ||
            this.adjList.get(vet1).indexOf(vet2) === -1
        ) {
            throw new Error('Illegal Argument Exception');
        }
        // Remove the edge vet1 - vet2
        this.adjList.get(vet1).splice(this.adjList.get(vet1).indexOf(vet2), 1);
        this.adjList.get(vet2).splice(this.adjList.get(vet2).indexOf(vet1), 1);
    }

    /* Add a vertex */
    addVertex(vet) {
        if (this.adjList.has(vet)) return;
        // Add a new linked list to the adjacency list
        this.adjList.set(vet, []);
    }

    /* Remove a vertex */
    removeVertex(vet) {
        if (!this.adjList.has(vet)) {
            throw new Error('Illegal Argument Exception');
        }
        // Remove the linked list for vertex vet from the adjacency list
        this.adjList.delete(vet);
        // Traverse the other vertices' lists and remove every edge incident to vet
        for (const set of this.adjList.values()) {
            const index = set.indexOf(vet);
            if (index > -1) {
                set.splice(index, 1);
            }
        }
    }

        for (const [key, value] of this.adjList) {
            const tmp = [];
            for (const vertex of value) {
                tmp.push(vertex.val);
            }

        }
    }

        this.adjList.get(vet1).push(vet2);
        this.adjList.get(vet2).push(vet1);
    }

    /* Remove an edge */
    removeEdge(vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex): void {
        if (
            !this.adjList.has(vet1) ||
            !this.adjList.has(vet2) ||
            vet1 === vet2 ||
            this.adjList.get(vet1).indexOf(vet2) === -1
        ) {
            throw new Error('Illegal Argument Exception');
        }
        // Remove the edge vet1 - vet2
        this.adjList.get(vet1).splice(this.adjList.get(vet1).indexOf(vet2), 1);
        this.adjList.get(vet2).splice(this.adjList.get(vet2).indexOf(vet1), 1);
    }

    /* Add a vertex */
    addVertex(vet: Vertex): void {
        if (this.adjList.has(vet)) return;
        // Add a new linked list to the adjacency list
        this.adjList.set(vet, []);
    }

    /* Remove a vertex */
    removeVertex(vet: Vertex): void {
        if (!this.adjList.has(vet)) {
            throw new Error('Illegal Argument Exception');
        }
        // Remove the linked list for vertex vet from the adjacency list
        this.adjList.delete(vet);
        // Traverse the other vertices' lists and remove every edge incident to vet
        for (const set of this.adjList.values()) {
            const index: number = set.indexOf(vet);
            if (index > -1) {
                set.splice(index, 1);
            }
        }
    }

    /* Print the adjacency list */
    print(): void {
        console.log('Adjacency list =');
        for (const [key, value] of this.adjList.entries()) {
            const tmp = [];
            for (const vertex of value) {
                tmp.push(vertex.val);
            }
            console.log(key.val + ': ' + tmp.join());
        }
    }
}

/* Undirected graph type represented by an adjacency list */
pub struct GraphAdjList {
    // Adjacency list: each vertex maps to its neighbors
    pub adj_list: HashMap<Vertex, Vec<Vertex>>, // Would HashSet<Vertex> be a better choice for the values?
}

impl GraphAdjList {
    /* Constructor */
    pub fn new(edges: Vec<[Vertex; 2]>) -> Self {
        let mut graph = GraphAdjList {
            adj_list: HashMap::new(),
        };
        // Add all vertices and edges
        for edge in edges {
            graph.add_vertex(edge[0]);
            graph.add_vertex(edge[1]);
            graph.add_edge(edge[0], edge[1]);
        }

        graph
    }

    /* Get the vertex count */
    #[allow(unused)]
    pub fn size(&self) -> usize {
        self.adj_list.len()
    }

    /* Add an edge */
    pub fn add_edge(&mut self, vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex) {
        if vet1 == vet2 {
            panic!("value error");
        }
        // Add the edge vet1 - vet2
        self.adj_list.entry(vet1).or_default().push(vet2);
        self.adj_list.entry(vet2).or_default().push(vet1);
    }

    /* Remove an edge */
    #[allow(unused)]
    pub fn remove_edge(&mut self, vet1: Vertex, vet2: Vertex) {
        if vet1 == vet2 {
            panic!("value error");
        }
        // Remove the edge vet1 - vet2
        self.adj_list
            .entry(vet1)
            .and_modify(|v| v.retain(|&e| e != vet2));
        self.adj_list
            .entry(vet2)
            .and_modify(|v| v.retain(|&e| e != vet1));
    }

    /* Add a vertex */
    pub fn add_vertex(&mut self, vet: Vertex) {
        if self.adj_list.contains_key(&vet) {
            return;
        }
        // Add a new linked list to the adjacency list
        self.adj_list.insert(vet, vec![]);
    }

    /* Remove a vertex */
    #[allow(unused)]
    pub fn remove_vertex(&mut self, vet: Vertex) {
        // Remove the linked list for vertex vet from the adjacency list
        self.adj_list.remove(&vet);
        // Traverse the other vertices' lists and remove every edge incident to vet
        for list in self.adj_list.values_mut() {
            list.retain(|&v| v != vet);
        }
    }

    /* Print the adjacency list */
    pub fn print(&self) {
        println!("Adjacency list =");
        for (vertex, list) in &self.adj_list {
            let list = list.iter().map(|vertex| vertex.val).collect::<Vec<i32>>();
            println!("{}: {:?},", vertex.val, list);
        }
    }
}

/* Node structure */
typedef struct AdjListNode {
    Vertex *vertex;           // Vertex
    struct AdjListNode *next; // Next node
} AdjListNode;

/* Find the node for a vertex */
AdjListNode *findNode(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet) {
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        if (graph->heads[i]->vertex == vet) {
            return graph->heads[i];
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

/* Helper for adding an edge */
void addEdgeHelper(AdjListNode *head, Vertex *vet) {
    AdjListNode *node = (AdjListNode *)malloc(sizeof(AdjListNode));
    node->vertex = vet;
    // Insert at the head
    node->next = head->next;
    head->next = node;
}

/* Helper for removing an edge */
void removeEdgeHelper(AdjListNode *head, Vertex *vet) {
    AdjListNode *pre = head;
    AdjListNode *cur = head->next;
    // Search the linked list for the node corresponding to vet
    while (cur != NULL && cur->vertex != vet) {
        pre = cur;
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    if (cur == NULL)
        return;
    // Remove the node corresponding to vet from the linked list
    pre->next = cur->next;
    // Free the memory
    free(cur);
}

/* Undirected graph represented by an adjacency list */
typedef struct {
    AdjListNode *heads[MAX_SIZE]; // Array of nodes
    int size;                     // Number of nodes
} GraphAdjList;

/* Constructor */
GraphAdjList *newGraphAdjList() {
    GraphAdjList *graph = (GraphAdjList *)malloc(sizeof(GraphAdjList));
    if (!graph) {
        return NULL;
    }
    graph->size = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < MAX_SIZE; i++) {
        graph->heads[i] = NULL;
    }
    return graph;
}

/* Destructor */
void delGraphAdjList(GraphAdjList *graph) {
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        AdjListNode *cur = graph->heads[i];
        while (cur != NULL) {
            AdjListNode *next = cur->next;
            if (cur != graph->heads[i]) {
                free(cur);
            }
            cur = next;
        }
        free(graph->heads[i]->vertex);
        free(graph->heads[i]);
    }
    free(graph);
}

/* Find the node for a vertex */
AdjListNode *findNode(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet) {
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        if (graph->heads[i]->vertex == vet) {
            return graph->heads[i];
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

/* Add an edge */
void addEdge(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet1, Vertex *vet2) {
    AdjListNode *head1 = findNode(graph, vet1);
    AdjListNode *head2 = findNode(graph, vet2);
    assert(head1 != NULL && head2 != NULL && head1 != head2);
    // Add the edge vet1 - vet2
    addEdgeHelper(head1, vet2);
    addEdgeHelper(head2, vet1);
}

/* Remove an edge */
void removeEdge(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet1, Vertex *vet2) {
    AdjListNode *head1 = findNode(graph, vet1);
    AdjListNode *head2 = findNode(graph, vet2);
    assert(head1 != NULL && head2 != NULL);
    // Remove the edge vet1 - vet2
    removeEdgeHelper(head1, head2->vertex);
    removeEdgeHelper(head2, head1->vertex);
}

/* Add a vertex */
void addVertex(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet) {
    assert(graph != NULL);
    if (findNode(graph, vet) != NULL)
        return;
    assert(graph->size < MAX_SIZE);
    AdjListNode *head = (AdjListNode *)malloc(sizeof(AdjListNode));
    head->vertex = vet;
    head->next = NULL;
    // Add a new linked list to the adjacency list
    graph->heads[graph->size++] = head;
}

/* Remove a vertex */
void removeVertex(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *vet) {
    AdjListNode *node = findNode(graph, vet);
    assert(node != NULL);
    // Shift the following vertices forward to fill the gap
    int i;
    for (i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        if (graph->heads[i] == node)
            break;
    }
    for (int j = i; j < graph->size - 1; j++) {
        graph->heads[j] = graph->heads[j + 1];
    }
    graph->size--;
    // Traverse the other vertices' lists and remove every edge incident to vet
    for (int i = 0; i < graph->size; i++) {
        AdjListNode *cur = graph->heads[i];
        while (cur->next != NULL) {
            AdjListNode *next = cur->next;
            if (next->vertex == vet) {
                cur->next = next->next;
                free(next);
            } else {
                cur = next;
            }
        }
    }
    // Remove the linked list for vertex vet from the adjacency list
    while (node != NULL) {
        AdjListNode *next = node->next;
        free(node);
        node = next;
    }
    free(vet);
}

items.title: 9.2.3   Efficiency comparison
items.text:
Consider a graph with \(n\) vertices and \(m\) edges. Table 9-2 compares the time and space costs of an adjacency matrix and an adjacency list. “Adjacency list (linked lists)” corresponds to the implementation described here. “Adjacency list (hash tables)” means that every linked list has been replaced with a hash table.

Table 9-2   Comparing adjacency matrices and adjacency lists

Adjacency matrix Adjacency list (linked lists) Adjacency list (hash tables) Check adjacency \(O(1)\) \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Add an edge \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\) Remove an edge \(O(1)\) \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) Add a vertex \(O(n)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\) Remove a vertex \(O(n^2)\) \(O(n + m)\) \(O(n)\) Memory usage \(O(n^2)\) \(O(n + m)\) \(O(n + m)\)

The adjacency list with hash tables appears to offer the best time and space efficiency in the table. In practice, however, edge operations are faster in an adjacency matrix because each takes just one array access or assignment. Overall, an adjacency matrix trades space for time, while an adjacency list trades time for space.

items.title: 9.3   Graph traversal
items.text:
A tree describes one-to-many relationships. A graph allows more flexible connections and can represent arbitrary many-to-many relationships. We can therefore view a tree as a special case of a graph. For the same reason, tree traversal is a special case of graph traversal.

Both trees and graphs use search algorithms for traversal. Graph traversal also has two main approaches: breadth-first traversal and depth-first traversal.

items.title: 9.3.1   Breadth-first traversal
items.text:
Breadth-first traversal starts at a vertex and visits the nearest vertices first, expanding outward one layer at a time. In Figure 9-9, we start at the upper-left vertex and visit all its neighbors. We then visit the neighbors of the next vertex and continue until every vertex has been visited.

Figure 9-9   Breadth-first traversal of a graph

items.title: 1.   Implementation
items.text:
BFS usually uses a queue, as in the code below. Its first-in, first-out order fits the way BFS visits nearby vertices before more distant ones.

  1. Enqueue the starting vertex startVet and begin the loop.
  2. On each iteration, dequeue the front vertex and record the visit, then add its unvisited neighbors to the back of the queue.
  3. Repeat step 2. until all vertices have been visited.

To avoid repeated visits, use a hash set visited to record which vertices have already been visited.

Tip

Think of a hash set as a hash table that stores only a key, without an associated value. Adding, removing, looking up, or updating a key takes \(O(1)\) time. Since each key is unique, hash sets are often used to remove duplicates.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby graph_bfs.py
def graph_bfs(graph: GraphAdjList, start_vet: Vertex) -> list[Vertex]:
    """Breadth-first traversal"""
    # Represent the graph with an adjacency list to look up all neighbors of a given vertex
    # Vertex traversal order
    res = []
    # Use a hash set to track visited vertices
    visited = set[Vertex]([start_vet])
    # Use a queue for BFS
    que = deque[Vertex]([start_vet])
    # Starting at vertex vet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while len(que) > 0:
        vet = que.popleft()  # Dequeue the front vertex
        res.append(vet)  # Record the visited vertex
        # Iterate over all neighbors of this vertex
        for adj_vet in graph.adj_list[vet]:
            if adj_vet in visited:
                continue  # Skip visited vertices
            que.append(adj_vet)  # Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            visited.add(adj_vet)  # Mark the vertex as visited
    # Return the vertex traversal order
    return res
