/* Breadth-first traversal */
// Represent the graph with an adjacency list to look up all neighbors of a given vertex
vector<Vertex *> graphBFS(GraphAdjList &graph, Vertex *startVet) {
    // Vertex traversal order
    vector<Vertex *> res;
    // Use a hash set to track visited vertices
    unordered_set<Vertex *> visited = {startVet};
    // Use a queue for BFS
    queue<Vertex *> que;
    que.push(startVet);
    // Starting at vertex vet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while (!que.empty()) {
        Vertex *vet = que.front();
        que.pop();          // Dequeue the front vertex
        res.push_back(vet); // Record the visited vertex
        // Iterate over all neighbors of this vertex
        for (auto adjVet : graph.adjList[vet]) {
            if (visited.count(adjVet))
                continue;            // Skip visited vertices
            que.push(adjVet);        // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            visited.emplace(adjVet); // Mark the vertex as visited
        }
    }
    // Return the vertex traversal order
    return res;
}

// Represent the graph with an adjacency list to look up all neighbors of a given vertex
func graphBFS(g *graphAdjList, startVet Vertex) []Vertex {
    // Vertex traversal order
    res := make([]Vertex, 0)
    // Use a hash set to track visited vertices
    visited := make(map[Vertex]struct{})
    visited[startVet] = struct{}{}
    // Use a slice as the BFS queue
    queue := make([]Vertex, 0)
    queue = append(queue, startVet)
    // Starting at vertex vet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    for len(queue) > 0 {
        // Dequeue the front vertex
        vet := queue[0]
        queue = queue[1:]
        // Record the visited vertex
        res = append(res, vet)
        // Iterate over all neighbors of this vertex
        for _, adjVet := range g.adjList[vet] {
            _, isExist := visited[adjVet]
            // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            if !isExist {
                queue = append(queue, adjVet)
                visited[adjVet] = struct{}{}
            }
        }
    }
    // Return the vertex traversal order
    return res
}

// Represent the graph with an adjacency list to look up all neighbors of a given vertex
function graphBFS(graph: GraphAdjList, startVet: Vertex): Vertex[] {
    // Vertex traversal order
    const res: Vertex[] = [];
    // Use a hash set to track visited vertices
    const visited: Set<Vertex> = new Set();
    visited.add(startVet);
    // Use a queue for BFS
    const que = [startVet];
    // Starting at vertex vet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while (que.length) {
        const vet = que.shift(); // Dequeue the front vertex
        res.push(vet); // Record the visited vertex
        // Iterate over all neighbors of this vertex
        for (const adjVet of graph.adjList.get(vet) ?? []) {
            if (visited.has(adjVet)) {
                continue; // Skip visited vertices
            }
            que.push(adjVet); // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
            visited.add(adjVet); // Mark the vertex as visited
        }
    }
    // Return the vertex traversal order
    return res;
}

graph_bfs.c
/* Node queue structure */
typedef struct {
    Vertex *vertices[MAX_SIZE];
    int front, rear, size;
} Queue;

/* Constructor */
Queue *newQueue() {
    Queue *q = (Queue *)malloc(sizeof(Queue));
    q->front = q->rear = q->size = 0;
    return q;
}

/* Check whether the queue is empty */
int isEmpty(Queue *q) {
    return q->size == 0;
}

/* Enqueue */
void enqueue(Queue *q, Vertex *vet) {
    q->vertices[q->rear] = vet;
    q->rear = (q->rear + 1) % MAX_SIZE;
    q->size++;
}

/* Dequeue */
Vertex *dequeue(Queue *q) {
    Vertex *vet = q->vertices[q->front];
    q->front = (q->front + 1) % MAX_SIZE;
    q->size--;
    return vet;
}

/* Check whether a vertex has been visited */
int isVisited(Vertex **visited, int size, Vertex *vet) {
    // Scan for the node in O(n) time
    for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
        if (visited[i] == vet)
            return 1;
    }
    return 0;
}

/* Breadth-first traversal */
// Represent the graph with an adjacency list to look up all neighbors of a given vertex
void graphBFS(GraphAdjList *graph, Vertex *startVet, Vertex **res, int *resSize, Vertex **visited, int *visitedSize) {
    // Use a queue for BFS
    Queue *queue = newQueue();
    enqueue(queue, startVet);
    visited[(*visitedSize)++] = startVet;
    // Starting at vertex vet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
    while (!isEmpty(queue)) {
        Vertex *vet = dequeue(queue); // Dequeue the front vertex
        res[(*resSize)++] = vet;      // Record the visited vertex
        // Iterate over all neighbors of this vertex
        AdjListNode *node = findNode(graph, vet);
        while (node != NULL) {
            // Skip visited vertices
            if (!isVisited(visited, *visitedSize, node->vertex)) {
                enqueue(queue, node->vertex);             // Enqueue only unvisited vertices
                visited[(*visitedSize)++] = node->vertex; // Mark the vertex as visited
            }
            node = node->next;
        }
    }
    // Free the memory
    free(queue);
}

def graph_bfs(graph, start_vet)
  # Represent the graph with an adjacency list to look up all neighbors of a given vertex
  # Vertex traversal order
  res = []
  # Use a hash set to track visited vertices
  visited = Set.new([start_vet])
  # Use a queue for BFS
  que = [start_vet]
  # Starting at vertex vet, loop until all reachable vertices have been visited
  while que.length > 0
    vet = que.shift # Dequeue the front vertex
    res << vet # Record the visited vertex
    # Iterate over all neighbors of this vertex
    for adj_vet in graph.adj_list[vet]
      next if visited.include?(adj_vet) # Skip visited vertices
      que << adj_vet # Enqueue only unvisited vertices
      visited.add(adj_vet) # Mark the vertex as visited
    end
  end
  # Return the vertex traversal order
  res
end

Is the breadth-first traversal order unique?

No. Breadth-first traversal requires only that nearer vertices be visited before farther ones. Vertices at the same distance can be visited in any order. In Figure 9-10, vertices \(1\) and \(3\) can switch places, and vertices \(2\), \(4\), and \(6\) can also be reordered.

items.title: 2.   Complexity analysis
items.text:
Time complexity: Each vertex enters and leaves the queue once, taking \(O(|V|)\) time in total. When checking neighbors in an undirected graph, we examine every edge \(2\) times, taking \(O(2|E|)\) time. The total is \(O(|V| + |E|)\).

Space complexity: The list res, hash set visited, and queue que each hold at most \(|V|\) vertices, so the space complexity is \(O(|V|)\).

items.title: 9.3.2   Depth-first traversal
items.text:
Depth-first traversal follows a path as far as it can before backtracking. In Figure 9-11, we start at the upper-left vertex and follow a neighbor of the current vertex. When we reach a dead end, we return and follow another branch as far as possible. We repeat this process until every vertex has been visited.

Figure 9-11   Depth-first traversal of a graph

items.title: 1.   Implementation
items.text:
Recursion is a natural way to explore a path to its end and then return. As in breadth-first traversal, we use a hash set visited to record visited vertices and avoid revisiting them.

Is the depth-first traversal order unique?

As with breadth-first traversal, there is more than one valid depth-first order. At any vertex, we can choose which direction to explore first. Reordering the neighbors still gives a depth-first traversal.

For example, the tree traversals “root \(\rightarrow\) left \(\rightarrow\) right,” “left \(\rightarrow\) root \(\rightarrow\) right,” and “left \(\rightarrow\) right \(\rightarrow\) root” are preorder, inorder, and postorder, respectively. They give different priorities to the visits, yet all three are depth-first traversals.

items.title: 2.   Complexity analysis
items.text:
Time complexity: Each vertex is visited exactly \(1\) time, taking \(O(|V|)\) time overall. Each edge is examined \(2\) times, taking \(O(2|E|)\) time overall. The total is \(O(|V| + |E|)\).

Space complexity: The list res and hash set visited each hold at most \(|V|\) vertices, and the recursion depth is at most \(|V|\), giving \(O(|V|)\) space.

items.title: 1.   Key points
items.text:
• A graph consists of vertices and edges and can be represented by a set of vertices and a set of edges.
  • A network (graph) allows more flexible connections than a linear structure (linked list) or a branching, divide-and-conquer structure (tree), which makes it more complex.
  • Edges in a directed graph have a direction. In a connected graph, every vertex is reachable from every other vertex. Every edge in a weighted graph carries a weight.
  • An adjacency matrix represents a graph with one row and column per vertex. Entries represent edges, with \(1\) or \(0\) indicating whether two vertices are connected by an edge. Adding, removing, looking up, and updating edges are efficient, but the matrix takes considerable space.
  • An adjacency list represents a graph with multiple linked lists. List \(i\) stores all neighbors of vertex \(i\). An adjacency list uses less space than an adjacency matrix, but finding an edge requires scanning a list, so lookups take longer.
  • If a linked list in an adjacency list becomes too long, replacing it with a red-black tree or hash table can speed up lookups.
  • An adjacency matrix trades space for time, while an adjacency list trades time for space.
  • Graphs can model real-world systems such as social networks and subway networks.
  • A tree is a special case of a graph, and tree traversal is a special case of graph traversal.
  • Breadth-first traversal searches a graph from near to far, expanding one layer at a time. It usually uses a queue.
  • Depth-first traversal searches a graph by following a path as far as possible, then backtracking. It is often implemented recursively.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: Is a path defined as a sequence of vertices or a sequence of edges?

Different language editions of Wikipedia give different definitions. The English edition describes a path as a sequence of edges, while the Chinese edition describes it as a sequence of vertices. The English text reads: In graph theory, a path in a graph is a finite or infinite sequence of edges which joins a sequence of vertices.

Here we treat a path as a sequence of edges rather than a sequence of vertices. Two vertices can be joined by multiple edges, in which case each edge gives a distinct path.

Q: Can some vertices be unreachable when traversing a disconnected graph?

In a disconnected graph, at least one vertex is unreachable from a given starting vertex. To visit every connected component, start traversals from multiple vertices.

Q: In an adjacency list, must the neighbors of a vertex appear in a particular order?

Any order is valid. In practice, you might sort the neighbors by a rule, such as the order in which the vertices were added or the values of the vertices. This can make it easier to find a vertex with a particular extreme value.

Abstract

A sunflower turns toward the sun, seeking the best conditions for growth at every moment.

In much the same way, a greedy strategy works toward the best answer one simple choice at a time.

items.title: 1.   Is taking the largest coin always best?
items.text:
The coin denominations are [1, 7, 10] and the target amount is 14.

  1. Write down the coins you take if you always choose the largest denomination that does not exceed the remaining amount.
  2. Can you make the same amount with fewer coins? Give one way if you can, or explain why you cannot.
  3. Does this show that the greedy strategy works for every set of denominations?
Sample answer

  1. The greedy strategy chooses 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 in that order, for a total of 5 coins.

  2. Yes. The combination 7 + 7 uses only 2 coins.

  3. No. This counterexample shows that choosing the largest coin you can take at each step does not always minimize the number of coins for an arbitrary set of denominations. Taking the largest coin now can rule out a better combination later.

items.title: 2.   Which item goes into the knapsack first?
items.text:
A knapsack can carry 4 kg. You may take any fraction of the following items, and the value you receive is proportional to the weight you take.

  • Item A weighs 4 kg and has a value of 20.
  • Item B weighs 3 kg and has a value of 18.
  1. What is the value per kilogram of each item? Which should you take first?
  2. What total value do you get when you fill the knapsack using the greedy strategy for fractional knapsack?
  3. When you can divide items and the knapsack limits total weight, should you compare total values or values per kilogram? Why?
Sample answer

  1. A's value per kilogram is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 and B's is 18 ÷ 3 = 6, so take B first because it has the higher value per kilogram.

  2. Take all of B first. This uses 3 kg of capacity and gives a value of 18. With 1 kg of capacity left, take 1 kg of A for a value of 5. The final value is 18 + 5 = 23.

  3. The knapsack limits total weight, and the items are divisible, so compare values per unit of weight. A has a higher total value but a lower value per kilogram than B. Filling the knapsack with A first would give a value of only 20.

items.title: 3.   Which pointer should move next?
items.text:
The board heights are [1, 8, 6, 2, 5]. Use two pointers starting at opposite ends to find the maximum capacity. Capacity equals the height of the shorter board times the distance between the two board indices.

  1. Initially, the left pointer is at index 0 and the right pointer is at index 4. What is the current capacity? Which pointer should move next?
  2. After the move you chose in part 1, what are the two pointer indices? What is the capacity now, and which pointer should move next?
  3. For the current pair of boards, you could move the pointer at the shorter board or the one at the taller board. Which move could still give you a larger capacity? Why?
Sample answer

  1. The current capacity is min(1, 5) × (4 - 0) = 4. The left board is shorter, so move the left pointer.

  2. After the left pointer moves, the pointers are at indices 1 and 4. The current capacity is min(8, 5) × (4 - 1) = 15. The right board is shorter, so move the right pointer next.

  3. Only moving the pointer at the shorter board can lead to a larger capacity. Moving the pointer at the taller board reduces the distance between the boards, and the shorter board that stays in place still limits the height of the container. That height can only stay the same or decrease, so the capacity cannot exceed its previous value. Only by moving away from the shorter board do we get a chance to replace it with a taller one.

items.title: 1.   Fractional knapsack
items.text:
You are given two arrays of equal length, wgt and val, with wgt[i] > 0 and val[i] >= 0, and a knapsack of capacity cap >= 0. There is one of each item, and you may take a fraction of it. The value you receive is proportional to the fraction of the item's weight you take. Use a greedy algorithm to find the maximum total value the knapsack can hold and return it as a real number.

Hints
  1. First compute each item's value per unit of weight, val[i] / wgt[i]. Keep the fractional part of the quotient.
  2. Take items with higher value per unit of weight first.
  3. If the remaining capacity is less than the weight of the current item, take just enough of it to fill the knapsack and stop.

items.title: 15.2   Fractional knapsack problem
items.text:
Question

You are given \(n\) items and a knapsack of capacity \(cap\). Item \(i\) has weight \(wgt[i-1]\) and value \(val[i-1]\). You can select each item only once, but you may take a fraction of it and receive the corresponding fraction of its value. What is the maximum total value you can pack within the weight limit? Figure 15-3 shows an example.

Figure 15-3   Example data for fractional knapsack

Fractional knapsack closely resembles 0-1 knapsack. The state includes the current item \(i\) and capacity \(c\), and the goal is to maximize total value within the capacity limit.

Here, however, we can take just part of an item. As Figure 15-4 shows, we can divide an item at any point and calculate the value of the portion in proportion to its weight.

  1. For item \(i\), the value per unit of weight is \(val[i-1] / wgt[i-1]\). We call this its unit value.
  2. If we take a portion of item \(i\) that weighs \(w\), it adds \(w \times val[i-1] / wgt[i-1]\) to the value in the knapsack.

Figure 15-4   Value per unit of weight

items.title: 1.   Choosing a greedy strategy
items.text:
To maximize total value in the knapsack, we want the greatest possible value for each unit of weight. This leads to the greedy strategy shown below.

  1. Sort the items in descending order of unit value.
  2. Go through the items, choosing the one with the highest remaining unit value at each step.
  3. If the current item does not fit, take just enough of it to fill the knapsack.

Figure 15-5   Greedy strategy for fractional knapsack

items.title: 2.   Implementation
items.text:
We define an Item class so we can sort the items by unit value. The loop makes one greedy choice at a time. Once the knapsack is full, we exit the loop and return the result:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby fractional_knapsack.py
class Item:
    """Item"""

    def __init__(self, w: int, v: int):
        self.w = w  # Item weight
        self.v = v  # Item value

def fractional_knapsack(wgt: list[int], val: list[int], cap: int) -> int:
    """Greedy fractional knapsack"""
    # Create a list of items, each with a weight and a value
    items = [Item(w, v) for w, v in zip(wgt, val)]
    # Sort by value per unit of weight, item.v / item.w, in descending order
    items.sort(key=lambda item: item.v / item.w, reverse=True)
    # Make greedy choices in a loop
    res = 0
    for item in items:
        if item.w <= cap:
            # If the whole item fits, put it in the knapsack
            res += item.v
            cap -= item.w
        else:
            # If the whole item does not fit, take a fraction of it
            res += (item.v / item.w) * cap
            # The knapsack is full, so exit the loop
            break
    return res

double fractionalKnapsack(vector<int> &wgt, vector<int> &val, int cap) {

    sort(items.begin(), items.end(), [](Item &a, Item &b) { return (double)a.v / a.w > (double)b.v / b.w; });
    // Make greedy choices in a loop
    double res = 0;

            res += item.v;
            cap -= item.w;

            // If the whole item does not fit, take a fraction of it
            res += (double)item.v / item.w * cap;
            // The knapsack is full, so exit the loop
            break;
        }
    }
    return res;
}

fn fractional_knapsack(wgt: &[i32], val: &[i32], mut cap: i32) -> f64 {

    let mut items = wgt
        .iter()

        .collect::<Vec<Item>>();
    // Sort by value per unit of weight, item.v / item.w, in descending order
    items.sort_by(|a, b| {

            .partial_cmp(&(a.v as f64 / a.w as f64))
            .unwrap()
    });
    // Make greedy choices in a loop

    for item in &items {

            // If the whole item fits, put it in the knapsack
            res += item.v as f64;
            cap -= item.w;
        } else {

            res += item.v as f64 / item.w as f64 * cap as f64;
            // The knapsack is full, so exit the loop
            break;

    }
    res
}

    // Create a list of items, each with a weight and a value

A built-in sort typically takes \(O(n \log n)\) time and \(O(\log n)\) or \(O(n)\) space, depending on the language's implementation.

After sorting, we may have to scan the entire list in the worst case, so the scan takes \(O(n)\) time, where \(n\) is the number of items.

We create a list of Item objects, so the space complexity is \(O(n)\).

items.title: 3.   Proof of correctness
items.text:
We use proof by contradiction. Suppose item \(x\) has the highest unit value and some algorithm finds a maximum value of res without including item \(x\).

Remove one unit of weight of any item in the knapsack and replace it with one unit of item \(x\). Since item \(x\) has the highest unit value, the new total must exceed res. This contradicts the assumption that res is optimal, so an optimal solution must include item \(x\).

We can make the same argument for the other items in the solution. In short, an item with a higher unit value is always a better choice, which establishes the greedy strategy.

Figure 15-6 plots weight on the horizontal axis and unit value on the vertical axis. In these terms, the fractional knapsack problem asks how much area we can cover within a fixed horizontal interval. This gives us a geometric way to see why the greedy strategy works.

Figure 15-6   A geometric view of fractional knapsack

items.title: 15.1   Greedy algorithms
items.text:
A greedy algorithm is a common way to solve optimization problems. At each decision point, it takes the option that looks best at that moment. The aim is to reach a globally optimal solution through locally optimal choices. Greedy algorithms are simple and efficient and have many practical applications.

Greedy algorithms and dynamic programming are both common approaches to optimization. They share some features, such as relying on optimal substructure, but they work differently.

  • Dynamic programming considers the full range of earlier decisions when making a decision at the current stage. It builds the solution to the current subproblem from solutions to earlier subproblems.
  • A greedy algorithm moves forward without reconsidering earlier decisions. Each greedy choice reduces the size of the remaining problem until the problem is solved.

Let's see how a greedy algorithm works by revisiting coin change, a problem we met in the section on unbounded knapsack.

Question

You are given \(n\) coin denominations. Denomination \(i\) is worth \(coins[i - 1]\), and the target amount is \(amt\). You may use each denomination repeatedly. What is the minimum number of coins needed to make the target amount? Return \(-1\) if the amount cannot be made.

Figure 15-1 shows the greedy strategy. Starting with the target amount, choose the largest coin that does not exceed the remaining amount. Repeat until the coins add up to the target.

Figure 15-1   Greedy strategy for coin change

Here is the implementation:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby coin_change_greedy.py
def coin_change_greedy(coins: list[int], amt: int) -> int:
    """Greedy coin change"""
    # Assume the coins list is sorted
    i = len(coins) - 1
    count = 0
    # Make greedy choices until no amount remains
    while amt > 0:
        # Find the largest denomination that does not exceed the remaining amount
        while i > 0 and coins[i] > amt:
            i -= 1
        # Choose coins[i]
        amt -= coins[i]
        count += 1
    # Return -1 if no feasible solution was found
    return count if amt == 0 else -1

items.title: 15.1.1   Strengths and limitations of greedy algorithms
items.text:
Greedy algorithms are straightforward to use, simple to implement, and often very efficient. In the code above, let \(\min(coins)\) be the smallest denomination. The greedy choice repeats at most \(amt / \min(coins)\) times, giving a time complexity of \(O(amt / \min(coins))\). This is an order of magnitude lower than the \(O(n \times amt)\) time complexity of the dynamic programming solution.

However, for some sets of denominations, the greedy algorithm fails to find an optimal solution. Figure 15-2 shows two examples.

  • Where greedy succeeds: \(coins = [1, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100]\). With these denominations, the greedy algorithm finds an optimal solution for any \(amt\).
  • Counterexample: \(coins = [1, 20, 50]\). Suppose \(amt = 60\). The greedy algorithm chooses \(50 + 1 \times 10\), using \(11\) coins. Dynamic programming finds the optimal combination \(20 + 20 + 20\), which takes only \(3\) coins.
  • Counterexample: \(coins = [1, 49, 50]\). Suppose \(amt = 98\). The greedy algorithm chooses \(50 + 1 \times 48\), using \(49\) coins. Dynamic programming finds the optimal combination \(49 + 49\), which takes only \(2\) coins.

Figure 15-2   Examples where greedy coin change misses the optimum

For coin change in general, a greedy algorithm cannot guarantee a global optimum and may give a very poor solution. Dynamic programming is a better fit for the general problem.

Greedy algorithms are generally useful in two situations.

  1. An optimal solution is guaranteed. A greedy algorithm is often the best choice here because it is usually more efficient than backtracking or dynamic programming.
  2. A near-optimal solution is possible. A greedy algorithm can still be useful here. For many complex problems, finding a global optimum is difficult, and an efficient way to get a good suboptimal solution is valuable.

items.title: 15.1.2   Properties of greedy algorithms
items.text:
What kinds of problems are good candidates for a greedy algorithm? In particular, when can we guarantee that it will find an optimal solution?

Greedy algorithms have stricter requirements than dynamic programming. Two properties of the problem are particularly important.

  • Greedy-choice property. A greedy algorithm can guarantee an optimal solution only if a locally optimal choice can always lead to a globally optimal solution.
  • Optimal substructure. An optimal solution to the original problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems.

We covered optimal substructure in the chapter on dynamic programming. One point worth keeping in mind is that some problems admit a greedy solution even when their optimal substructure is hard to see.

Let's focus on how to recognize the greedy-choice property. The property is simple to state, but for many problems it is difficult to prove.

Take coin change. It is easy to give a counterexample that disproves the greedy-choice property, but proving the property is harder. What conditions must a set of denominations satisfy for greedy coin change to work? Intuition and examples may suggest an answer, but turning it into a rigorous mathematical proof is difficult.

Quote

One paper gives an \(O(n^3)\)-time algorithm for deciding whether greedy coin change is optimal for every amount with a given set of denominations.

Pearson, D. A polynomial-time algorithm for the change-making problem[J]. Operations Research Letters, 2005, 33(3): 231-234.

items.title: 15.1.3   Steps for solving a problem with a greedy algorithm
items.text:
Solving a problem with a greedy algorithm generally involves three steps.

  1. Analyze the problem. Identify the states, the objective to optimize, and the constraints. This step also comes up in backtracking and dynamic programming.
  2. Choose a greedy strategy. Decide how to make the greedy choice at each step. Each choice should reduce the size of the remaining problem until the entire problem is solved.
  3. Prove correctness. Typically, you need to show that the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. This may require a mathematical proof, for example by induction or contradiction.

Choosing the greedy strategy is central to solving the problem, but it can be difficult for two main reasons.

  • Greedy strategies vary widely from one problem to another. For many problems, a little thought and experimentation reveal a straightforward strategy. For more complex problems, the strategy can be hard to spot, putting your problem-solving experience and algorithm design skills to the test.
  • Some greedy strategies are deceptive. You may feel confident in a strategy, implement it, and submit the code only to find that it fails some test cases. Such a strategy works only some of the time. Coin change is a classic example.

To establish correctness, we should give a rigorous mathematical proof of the greedy strategy, typically by contradiction or induction.

Finding a proof can itself be difficult. When we are stuck, we often debug the code against test cases, revising and checking the strategy one step at a time.

items.title: 15.1.4   Common greedy algorithm problems
items.text:
Greedy algorithms often solve optimization problems with the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. Here are some typical examples.

  • Coin change. For certain sets of denominations, the greedy algorithm always gives an optimal solution.
  • Interval scheduling. Each task occupies a time interval, and you want to complete as many tasks as possible. Always choosing the available task that finishes earliest gives an optimal schedule.
  • Fractional knapsack. Given items and a weight limit, choose items to maximize total value without exceeding that limit. In some settings, always taking the item with the greatest value-to-weight ratio (value / weight) gives an optimal solution.
  • Buying and selling stock. Given a stock's historical prices, you may buy and sell multiple times. Once you buy, you must sell before buying again. The goal is to maximize profit.
  • Huffman coding. This greedy algorithm performs lossless data compression. To build a Huffman tree, repeatedly merge the two nodes with the lowest frequencies. The resulting tree minimizes the weighted path length (the encoded length).
  • Dijkstra's algorithm. In a graph with nonnegative edge weights, this greedy algorithm finds the shortest paths from a given source vertex to all other vertices.

items.title: 15.3   Maximum capacity problem
items.text:
Question

You are given an array \(ht\) in which each element is the height of a vertical board. Any two boards and the space between them form a container.

The container's capacity is its area: height times width. The shorter board sets the height, and the difference between the boards' array indices gives the width.

Choose two boards that form a container of maximum capacity and return that capacity. Figure 15-7 shows an example.

Figure 15-7   Example data for the maximum capacity problem

Any pair of boards forms a container, so the state is the pair of board indices, denoted by \([i, j]\).

Capacity is height times width. The shorter board sets the height, and the difference between the board indices gives the width. Writing the capacity as \(cap[i, j]\) gives the formula:

\[ cap[i, j] = \min(ht[i], ht[j]) \times (j - i) \]

For an array of length \(n\), there are \(C_n^2 = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}\) pairs of boards, one for each possible state. The most direct approach is to try every state and return the largest capacity. This takes \(O(n^2)\) time.

items.title: 1.   Choosing a greedy strategy
items.text:
There is a more efficient solution. Consider a state \([i, j]\) with indices \(i < j\) and heights \(ht[i] < ht[j]\), as shown below. The board at \(i\) is shorter and the one at \(j\) is taller.

Figure 15-8   Initial state

As Figure 15-9 shows, moving inward from the taller board at \(j\) toward the shorter board at \(i\) must reduce capacity.

Moving the pointer at the taller board \(j\) reduces the width \(j-i\). The shorter board sets the height, so the height can only stay the same (if \(i\) is still the shorter board) or decrease (if the new board at \(j\) is shorter).

Figure 15-9   State after moving inward from the taller board

Conversely, the only move that can increase capacity is to move inward from the shorter board at \(i\). Although the width must decrease, the height might increase if the new board at \(i\) is taller. In Figure 15-10, for example, moving from the shorter board increases the area.

Figure 15-10   State after moving inward from the shorter board

This gives us a greedy strategy. Start the two pointers at opposite ends of the container. At each step, move the pointer at the shorter board inward until the pointers meet.

Figure 15-11 shows the greedy strategy in action.

  1. Start with the pointers \(i\) and \(j\) at opposite ends of the array.
  2. Calculate the capacity \(cap[i, j]\) for the current state and update the maximum capacity so far.
  3. Compare the heights of boards \(i\) and \(j\) and move the pointer at the shorter board one position inward.
  4. Repeat steps 2. and 3. until \(i\) and \(j\) meet.
<1><2><3><4><5><6><7><8><9>

Figure 15-11   Greedy search for maximum capacity

items.title: 2.   Implementation
items.text:
The loop runs at most \(n\) times, so the time complexity is \(O(n)\).

The variables \(i\), \(j\), and \(res\) use a constant amount of extra space, so the space complexity is \(O(1)\).

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby max_capacity.py
def max_capacity(ht: list[int]) -> int:
    """Greedy maximum capacity algorithm"""
    # Start i and j at opposite ends of the array
    i, j = 0, len(ht) - 1
    # The initial maximum capacity is 0
    res = 0
    # Make greedy choices until the two pointers meet
    while i < j:
        # Update the maximum capacity
        cap = min(ht[i], ht[j]) * (j - i)
        res = max(res, cap)
        # Move the pointer at the shorter board inward
        if ht[i] < ht[j]:
            i += 1
        else:
            j -= 1
    return res

items.title: 3.   Proof of correctness
items.text:
The greedy search is faster than exhaustive search because each greedy choice skips some states.

For example, in state \(cap[i, j]\), the board at \(i\) is shorter than the one at \(j\). Moving one position inward from the shorter board at \(i\) skips the states shown below. The algorithm can no longer check the capacities of those states.

\[ cap[i, i+1], cap[i, i+2], \dots, cap[i, j-2], cap[i, j-1] \]

Figure 15-12   States skipped when moving inward from the shorter board

The skipped states are exactly the ones we would reach by moving inward from the taller board at \(j\). We have already shown that such a move reduces capacity. None of these states can be optimal, so skipping them cannot cause us to miss the optimum.

Moving inward from the shorter board is therefore safe, and the greedy strategy is valid.

items.title: 15.4   Maximum product after cutting
items.text:
Question

Given a positive integer \(n\), write it as a sum of at least two positive integers. What is the largest possible product of those integers? Figure 15-13 illustrates the problem.

Figure 15-13   Defining the maximum product after cutting

Suppose we split \(n\) into \(m\) integer pieces, with piece \(i\) denoted by \(n_i\). Then

\[ n = \sum_{i=1}^{m}n_i \]

Our goal is to maximize the product of all the pieces:

\[ \max(\prod_{i=1}^{m}n_i) \]

How many pieces should we make (\(m\)), and how large should each piece \(n_i\) be?

items.title: 1.   Choosing a greedy strategy
items.text:
The product of two integers is often greater than their sum. If we cut a piece of size \(2\) from \(n\), the two pieces have product \(2(n-2)\). Let's compare this product with \(n\):

\[ \begin{aligned} 2(n-2) & \geq n \newline 2n - n - 4 & \geq 0 \newline n & \geq 4 \end{aligned} \]

As Figure 15-14 shows, when \(n \geq 4\), cutting off a piece of size \(2\) increases the product. This suggests that every integer greater than or equal to \(4\) should be split.

First greedy rule. If a split contains a factor \(\geq 4\), split it again. The final split should contain only factors of \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\).

Figure 15-14   Cutting increases the product

Which factor is best? Of \(1\), \(2\), and \(3\), the worst is \(1\), because \(1 \times (n-1) < n\) always holds. Cutting off a piece of size \(1\) actually reduces the product.

As shown below, when \(n = 6\), we have \(3 \times 3 > 2 \times 2 \times 2\). This means pieces of size \(3\) are preferable to pieces of size \(2\).

Second greedy rule. A split should contain at most two factors of \(2\). Three factors of \(2\) can always be replaced by two factors of \(3\) to obtain a larger product.

Figure 15-15   Optimal factors for the split

These observations give us the following greedy strategy.

  1. Given the integer \(n\), repeatedly cut off pieces of size \(3\) until the remainder is \(0\), \(1\), or \(2\).
  2. If the remainder is \(0\), then \(n\) is a multiple of \(3\), so no adjustment is needed.
  3. If the remainder is \(2\), keep it as a piece without splitting it further.
  4. If the remainder is \(1\), then because \(2 \times 2 > 1 \times 3\), replace the last \(3\) and the leftover \(1\) with two pieces of size \(2\).

items.title: 2.   Implementation
items.text:
As Figure 15-16 shows, we can skip the loop that cuts individual pieces. Floor division gives the number \(a\) of pieces of size \(3\), and the remainder operation gives the leftover amount \(b\). Thus:

\[ n = 3 a + b \]

For the boundary cases \(n \leq 3\), we must cut off a piece of size \(1\), giving a product of \(1 \times (n - 1)\).

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby max_product_cutting.py
def max_product_cutting(n: int) -> int:
    """Greedy maximum product algorithm"""
    # When n <= 3, one piece must be 1
    if n <= 3:
        return 1 * (n - 1)
    # Greedily cut off pieces of size 3. Let a be their count and b the remainder
    a, b = n // 3, n % 3
    if b == 1:
        # If the remainder is 1, replace one pair 1 * 3 with 2 * 2
        return int(math.pow(3, a - 1)) * 2 * 2
    if b == 2:
        # If the remainder is 2, leave it as is
        return int(math.pow(3, a)) * 2
    # If the remainder is 0, no adjustment is needed
    return int(math.pow(3, a))

items.title: 3.   Proof of correctness
items.text:
We use proof by contradiction and consider only \(n \geq 4\).

  1. All factors are \(\leq 3\). Suppose an optimal split contains a factor \(x\) that is \(\geq 4\). We can split it again to obtain the product \(2(x-2)\), giving a larger or equal product. This contradicts the assumption.
  2. The split contains no factor of \(1\). Suppose an optimal split contains a factor of \(1\). We can merge it into another piece to obtain a larger product, contradicting optimality.
  3. The split contains at most two factors of \(2\). Suppose an optimal split contains three factors of \(2\). Replacing them with two factors of \(3\) gives a larger product, contradicting optimality.

items.title: 1.   Key points
items.text:
• Greedy algorithms typically solve optimization problems by making a locally optimal choice at each decision point in the hope of reaching a global optimum.
  • A greedy algorithm makes one choice after another. Each choice reduces the problem to a smaller subproblem, and the process continues until the problem is solved.
  • Greedy algorithms are easy to implement and efficient. They usually have lower time complexity than dynamic programming.
  • For some sets of coin denominations, greedy coin change is guaranteed to find an optimal solution. For other sets, it can give a very poor solution.
  • Problems suited to greedy algorithms have two properties: the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. The greedy-choice property is what makes the greedy strategy valid.
  • For some complex problems, the greedy-choice property is difficult to prove. It can be easier to disprove, as the coin change example shows.
  • Solving a greedy problem involves three main steps: analyze the problem, choose a greedy strategy, and prove correctness. Choosing the strategy is the central step, and proving correctness is often the hardest part.
  • Fractional knapsack extends 0-1 knapsack by allowing a fraction of an item to be taken. This makes a greedy solution possible. Its correctness can be proved by contradiction.
  • An exhaustive search for maximum capacity takes \(O(n^2)\) time. Moving the pointer at the shorter board inward at each step gives a greedy strategy that reduces the time to \(O(n)\).
  • For the maximum product after cutting, we derived two greedy rules: keep splitting integers \(\geq 4\), and favor factors of \(3\). The code uses exponentiation, so its time complexity depends on the implementation of that operation, usually \(O(1)\) or \(O(\log n)\).

items.title: 1.   Looking up an element after a hash collision
items.text:
A hash table has 5 buckets and uses the hash function \(h(x)=x \bmod 5\). When elements collide, append them to the list in that bucket in insertion order. Insert the elements of [1, 6, 11, 7] in order.

  1. Write down the contents of buckets 0 through 4.
  2. When looking up 6, which bucket do you visit first, and which elements do you check, in what order?
  3. Look at the buckets you wrote down in part 1. Did any later insertion overwrite an earlier element? Explain how this collision resolution method accounts for your answer.
Sample answer

  1. Since \(1\bmod5=6\bmod5=11\bmod5=1\) and \(7\bmod5=2\), the buckets contain the following elements:

    0: []
1: [1, 6, 11]
2: [7]
3: []
4: []

  2. To find 6, go to bucket 1 and compare the target with 1, then 6. The second comparison finds a match.

  3. Equal hash values tell us only that the elements land in the same bucket. The elements themselves can differ. Chaining keeps all the colliding elements in the bucket and compares them one at a time during lookup, so 1, 6, and 11 do not overwrite one another.

items.title: 2.   Where do elements go when a hash table grows?
items.text:
A hash table that uses chaining starts with 5 buckets and the hash function \(h(x)=x\bmod5\). The keys [1, 6, 11] are all in bucket 1.

Now expand the table to 7 buckets and change the hash function accordingly to \(h(x)=x\bmod7\).

  1. Calculate the new bucket numbers for 1, 6, and 11.
  2. Which buckets contain elements after the table grows?
  3. Can you copy the original list in bucket 1 directly into the new bucket 1? Use your results from parts 1 and 2 to explain.
Sample answer

  1. The new bucket numbers are as follows:

    • \(1\bmod7=1\),
    • \(6\bmod7=6\),
    • \(11\bmod7=4\).

  2. Bucket 1 holds 1, bucket 4 holds 11, and bucket 6 holds 6. The three keys no longer share a bucket.

  3. No. The bucket number is the remainder when the key is divided by the number of buckets. Increasing the number of buckets from 5 to 7 can change the bucket number for a given key, so you must recalculate each key’s position. If you copied the old bucket 1 as is, later lookups for 6 and 11 would use the new formula and go to buckets 6 and 4, respectively, where neither key would be found.

items.title: 3.   Can you still find 11 after deleting 6?
items.text:
A hash table has 5 slots indexed 0–4 and uses the hash function \(h(x)=x\bmod5\). When a collision occurs, start at the index given by the hash function and move right until you find an empty slot.

Insert the elements of [1, 6, 11] in order.

  1. At which index does each of the three numbers end up?
  2. Which indices do you check, in order, when looking up 11?
  3. Suppose that deleting 6 marks its slot as empty and never used, and that a lookup stops at an empty slot. What happens when you look up 11 again? Is the result correct? If there is a problem, how can you avoid it?
Sample answer

  1. Place 1 at index 1. The number 6 also maps to index 1, so the collision sends it to index 2. The number 11 also starts at index 1. It skips occupied indices 1 and 2 in turn and ends up at index 3.

  2. To look up 11, check the indices in the order 1, 2, 3. You find it at index 3.

  3. If you mark index 2 as empty and never used, a lookup for 11 checks index 1 and stops at index 2, incorrectly concluding that 11 is absent. Leave a “deleted” marker when removing an element: a lookup that encounters the marker continues to the next index (wrapping from index 4 to index 0), and a later insertion can reuse the slot.

items.title: 1.   Comparing the letters in two strings
items.text:
You are given two strings, s and t, that contain only lowercase English letters. You may rearrange the characters in s in any order, but you cannot add, remove, or replace characters.

Can you obtain t this way? Return true if you can and false otherwise. Use a hash table to count the occurrences of each letter without sorting the characters in either string.

Hints
  1. If the strings have different lengths, their letter counts cannot all match.
  2. Use a hash table to count each letter. As you scan s, add 1 to the count for each letter you encounter.
  3. As you scan t, subtract 1 from the corresponding count. The strings contain the same letters with the same frequencies only if all counts end at 0.

items.title: 6.3   Hash algorithms
items.text:
The previous two sections explained how hash tables work and how they handle collisions. Both open addressing and chaining keep a hash table working correctly when collisions occur, but neither reduces the number of collisions.

Frequent collisions can sharply degrade hash table performance. Figure 6-8 shows a hash table with chaining. Ideally, the pairs are evenly distributed across buckets, giving the fastest lookups. In the worst case, all pairs land in a single bucket, and lookup time degrades to \(O(n)\).

Figure 6-8   Best and worst cases for hash collisions

The hash function determines how the key-value pairs are distributed. Recall its two steps: compute the hash value, then take the remainder modulo the array length.

index = hash(key) % capacity

In this formula, when the table capacity capacity is fixed, the hash algorithm hash() determines the output and thus how the key-value pairs are distributed across the table.

To reduce the likelihood of collisions, we therefore need to focus on the design of the hash algorithm hash().

items.title: 6.3.1   Goals of a hash algorithm
items.text:
A fast, reliable hash table needs a hash algorithm with the following properties.

  • Determinism. The same input should always produce the same output so that the table works reliably.
  • Efficiency. Computing a hash value should be fast. The lower the cost, the more practical the table is to use.
  • Uniform distribution. The algorithm should spread key-value pairs evenly across the table. The more uniform the distribution, the less likely a collision becomes.

Hash algorithms also have many uses beyond implementing hash tables.

  • Password storage. To protect passwords, systems typically store a hash of each password instead of the plaintext. When a user enters a password, the system hashes it and compares the result with the stored hash. If they match, the system accepts the password.
  • Data integrity checks. A sender can compute a hash of the data and send it along with the data. The recipient hashes the data received and compares the result with the hash received. If they match, the data is considered intact.

Cryptographic applications need stronger security properties to prevent someone from working backward from a hash, for example to recover the original password.

  • One-way operation. It should be infeasible to work backward from the hash value to recover information about the input.
  • Collision resistance. Finding two different inputs with the same hash value should be extremely difficult.
  • Avalanche effect. A small change to the input should cause a large, unpredictable change in the output.

Uniform distribution and collision resistance are distinct properties. A uniform distribution does not guarantee collision resistance. For example, with random inputs key, the function key % 100 can produce uniformly distributed outputs. Yet this algorithm is so simple that every key with the same last two digits gives the same output. Given a hash, it is easy to find a key that works and thereby defeat the password check.

items.title: 6.3.2   Designing a hash algorithm
items.text:
Designing a hash algorithm is complex and requires balancing many factors. For less demanding applications, however, we can design simple algorithms.

  • Additive hashing adds the ASCII codes of all the input characters and uses the sum as the hash value.
  • Multiplicative hashing mixes the character contributions by multiplying the running hash by a constant each round and accumulating each character’s ASCII code.
  • XOR hashing combines each input element with the running hash using XOR.
  • Rotation hashing rotates the running hash before incorporating the ASCII code of each character.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby simple_hash.py
def add_hash(key: str) -> int:
    """Additive hashing"""
    hash = 0
    modulus = 1000000007
    for c in key:
        hash += ord(c)
    return hash % modulus

def mul_hash(key: str) -> int:
    """Multiplicative hashing"""
    hash = 0
    modulus = 1000000007
    for c in key:
        hash = 31 * hash + ord(c)
    return hash % modulus

def xor_hash(key: str) -> int:
    """XOR hashing"""
    hash = 0
    modulus = 1000000007
    for c in key:
        hash ^= ord(c)
    return hash % modulus

def rot_hash(key: str) -> int:
    """Rotation hashing"""
    hash = 0
    modulus = 1000000007
    for c in key:
        hash = (hash << 4) ^ (hash >> 28) ^ ord(c)
    return hash % modulus

Each algorithm takes the result modulo the large prime \(1000000007\) as its final step to keep the hash in a suitable range. Why use a prime modulus? What can go wrong with a composite modulus?

A large prime modulus gives the best chance of distributing hash values evenly. Because a prime shares no nontrivial factor with numbers that are not its multiples, it can reduce periodic patterns introduced by the remainder operation and help avoid collisions.

For example, suppose we choose the composite modulus \(9\). It is divisible by \(3\), so every key divisible by \(3\) maps to one of just three hash values: \(0\), \(3\), or \(6\).

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{modulus} & = 9 \newline \text{key} & = \{ 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, \dots \} \newline \text{hash} & = \{ 0, 3, 6, 0, 3, 6, 0, 3, 6, 0, 3, 6,\dots \} \end{aligned} \]

If the input values of key follow this arithmetic progression, the hashes cluster, leading to more collisions. Now set modulus to the prime \(13\). The step between successive key values has no common factor greater than one with modulus, so the hash values are much more evenly distributed.

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{modulus} & = 13 \newline \text{key} & = \{ 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30, 33, \dots \} \newline \text{hash} & = \{ 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 2, 5, 8, 11, 1, 4, 7, \dots \} \end{aligned} \]

If key is uniformly random, either a prime or a composite modulus can produce evenly distributed hash values. When key follows a periodic pattern, however, a composite modulus is more likely to produce clusters.

We therefore usually choose a prime modulus, preferably a large one, to suppress periodic patterns as much as possible and make the algorithm more robust.

items.title: 6.3.3   Common hash algorithms
items.text:
The simple algorithms above are fragile and fall well short of the design goals. For example, addition and XOR are commutative, so additive and XOR hashing cannot distinguish strings that contain the same characters in different orders. This can increase collisions and cause security problems.

In practice, standard hash algorithms include MD5, SHA-1, SHA-2, and SHA-3. They map inputs of any length to fixed-length hash values.

Over nearly a century, hash algorithms have undergone continual refinement. Some researchers work to improve their performance, while other researchers and hackers look for security weaknesses. Table 6-2 lists common hash algorithms used in practice.

  • Successful attacks against MD5 and SHA-1 have led security applications to phase them out.
  • SHA-256, a member of the SHA-2 family, is among the most secure hash algorithms. It has withstood attacks to date and is widely used in security applications and protocols.
  • SHA-3 has lower implementation overhead and higher computational efficiency than SHA-2, but the SHA-2 family is still more widely used.

Table 6-2   Common hash algorithms

MD5 SHA-1 SHA-2 SHA-3 Year introduced 1992 1995 2002 2008 Output length 128 bit 160 bit 256/512 bit 224/256/384/512 bit Hash collisions Relatively frequent Relatively frequent Rare Rare Security level Low; successful attacks exist Low; successful attacks exist High High Applications Deprecated, still used for data integrity checks Deprecated Cryptocurrency transaction verification, digital signatures, and more Can serve as an alternative to SHA-2

items.title: 6.3.4   Hash values of data structures
items.text:
A hash table’s key can be an integer, a floating-point number, a string, or another data type. Programming languages typically provide built-in hashing for these types so a table can compute a bucket index. In Python, for example, we can call hash() to compute hash values for several data types.

  • Integers and Booleans hash to their own numeric values.
  • Hashing floating-point numbers and strings is more involved. Interested readers can explore these calculations further.
  • To hash a tuple, hash each element and combine the results into a single hash value.
  • An object’s hash value is based on its memory address. You can override its hash method to generate a hash based on its contents.

Tip

Programming languages differ in how they define and implement their built-in hash functions.

In many programming languages, only immutable objects can serve as a hash table’s key. Suppose we used a list (a dynamic array) as a key. Changing the contents of the list would change its hash value, and we would no longer be able to look up the original value in the table.

A user-defined object, such as a linked list node, can be hashable even though its fields can change. An object’s hash is typically based on its memory address. Changes to its contents leave its address, and therefore its hash, unchanged.

You may notice different hash values when you run the program in different consoles. Each time the Python interpreter starts, it supplies a random salt to the string hash function. This helps prevent HashDoS attacks and makes hashing more secure.

items.title: 6.2   Hash collisions
items.text:
As the previous section explained, a hash function typically has far more possible inputs than outputs, so collisions are theoretically unavoidable. For example, if the inputs are all integers and the number of possible outputs equals the array capacity, multiple integers must map to the same bucket index.

Collisions can lead to incorrect lookup results, severely limiting the usefulness of our hash table. One solution is to expand the table whenever a collision occurs and keep expanding until the collision disappears. This brute-force approach works, but it is inefficient because resizing requires moving many entries and recomputing their hashes. We can improve efficiency with the following strategies.

  1. Change the structure of the table so it works correctly even when collisions occur.
  2. Expand the table only when necessary, once collisions become a significant problem.

The two main structural approaches are separate chaining and open addressing.

items.title: 6.2.1   Separate chaining
items.text:
In the original table, each bucket holds only one key-value pair. With separate chaining, a linked list replaces the single entry. Each node holds a key-value pair, and all pairs that collide go into the same list. Figure 6-5 shows an example.

Figure 6-5   Hash table with chaining

With chaining, hash table operations change as follows.

  • Lookup. Pass key to the hash function to get the bucket index and access the head of its list. Walk the list, comparing each node’s key with key to find the target pair.
  • Insertion. Use the hash function to locate the head of the list, then add a node containing the key-value pair to the list.
  • Deletion. Use the hash function to reach the head of the list. Walk the list to find the target node and remove it.

Chaining has the following limitations.

  • Higher memory usage. A linked list needs pointers to link its nodes, so it uses more memory than an array.
  • Slower lookups. Finding a particular element requires scanning the list linearly.

The following code implements a simple hash table with chaining. Two details are worth noting.

  • To simplify the code, we use lists (dynamic arrays) in place of linked lists. The hash table is an array of buckets, each of which is itself a list.
  • The implementation includes a method for expanding the table. When the load factor exceeds \(\frac{2}{3}\), we increase the capacity to \(2\) times its previous value.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby hash_map_chaining.py
class HashMapChaining:
    """Hash table with chaining"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self.size = 0  # Number of key-value pairs
        self.capacity = 4  # Hash table capacity
        self.load_thres = 2.0 / 3.0  # Load factor threshold for resizing
        self.extend_ratio = 2  # Growth factor
        self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(self.capacity)]  # Bucket array

    def hash_func(self, key: int) -> int:
        """Hash function"""
        return key % self.capacity

    def load_factor(self) -> float:
        """Load factor"""
        return self.size / self.capacity

    def get(self, key: int) -> str | None:
        """Look up a value"""
        index = self.hash_func(key)
        bucket = self.buckets[index]
        # Scan the bucket and return the corresponding val if key is found
        for pair in bucket:
            if pair.key == key:
                return pair.val
        # Return None if key is absent
        return None

    def put(self, key: int, val: str):
        """Insert a key-value pair"""
        # Expand the table when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if self.load_factor() > self.load_thres:
            self.extend()
        index = self.hash_func(key)
        bucket = self.buckets[index]
        # Scan the bucket. If the specified key is found, update its val and return
        for pair in bucket:
            if pair.key == key:
                pair.val = val
                return
        # If key is absent, append the pair to the end of the list
        pair = Pair(key, val)
        bucket.append(pair)
        self.size += 1

    def remove(self, key: int):
        """Remove a key-value pair"""
        index = self.hash_func(key)
        bucket = self.buckets[index]
        # Scan the bucket and remove the pair
        for pair in bucket:
            if pair.key == key:
                bucket.remove(pair)
                self.size -= 1
                break

    def extend(self):
        """Expand the hash table"""
        # Save the original hash table
        buckets = self.buckets
        # Initialize the larger hash table
        self.capacity *= self.extend_ratio
        self.buckets = [[] for _ in range(self.capacity)]
        self.size = 0
        # Move the key-value pairs from the old table into the new one
        for bucket in buckets:
            for pair in bucket:
                self.put(pair.key, pair.val)

    def print(self):
        """Print the hash table"""
        for bucket in self.buckets:
            res = []
            for pair in bucket:
                res.append(str(pair.key) + " -> " + pair.val)
            print(res)

/* Hash table with chaining */
class HashMapChaining {
  private:
    int size;                       // Number of key-value pairs
    int capacity;                   // Hash table capacity
    double loadThres;               // Load factor threshold for resizing
    int extendRatio;                // Growth factor
    vector<vector<Pair *>> buckets; // Bucket array

}

func (m *hashMapChaining) get(key int) string {

        }
    }

}

func (m *hashMapChaining) put(key int, val string) {

    if m.loadFactor() > m.loadThres {
        m.extend()
    }
    idx := m.hashFunc(key)
    // Scan the bucket. If the specified key is found, update its val and return
    for i := range m.buckets[idx] {
        if m.buckets[idx][i].key == key {
            m.buckets[idx][i].val = val
            return
        }
    }
    // If key is absent, append the pair to the end of the list
    p := pair{
        key: key,
        val: val,
    }
    m.buckets[idx] = append(m.buckets[idx], p)
    m.size += 1
}

/* Remove a key-value pair */
func (m *hashMapChaining) remove(key int) {
    idx := m.hashFunc(key)
    // Scan the bucket and remove the pair
    for i, p := range m.buckets[idx] {
        if p.key == key {
            // Delete from the slice
            m.buckets[idx] = append(m.buckets[idx][:i], m.buckets[idx][i+1:]...)
            m.size -= 1
            break
        }
    }
}

func (m *hashMapChaining) extend() {
    // Save the original hash table
    tmpBuckets := make([][]pair, len(m.buckets))
    for i := 0; i < len(m.buckets); i++ {
        tmpBuckets[i] = make([]pair, len(m.buckets[i]))
        copy(tmpBuckets[i], m.buckets[i])
    }
    // Initialize the larger hash table
    m.capacity *= m.extendRatio
    m.buckets = make([][]pair, m.capacity)
    for i := 0; i < m.capacity; i++ {

    }

    fn extend(&mut self) {
        // Save the original hash table
        let buckets_tmp = std::mem::take(&mut self.buckets);

        // Initialize the larger hash table
        self.capacity *= self.extend_ratio;
        self.buckets = vec![Vec::new(); self.capacity as usize];
        self.size = 0;

        // Move the key-value pairs from the old table into the new one
        for bucket in buckets_tmp {
            for pair in bucket {
                self.put(pair.key, pair.val);
            }
        }
    }

    /* Print the hash table */
    fn print(&self) {
        for bucket in &self.buckets {
            let mut res = Vec::new();
            for pair in bucket {
                res.push(format!("{} -> {}", pair.key, pair.val));
            }
            println!("{:?}", res);
        }
    }

    /* Insert a key-value pair */
    fn put(&mut self, key: i32, val: String) {
        // Expand the table when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if self.load_factor() > self.load_thres {
            self.extend();
        }

        let index = self.hash_func(key);

        // Scan the bucket. If the specified key is found, update its val and return
        for pair in self.buckets[index].iter_mut() {
            if pair.key == key {
                pair.val = val;
                return;
            }
        }

        // If key is absent, append the pair to the end of the list
        let pair = Pair { key, val };
        self.buckets[index].push(pair);
        self.size += 1;
    }

    /* Look up a value */
    fn get(&self, key: i32) -> Option<&str> {
        let index = self.hash_func(key);

        // Scan the bucket and return the corresponding val if key is found
        for pair in self.buckets[index].iter() {
            if pair.key == key {
                return Some(&pair.val);
            }
        }

        // Return None if key is absent
        None
    }
}

        hashMap->buckets[i] = NULL;
    }

}

/* Destructor */

    for (int i = 0; i < hashMap->capacity; i++) {
        Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[i];
        while (cur) {

            cur = cur->next;

        }
    }

    free(hashMap);
}

/* Hash function */

}

/* Load factor */

    return (double)hashMap->size / (double)hashMap->capacity;
}

/* Look up a value */
char *get(HashMapChaining *hashMap, int key) {

    // Scan the bucket and return the corresponding val if key is found
    Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[index];
    while (cur) {
        if (cur->pair->key == key) {
            return cur->pair->val;
        }
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    return ""; // Return an empty string if key is absent
}

/* Insert a key-value pair */
void put(HashMapChaining *hashMap, int key, const char *val) {
    // Expand the table when the load factor exceeds the threshold
    if (loadFactor(hashMap) > hashMap->loadThres) {
        extend(hashMap);
    }
    int index = hashFunc(hashMap, key);
    // Scan the bucket. If the specified key is found, update its val and return
    Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[index];
    while (cur) {
        if (cur->pair->key == key) {
            strcpy(cur->pair->val, val); // If the specified key is found, update its val and return
            return;
        }
        cur = cur->next;
    }
    // If key is absent, insert the pair at the head of the list
    Pair *newPair = (Pair *)malloc(sizeof(Pair));
    newPair->key = key;
    strcpy(newPair->val, val);
    Node *newNode = (Node *)malloc(sizeof(Node));
    newNode->pair = newPair;
    newNode->next = hashMap->buckets[index];
    hashMap->buckets[index] = newNode;
    hashMap->size++;
}

/* Expand the hash table */
void extend(HashMapChaining *hashMap) {
    // Save the original hash table
    int oldCapacity = hashMap->capacity;
    Node **oldBuckets = hashMap->buckets;
    // Initialize the larger hash table
    hashMap->capacity *= hashMap->extendRatio;
    hashMap->buckets = (Node **)malloc(hashMap->capacity * sizeof(Node *));
    for (int i = 0; i < hashMap->capacity; i++) {
        hashMap->buckets[i] = NULL;
    }
    hashMap->size = 0;
    // Move the key-value pairs from the old table into the new one
    for (int i = 0; i < oldCapacity; i++) {
        Node *cur = oldBuckets[i];
        while (cur) {
            put(hashMap, cur->pair->key, cur->pair->val);
            Node *temp = cur;
            cur = cur->next;
            // Free the memory
            free(temp->pair);
            free(temp);
        }
    }

    free(oldBuckets);
}

/* Remove a key-value pair */
void removeItem(HashMapChaining *hashMap, int key) {
    int index = hashFunc(hashMap, key);
    Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[index];
    Node *pre = NULL;
    while (cur) {
        if (cur->pair->key == key) {
            // Remove the pair from the list
            if (pre) {
                pre->next = cur->next;
            } else {
                hashMap->buckets[index] = cur->next;
            }
            // Free the memory
            free(cur->pair);
            free(cur);
            hashMap->size--;
            return;
        }
        pre = cur;
        cur = cur->next;
    }
}

/* Print the hash table */
void print(HashMapChaining *hashMap) {
    for (int i = 0; i < hashMap->capacity; i++) {
        Node *cur = hashMap->buckets[i];
        printf("[");
        while (cur) {
            printf("%d -> %s, ", cur->pair->key, cur->pair->val);
            cur = cur->next;
        }
        printf("]\n");
    }
}

items.title: 6.2.2   Open addressing
items.text:
Open addressing handles collisions by probing multiple positions within the table, without introducing another data structure. Common methods include linear probing, quadratic probing, and probing with multiple hash functions.

We will use linear probing to see how a hash table with open addressing works.

items.title: 1.   Linear probing
items.text:
Linear probing searches in fixed-size steps. Its operations differ from those of the basic hash table.

  • Insertion. Compute the bucket index with the hash function. If the bucket is occupied, scan forward from that position in fixed steps (usually \(1\)) and insert the element in the first empty bucket.
  • Lookup. If a collision occurs, scan forward using the same step size. When you find the matching element, return its value. If you reach an empty bucket, the element is absent, so return None.

Figure 6-6 shows how open addressing with linear probing distributes key-value pairs. With this hash function, all key inputs with the same last two digits map to the same bucket. Linear probing stores them successively in that bucket and those below it.

Figure 6-6   Distribution of key-value pairs with open addressing and linear probing

However, linear probing tends to create clusters. The longer a run of occupied slots, the more likely a new key is to collide with an entry in that run. Each collision can extend the run, reinforcing the pattern. Eventually, insertions, deletions, lookups, and updates all slow down.

We cannot simply remove an element from an open-addressed hash table. Doing so leaves an empty bucket, None, where a linear search will stop. Elements farther along that probe sequence become unreachable, and the program may incorrectly report that they are absent, as Figure 6-7 shows.

Figure 6-7   How deletion can break lookup with open addressing

We can solve this problem with lazy deletion. Instead of simply removing the element and emptying its bucket, we mark the bucket with a constant, TOMBSTONE. Both None and TOMBSTONE represent available buckets that can hold a new pair. With linear probing, we must continue past TOMBSTONE because more pairs may lie farther along the probe sequence.

However, lazy deletion can make hash table performance degrade faster. Each deletion leaves a marker. As the number of TOMBSTONE markers grows, searches take longer because linear probing may have to skip several TOMBSTONE markers to reach the target.

To address this, record the index of the first TOMBSTONE encountered while probing. When you find the target, swap it with that TOMBSTONE. A lookup or insertion can thus move an element closer to its ideal position, the starting bucket for probing, and speed up later lookups.

The following code implements an open-addressed hash table with linear probing and lazy deletion. To make fuller use of the available space, we treat the table as a circular array: when probing passes the last slot, it continues at the first.

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby hash_map_open_addressing.py
class HashMapOpenAddressing:
    """Hash table with open addressing"""

    def __init__(self):
        """Constructor"""
        self.size = 0  # Number of key-value pairs
        self.capacity = 4  # Hash table capacity
        self.load_thres = 2.0 / 3.0  # Load factor threshold for resizing
        self.extend_ratio = 2  # Growth factor
        self.buckets: list[Pair | None] = [None] * self.capacity  # Bucket array
        self.TOMBSTONE = Pair(-1, "-1")  # Deletion marker

    def hash_func(self, key: int) -> int:
        """Hash function"""
        return key % self.capacity

    def load_factor(self) -> float:
        """Load factor"""
        return self.size / self.capacity

    def find_bucket(self, key: int) -> int:
        """Find the bucket index for key"""
        index = self.hash_func(key)
        first_tombstone = -1
        for _ in range(self.capacity):
            bucket = self.buckets[index]
            if bucket is None:
                break
            # Record the first deletion marker encountered
            if bucket is self.TOMBSTONE:
                if first_tombstone == -1:
                    first_tombstone = index
            # If key is found, return its bucket index
            elif bucket.key == key:
                # If a deletion marker was found earlier, move the pair to that index
                if first_tombstone != -1:
                    self.buckets[first_tombstone] = bucket
                    self.buckets[index] = self.TOMBSTONE
                    return first_tombstone  # Return the new bucket index
                return index  # Return the bucket index
            # Compute the next bucket index, wrapping to the start at the end
            index = (index + 1) % self.capacity
        # If key is absent, return the index for insertion
        return index if first_tombstone == -1 else first_tombstone

    def get(self, key: int) -> str:
        """Look up a value"""
        # Find the bucket index for key
        index = self.find_bucket(key)
        # If the pair is found, return its val
        if self.buckets[index] not in [None, self.TOMBSTONE]:
            return self.buckets[index].val
        # Return None if the pair is absent
        return None

    def put(self, key: int, val: str):
        """Insert a key-value pair"""
        # Expand the table when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if self.load_factor() > self.load_thres:
            self.extend()
        # Find the bucket index for key
        index = self.find_bucket(key)
        # If the pair is found, overwrite val and return
        if self.buckets[index] not in [None, self.TOMBSTONE]:
            self.buckets[index].val = val
            return
        # If the pair is absent, insert it
        self.buckets[index] = Pair(key, val)
        self.size += 1

    def remove(self, key: int):
        """Remove a key-value pair"""
        # Find the bucket index for key
        index = self.find_bucket(key)
        # If the pair is found, replace it with a deletion marker
        if self.buckets[index] not in [None, self.TOMBSTONE]:
            self.buckets[index] = self.TOMBSTONE
            self.size -= 1

    def extend(self):
        """Expand the hash table"""
        # Save the original hash table
        buckets_tmp = self.buckets
        # Initialize the larger hash table
        self.capacity *= self.extend_ratio
        self.buckets = [None] * self.capacity
        self.size = 0
        # Move the key-value pairs from the old table into the new one
        for pair in buckets_tmp:
            if pair not in [None, self.TOMBSTONE]:
                self.put(pair.key, pair.val)

    def print(self):
        """Print the hash table"""
        for pair in self.buckets:
            if pair is None:
                print("None")
            elif pair is self.TOMBSTONE:
                print("TOMBSTONE")
            else:
                print(pair.key, "->", pair.val)

/* Hash table with open addressing */
class HashMapOpenAddressing {
  private:
    int size;                             // Number of key-value pairs
    int capacity = 4;                     // Hash table capacity
    const double loadThres = 2.0 / 3.0;     // Load factor threshold for resizing
    const int extendRatio = 2;            // Growth factor
    vector<Pair *> buckets;               // Bucket array
    Pair *TOMBSTONE = new Pair(-1, "-1"); // Deletion marker

  public:
    /* Constructor */
    HashMapOpenAddressing() : size(0), buckets(capacity, nullptr) {
    }

    /* Destructor */
    ~HashMapOpenAddressing() {
        for (Pair *pair : buckets) {
            if (pair != nullptr && pair != TOMBSTONE) {
                delete pair;
            }
        }
        delete TOMBSTONE;
    }

    /* Hash function */
    int hashFunc(int key) {
        return key % capacity;
    }

    /* Load factor */
    double loadFactor() {
        return (double)size / capacity;
    }

    /* Find the bucket index for key */
    int findBucket(int key) {
        int index = hashFunc(key);
        int firstTombstone = -1;
        // Probe linearly until an empty bucket is reached
        while (buckets[index] != nullptr) {
            // If key is found, return its bucket index
            if (buckets[index]->key == key) {
                // If a deletion marker was found earlier, move the pair to that index
                if (firstTombstone != -1) {
                    buckets[firstTombstone] = buckets[index];
                    buckets[index] = TOMBSTONE;
                    return firstTombstone; // Return the new bucket index
                }
                return index; // Return the bucket index
            }
            // Record the first deletion marker encountered
            if (firstTombstone == -1 && buckets[index] == TOMBSTONE) {
                firstTombstone = index;
            }
            // Compute the next bucket index, wrapping to the start at the end
            index = (index + 1) % capacity;
        }
        // If key is absent, return the index for insertion
        return firstTombstone == -1 ? index : firstTombstone;
    }

    /* Look up a value */
    string get(int key) {
        // Find the bucket index for key
        int index = findBucket(key);
        // If the pair is found, return its val
        if (buckets[index] != nullptr && buckets[index] != TOMBSTONE) {
            return buckets[index]->val;
        }
        // If the pair is absent, return an empty string
        return "";
    }

    /* Insert a key-value pair */
    void put(int key, string val) {
        // Expand the table when the load factor exceeds the threshold
        if (loadFactor() > loadThres) {
            extend();
        }
        // Find the bucket index for key
        int index = findBucket(key);
        // If the pair is found, overwrite val and return
        if (buckets[index] != nullptr && buckets[index] != TOMBSTONE) {
            buckets[index]->val = val;
            return;
        }
        // If the pair is absent, insert it
        buckets[index] = new Pair(key, val);
        size++;
    }

    /* Remove a key-value pair */
    void remove(int key) {
        // Find the bucket index for key
        int index = findBucket(key);
        // If the pair is found, replace it with a deletion marker
        if (buckets[index] != nullptr && buckets[index] != TOMBSTONE) {
            delete buckets[index];
            buckets[index] = TOMBSTONE;
            size--;
        }
    }

    /* Expand the hash table */
    void extend() {
        // Save the original hash table
        vector<Pair *> bucketsTmp = buckets;
        // Initialize the larger hash table
        capacity *= extendRatio;
        buckets = vector<Pair *>(capacity, nullptr);
        size = 0;
        // Move the key-value pairs from the old table into the new one
        for (Pair *pair : bucketsTmp) {
            if (pair != nullptr && pair != TOMBSTONE) {
                put(pair->key, pair->val);
                delete pair;
            }
        }
    }

    /* Print the hash table */
    void print() {
        for (Pair *pair : buckets) {
            if (pair == nullptr) {
                cout << "nullptr" << endl;
            } else if (pair == TOMBSTONE) {
                cout << "TOMBSTONE" << endl;
            } else {
                cout << pair->key << " -> " << pair->val << endl;
            }
        }
    }
};

        }
