Why start with the least significant digit?

Each pass takes precedence over the one before it. For example, if the first pass orders two elements as \(a < b\) but the second orders them as \(a > b\), the second order prevails. Since more significant digits have higher priority, sort by the less significant digits first.

items.title: 11.10.2   Algorithm properties
items.text:
Compared with counting sort, radix sort handles a larger range of values, provided that the data can be represented with a fixed number of digits and that this number is not too large. For example, floating-point numbers are a poor fit here because their digit count \(k\) can be so large that the time complexity satisfies \(O(nk) \gg O(n^2)\).

  • Time complexity: \(O(nk)\), nonadaptive. Suppose there are \(n\) elements in base \(d\), each with at most \(k\) digits. Counting sort takes \(O(n + d)\) time for one digit, so sorting by all \(k\) digits takes \(O((n + d)k)\) time. Typically, \(d\) and \(k\) are both small and the time complexity approaches \(O(n)\).
  • Space complexity: \(O(n + d)\), out-of-place. As in counting sort, radix sort uses an array res of length \(n\) and an array counter of length \(d\).
  • Stable. If the counting sort used for each digit is stable, radix sort is stable too. If counting sort is unstable, radix sort may produce an incorrect result.

items.title: 11.2   Selection sort
items.text:
Selection sort uses a simple loop. On each pass, it selects the smallest element in the unsorted range and places it at the end of the sorted range.

For an array of length \(n\), selection sort proceeds as shown below.

  1. Initially, all elements are unsorted, so the unsorted indices span the closed interval \([0, n-1]\).
  2. Find the smallest element in \([0, n-1]\) and swap it with the element at index \(0\). The first element is now in its final position.
  3. Find the smallest element in \([1, n-1]\) and swap it with the element at index \(1\). The first two elements are now in their final positions.
  4. Continue in the same way. After \(n - 1\) rounds of selection and swapping, the first \(n - 1\) elements are in their final positions.
  5. The only remaining element must be the largest. It is already in place, so the array is sorted.

def selection_sort(nums: list[int]):
    """Selection sort"""
    n = len(nums)
    # Outer loop: the unsorted range is [i, n-1]
    for i in range(n - 1):
        # Inner loop: find the smallest element in the unsorted range
        k = i
        for j in range(i + 1, n):
            if nums[j] < nums[k]:
                k = j  # Record the index of the smallest element
        # Swap the smallest element with the first element of the unsorted range
        nums[i], nums[k] = nums[k], nums[i]

items.title: 11.2.1   Algorithm properties
items.text:
• Time complexity: \(O(n^2)\), nonadaptive. The outer loop runs \(n - 1\) times. The inner loop runs \(n - 1\) times on the first pass and \(1\) time on the last. The counts for successive passes are \(n - 1\), \(n - 2\), \(\dots\), \(2\), and \(1\), adding up to \(\frac{n(n - 1)}{2}\).
  • Space complexity: \(O(1)\), in-place. The two indices \(i\) and \(j\) use a constant amount of extra space.
  • Unstable. As shown below, a swap can move nums[i] to the right of an equal element, reversing their relative order.

Figure 11-3   Example of instability in selection sort

items.title: 11.1   Sorting algorithms
items.text:
A sorting algorithm arranges data in a specified order. Sorting is widely used because ordered data is usually easier to search, analyze, and process efficiently.

As Figure 11-1 shows, we can sort integers, floating-point numbers, characters, strings, and other types of data. We choose the ordering rule to suit the task, whether it uses numeric value, ASCII character codes, or a custom rule.

Figure 11-1   Examples of data types and ordering rules

items.title: 11.1.1   Criteria for comparing sorting algorithms
items.text:
Running time. We want low time complexity and a small total number of operations (a small constant factor in the running time). Speed is especially important for large datasets.

In-place operation. An in-place sort works directly on the original array, saving memory by avoiding an auxiliary array. In-place sorts usually move data less and run faster.

Stability. A stable sort preserves the relative order of equal elements in the array.

Stability is essential when sorting successively by multiple keys. Suppose a table of students contains names in the first column and ages in the second. An unstable sort can discard ordering information from the input:

# The input is sorted by name
# (name, age)
  ('A', 19)
  ('B', 18)
  ('C', 21)
  ('D', 19)
  ('E', 23)

# Suppose we sort the list by age using an unstable algorithm
# The relative order of ('D', 19) and ('A', 19) changes
# Students of the same age are no longer sorted by name
  ('B', 18)
  ('D', 19)
  ('A', 19)
  ('C', 21)
  ('E', 23)

Adaptivity. An adaptive sort takes advantage of existing order in the input to do less work and run faster. Its best-case time complexity is usually better than its average time complexity.

Use of comparisons. A comparison sort uses comparison operators (\(<\), \(=\), \(>\)) to establish the relative order of elements and sort the array. Its worst-case time complexity has a lower bound of \(\Omega(n \log n)\). A non-comparison sort does not rely on these comparisons and can run in \(O(n)\) time, but it applies to a narrower range of inputs.

items.title: 11.1.2   The ideal sorting algorithm
items.text:
Fast, in-place, stable, adaptive, and broadly applicable. So far, no known sorting algorithm has all these properties. The choice therefore depends on the data and the requirements of the problem.

In the following sections, we will study several sorting algorithms and use these criteria to analyze their strengths and weaknesses.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• Bubble sort swaps adjacent elements. Adding a flag that lets it return early improves its best-case time complexity to \(O(n)\).
  • On each pass, insertion sort takes an element from the unsorted range and inserts it at the correct position in the sorted range. Although it takes \(O(n^2)\) time, it performs relatively few elementary operations, making it a popular choice for small inputs.
  • Quicksort sorts by partitioning with two pointers. Choosing the worst possible pivot at every partition can degrade its running time to \(O(n^2)\). A median-of-three or random pivot makes this less likely. Recursing on the shorter subarray limits recursion depth and reduces space complexity to \(O(\log n)\).
  • Merge sort illustrates divide and conquer in two phases: divide and merge. Sorting an array requires an auxiliary array and takes \(O(n)\) space. For a linked list, the space complexity can be reduced to \(O(1)\).
  • Bucket sort has three steps: distribute the data among buckets, sort each bucket, and combine the results. It also uses divide and conquer and is suitable for very large datasets. Its efficiency depends on distributing the data evenly.
  • Counting sort is a special case of bucket sort that sorts values by counting their occurrences. It works well with large datasets whose values cover a limited range and can be converted to positive integers.
  • Radix sort sorts data one digit at a time. It requires values that can be represented with a fixed number of digits.
  • Ideally, a sorting algorithm would be efficient, stable, in-place, and adaptive. As with other data structures and algorithms, no single sort satisfies all these requirements. In practice, we choose an algorithm that suits the data.
  • Figure 11-19 compares common sorting algorithms in terms of efficiency, stability, in-place operation, and adaptivity.

Figure 11-19   Comparison of sorting algorithms

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: When does a sorting algorithm need to be stable?

In practice, we often sort objects by an attribute. Suppose each student has a name and a height, and we want to sort by multiple keys. First we sort by name, obtaining (A, 180) (B, 185) (C, 170) (D, 170). Then we sort by height. An unstable sort might produce (D, 170) (C, 170) (A, 180) (B, 185).

Students D and C have switched places. They are no longer in name order within their height group, which is precisely the ordering we wanted to preserve.

Q: In two-pointer partitioning, can we reverse the order of the right-to-left and left-to-right scans?

No. With the leftmost element as the pivot, we must scan from right to left first, then from left to right. Let's examine why this seemingly counterintuitive order matters.

The last step in partition() swaps nums[left] and nums[i]. After the swap, every element to the left of the pivot must be <= the pivot, so nums[left] >= nums[i] must hold before the swap. Suppose we scan from left to right first. If we find no larger element before the pointers meet, the loop exits at i == j, and we may have nums[j] == nums[i] > nums[left]. The final swap would then move an element larger than the pivot to the far left, breaking the partition.

For example, given [0, 0, 0, 0, 1], scanning from left to right first leaves the array as [1, 0, 0, 0, 0] after partitioning, which is incorrect.

The argument works in reverse if we choose nums[right] as the pivot: in that case, we must scan from left to right first.

Q: In quicksort, why does recursing on the shorter subarray limit recursion depth to \(\log n\)?

Recursion depth is the number of recursive calls that have not yet returned. Each partition splits the array into two subarrays. With the depth optimization, the subarray passed to the next recursive call is at most half the length of the current array. Even in the worst case, where the length is halved every time, the recursion depth is \(\log n\).

In the original quicksort, successive calls may keep taking the longer subarray. In the worst case, their lengths are \(n\), \(n - 1\), \(\dots\), \(2\), and \(1\), giving a recursion depth of \(n\). The depth optimization prevents this.

Q: Does quicksort take \(O(n^2)\) time when all the elements are equal? How can we handle this case?

Yes. We can handle it by partitioning the array into three parts: elements smaller than the pivot, elements equal to it, and elements larger than it. Recurse only on the smaller and larger groups. When all elements are equal, a single partition then sorts the entire array.

Q: Why is the worst-case time complexity of bucket sort \(O(n^2)\)?

In the worst case, all elements land in the same bucket. If we sort its contents with an \(O(n^2)\) algorithm, the time complexity is \(O(n^2)\).

items.title: Chapter 5.   Stacks and queues
items.text:
Abstract

Picture cats piled on top of one another for a stack, and cats standing in line for a queue.

A stack follows the last-in, first-out rule, and a queue follows the first-in, first-out rule.

items.title: 5.3   Deques
items.text:
An ordinary queue allows removal only at the front and insertion only at the rear. A double-ended queue (deque) is more flexible: as shown below, it allows insertion and removal at either end.

Figure 5-7   Deque operations

items.title: 5.3.2   Implementing a deque *
items.text: Like an ordinary queue, a deque can use either a linked list or an array as its underlying data structure.

items.title: 1.   Doubly linked list implementation
items.text:
In the previous section, we used a singly linked list for a queue because it makes it easy to remove the head node when dequeueing and to add a new node after the tail when enqueueing.

A deque supports enqueueing and dequeueing at both ends, so it also needs the mirror image of each queue operation. To support these operations, we use a doubly linked list.

As shown below, the head and tail of the doubly linked list serve as the front and rear of the deque. We implement insertion and removal at both ends.

<1><2><3><4><5>

Figure 5-8   Enqueueing and dequeueing at either end of a linked list

The following code implements the deque:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linkedlist_deque.py
class ListNode:
    """Doubly linked list node."""

    def __init__(self, val: int):
        """Initialize the node."""
        self.val: int = val
        self.next: ListNode | None = None  # Reference to the next node
        self.prev: ListNode | None = None  # Reference to the previous node

class LinkedListDeque:
    """Deque backed by a doubly linked list."""

    def __init__(self):
        """Initialize the deque."""
        self._front: ListNode | None = None  # Head node (_front)
        self._rear: ListNode | None = None  # Tail node (_rear)
        self._size: int = 0  # Deque size

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the deque size."""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the deque is empty."""
        return self._size == 0

    def push(self, num: int, is_front: bool):
        """Add an element at either end."""
        node = ListNode(num)
        # If the list is empty, point both _front and _rear at node
        if self.is_empty():
            self._front = self._rear = node
        # Add at the front
        elif is_front:
            # Link node at the head of the list
            self._front.prev = node
            node.next = self._front
            self._front = node  # Update the head
        # Add at the rear
        else:
            # Link node at the tail of the list
            self._rear.next = node
            node.prev = self._rear
            self._rear = node  # Update the tail
        self._size += 1  # Update the deque size

    def push_first(self, num: int):
        """Add an element at the front."""
        self.push(num, True)

    def push_last(self, num: int):
        """Add an element at the rear."""
        self.push(num, False)

    def pop(self, is_front: bool) -> int:
        """Remove an element from either end."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Deque is empty")
        # When the deque contains one element, the head and tail point to the same node
        if self._size == 1:
            val: int = self._front.val
            self._front = None
            self._rear = None
        # Remove from the front
        elif is_front:
            val: int = self._front.val  # Save the head node's value
            # Remove the head node
            fnext: ListNode | None = self._front.next
            fnext.prev = None
            self._front.next = None
            self._front = fnext  # Update the head
        # Remove from the rear
        else:
            val: int = self._rear.val  # Save the tail node's value
            # Remove the tail node
            rprev: ListNode | None = self._rear.prev
            rprev.next = None
            self._rear.prev = None
            self._rear = rprev  # Update the tail
        self._size -= 1  # Update the deque size
        return val

    def pop_first(self) -> int:
        """Remove and return the front element."""
        return self.pop(True)

    def pop_last(self) -> int:
        """Remove and return the rear element."""
        return self.pop(False)

    def peek_first(self) -> int:
        """Peek at the front element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Deque is empty")
        return self._front.val

    def peek_last(self) -> int:
        """Peek at the rear element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Deque is empty")
        return self._rear.val

    def to_array(self) -> list[int]:
        """Return a list for printing."""
        node = self._front
        res = [0] * self.size()
        for i in range(self.size()):
            res[i] = node.val
            node = node.next
        return res
linkedlist_deque.cpp
/* Doubly linked list node */
struct DoublyListNode {
    int val;              // Node value
    DoublyListNode *next; // Pointer to the next node
    DoublyListNode *prev; // Pointer to the previous node
    DoublyListNode(int val) : val(val), prev(nullptr), next(nullptr) {
    }
};

/* Deque backed by a doubly linked list */
class LinkedListDeque {
  private:
    DoublyListNode *front, *rear; // front points to the head node and rear to the tail node
    int queSize = 0;              // Deque size

  public:
    /* Constructor */
    LinkedListDeque() : front(nullptr), rear(nullptr) {
    }

    /* Destructor */
    ~LinkedListDeque() {
        // Walk the list and delete each node to free its memory
        DoublyListNode *pre, *cur = front;
        while (cur != nullptr) {
            pre = cur;
            cur = cur->next;
            delete pre;
        }
    }

    /* Get the deque size */
    int size() {
        return queSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the deque is empty */
    bool isEmpty() {
        return size() == 0;
    }

    /* Add an element at either end */
    void push(int num, bool isFront) {
        DoublyListNode *node = new DoublyListNode(num);
        // If the list is empty, point both front and rear at node
        if (isEmpty())
            front = rear = node;
        // Add at the front
        else if (isFront) {
            // Link node at the head of the list
            front->prev = node;
            node->next = front;
            front = node; // Update the head
        // Add at the rear
        } else {
            // Link node at the tail of the list
            rear->next = node;
            node->prev = rear;
            rear = node; // Update the tail
        }
        queSize++; // Update the deque size
    }

    /* Add an element at the front */
    void pushFirst(int num) {
        push(num, true);
    }

    /* Add an element at the rear */
    void pushLast(int num) {
        push(num, false);
    }

    /* Remove an element from either end */
    int pop(bool isFront) {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Queue is empty");
        int val;
        // When the deque contains one element, the head and tail point to the same node
        if (queSize == 1) {
            val = front->val;
            delete front; // Both point to the same node, so free it only once
            front = nullptr;
            rear = nullptr;
        }
        // Remove from the front
        else if (isFront) {
            val = front->val; // Save the head node's value
            // Remove the head node
            DoublyListNode *fNext = front->next;
            fNext->prev = nullptr;
            front->next = nullptr;
            delete front;
            front = fNext; // Update the head
        // Remove from the rear
        } else {
            val = rear->val; // Save the tail node's value
            // Remove the tail node
            DoublyListNode *rPrev = rear->prev;
            rPrev->next = nullptr;
            rear->prev = nullptr;
            delete rear;
            rear = rPrev; // Update the tail
        }
        queSize--; // Update the deque size
        return val;
    }

    /* Remove and return the front element */
    int popFirst() {
        return pop(true);
    }

    /* Remove and return the rear element */
    int popLast() {
        return pop(false);
    }

    /* Peek at the front element */
    int peekFirst() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Deque is empty");
        return front->val;
    }

    /* Peek at the rear element */
    int peekLast() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Deque is empty");
        return rear->val;
    }

    /* Return a vector for printing */
    vector<int> toVector() {
        DoublyListNode *node = front;
        vector<int> res(size());
        for (int i = 0; i < res.size(); i++) {
            res[i] = node->val;
            node = node->next;
        }
        return res;
    }
};

    private ListNode front, rear; // front points to the head node and rear to the tail node
    private int queSize = 0; // Deque size

    public LinkedListDeque() {
        front = rear = null;
    }

                match old_front.borrow_mut().next.take() {
                    Some(new_front) => {
                        new_front.borrow_mut().prev.take();
                        self.front = Some(new_front); // Update the head
                    }
                    None => {
                        self.rear.take();
                    }
                }
                self.que_size -= 1; // Update the deque size
                old_front.borrow().val
            })
        }
        // Remove from the rear
        else {
            self.rear.take().map(|old_rear| {
                match old_rear.borrow_mut().prev.take() {
                    Some(new_rear) => {
                        new_rear.borrow_mut().next.take();
                        self.rear = Some(new_rear); // Update the tail
                    }
                    None => {
                        self.front.take();
                    }
                }
                self.que_size -= 1; // Update the deque size
                old_rear.borrow().val
            })
        }
    }

    /* Remove and return the front element */
    pub fn pop_first(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        return self.pop(true);
    }

    /* Remove and return the rear element */
    pub fn pop_last(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        return self.pop(false);
    }

    /* Get a reference to the front node */
    pub fn peek_first(&self) -> Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>> {
        self.front.as_ref()
    }

    /* Get a reference to the rear node */
    pub fn peek_last(&self) -> Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>> {
        self.rear.as_ref()
    }

    /* Return a vector for printing */
    pub fn to_array(&self, head: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>) -> Vec<T> {
        let mut res: Vec<T> = Vec::new();
        fn recur<T: Copy>(cur: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, res: &mut Vec<T>) {
            if let Some(cur) = cur {
                res.push(cur.borrow().val);
                recur(cur.borrow().next.as_ref(), res);
            }
        }

        recur(head, &mut res);
        res
    }
}

/* Doubly linked list node */
typedef struct DoublyListNode {
    int val;                     // Node value
    struct DoublyListNode *next; // Next node
    struct DoublyListNode *prev; // Previous node
} DoublyListNode;

/* Constructor */
DoublyListNode *newDoublyListNode(int num) {
    DoublyListNode *new = (DoublyListNode *)malloc(sizeof(DoublyListNode));
    new->val = num;
    new->next = NULL;
    new->prev = NULL;
    return new;
}

/* Destructor */
void delDoublyListNode(DoublyListNode *node) {
    free(node);
}

/* Deque backed by a doubly linked list */
typedef struct {
    DoublyListNode *front, *rear; // front points to the head node and rear to the tail node
    int queSize;                  // Deque size
} LinkedListDeque;

/* Constructor */
LinkedListDeque *newLinkedListDeque() {
    LinkedListDeque *deque = (LinkedListDeque *)malloc(sizeof(LinkedListDeque));
    deque->front = NULL;
    deque->rear = NULL;
    deque->queSize = 0;
    return deque;
}

/* Destructor */
void delLinkedListdeque(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    // Free all the nodes
    for (int i = 0; i < deque->queSize && deque->front != NULL; i++) {
        DoublyListNode *tmp = deque->front;
        deque->front = deque->front->next;
        free(tmp);
    }
    // Free the deque structure
    free(deque);
}

/* Get the deque size */
int size(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    return deque->queSize;
}

/* Check whether the deque is empty */
bool empty(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    return (size(deque) == 0);
}

/* Enqueue an element */
void push(LinkedListDeque *deque, int num, bool isFront) {
    DoublyListNode *node = newDoublyListNode(num);
    // If the list is empty, point both front and rear at node
    if (empty(deque)) {
        deque->front = deque->rear = node;
    }
    // Add at the front
    else if (isFront) {
        // Link node at the head of the list
        deque->front->prev = node;
        node->next = deque->front;
        deque->front = node; // Update the head
    }
    // Add at the rear
    else {
        // Link node at the tail of the list
        deque->rear->next = node;
        node->prev = deque->rear;
        deque->rear = node;
    }
    deque->queSize++; // Update the deque size
}

/* Add an element at the front */
void pushFirst(LinkedListDeque *deque, int num) {
    push(deque, num, true);
}

/* Add an element at the rear */
void pushLast(LinkedListDeque *deque, int num) {
    push(deque, num, false);
}

/* Peek at the front element */
int peekFirst(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    assert(size(deque) && deque->front);
    return deque->front->val;
}

/* Peek at the rear element */
int peekLast(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    assert(size(deque) && deque->rear);
    return deque->rear->val;
}

/* Remove and return an element from either end of the deque */
int pop(LinkedListDeque *deque, bool isFront) {
    if (empty(deque))
        return -1;
    int val;
    // When the deque contains one element, the head and tail point to the same node
    if (deque->queSize == 1) {
        val = deque->front->val;
        delDoublyListNode(deque->front); // Both point to the same node, so free it only once
        deque->front = NULL;
        deque->rear = NULL;
    }
    // Remove from the front
    else if (isFront) {
        val = peekFirst(deque); // Save the head node's value
        DoublyListNode *fNext = deque->front->next;
        fNext->prev = NULL;
        deque->front->next = NULL;
        delDoublyListNode(deque->front);
        deque->front = fNext; // Update the head
    }
    // Remove from the rear
    else {
        val = peekLast(deque); // Save the tail node's value
        DoublyListNode *rPrev = deque->rear->prev;
        rPrev->next = NULL;
        deque->rear->prev = NULL;
        delDoublyListNode(deque->rear);
        deque->rear = rPrev; // Update the tail
    }
    deque->queSize--; // Update the deque size
    return val;
}

/* Remove and return the front element */
int popFirst(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    return pop(deque, true);
}

/* Remove and return the rear element */
int popLast(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    return pop(deque, false);
}

/* Print the deque */
void printLinkedListDeque(LinkedListDeque *deque) {
    int *arr = malloc(sizeof(int) * deque->queSize);
    // Copy the values from the linked list into an array
    int i;
    DoublyListNode *node;
    for (i = 0, node = deque->front; i < deque->queSize; i++) {
        arr[i] = node->val;
        node = node->next;
    }
    printArray(arr, deque->queSize);
    free(arr);
}

/* Deque backed by a doubly linked list */
class LinkedListDeque {
    private var front: ListNode? = null // Head node (front)
    private var rear: ListNode? = null // Tail node (rear)
    private var queSize: Int = 0 // Deque size

    /* Get the deque size */
    fun size(): Int {
        return queSize
    }

    fun isEmpty(): Boolean {
        return size() == 0
    }

    /* Add an element at either end */
    fun push(num: Int, isFront: Boolean) {
        val node = ListNode(num)
        // If the list is empty, point both front and rear at node
        if (isEmpty()) {
            rear = node
            front = rear
            // Add at the front
        } else if (isFront) {
            // Link node at the head of the list
            front?.prev = node
            node.next = front
            front = node // Update the head
            // Add at the rear
        } else {
            // Link node at the tail of the list
            rear?.next = node
            node.prev = rear
            rear = node // Update the tail
        }
        queSize++ // Update the deque size
    }

    /* Add an element at the front */
    fun pushFirst(num: Int) {
        push(num, true)
    }

    /* Add an element at the rear */
    fun pushLast(num: Int) {
        push(num, false)
    }

    /* Remove an element from either end */
    fun pop(isFront: Boolean): Int {
        if (isEmpty()) 
            throw IndexOutOfBoundsException()
        val _val: Int
        // When the deque contains one element, the head and tail point to the same node
        if (queSize == 1) {
            _val = front!!._val
            front = null
            rear = null
        }
        // Remove from the front
        else if (isFront) {
            _val = front!!._val // Save the head node's value
            // Remove the head node
            val fNext = front!!.next
            fNext!!.prev = null
            front!!.next = null
            front = fNext // Update the head
            // Remove from the rear
        } else {
            _val = rear!!._val // Save the tail node's value
            // Remove the tail node
            val rPrev = rear!!.prev
            rPrev!!.next = null
            rear!!.prev = null
            rear = rPrev // Update the tail
        }
        queSize-- // Update the deque size
        return _val
    }

    /* Remove and return the front element */
    fun popFirst(): Int {
        return pop(true)
    }

    /* Remove and return the rear element */
    fun popLast(): Int {
        return pop(false)
    }

    /* Peek at the front element */
    fun peekFirst(): Int {
        if (isEmpty()) throw IndexOutOfBoundsException()
        return front!!._val
    }

    /* Peek at the rear element */
    fun peekLast(): Int {
        if (isEmpty()) throw IndexOutOfBoundsException()
        return rear!!._val
    }

    /* Return an array for printing */
    fun toArray(): IntArray {
        var node = front
        val res = IntArray(size())
        for (i in res.indices) {
            res[i] = node!!._val
            node = node.next
        }
        return res
    }
}

class ArrayDeque:
    """Deque backed by a circular array."""

    def __init__(self, capacity: int):
        """Initialize the deque."""
        self._nums: list[int] = [0] * capacity
        self._front: int = 0
        self._size: int = 0

    def capacity(self) -> int:
        """Get the deque capacity."""
        return len(self._nums)

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the deque size."""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the deque is empty."""
        return self._size == 0

    def index(self, i: int) -> int:
        """Compute the circular array index."""
        # Use the remainder to wrap indices around the array
        # When i goes past the end, wrap it back to the start
        # When i goes before the start, wrap it around to the end
        return (i + self.capacity()) % self.capacity()

    def push_first(self, num: int):
        """Add an element at the front."""
        if self._size == self.capacity():
            print("Deque is full")
            return
        # Move the front index one slot to the left
        # Use the remainder to wrap front to the end if it goes before the start
        self._front = self.index(self._front - 1)
        # Add num at the front
        self._nums[self._front] = num
        self._size += 1

    def push_last(self, num: int):
        """Add an element at the rear."""
        if self._size == self.capacity():
            print("Deque is full")
            return
        # Compute the index one slot past the rear element
        rear = self.index(self._front + self._size)
        # Add num at the rear
        self._nums[rear] = num
        self._size += 1

    def pop_first(self) -> int:
        """Remove and return the front element."""
        num = self.peek_first()
        # Advance the front index by one
        self._front = self.index(self._front + 1)
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def pop_last(self) -> int:
        """Remove and return the rear element."""
        num = self.peek_last()
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def peek_first(self) -> int:
        """Peek at the front element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Deque is empty")
        return self._nums[self._front]

    def peek_last(self) -> int:
        """Peek at the rear element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Deque is empty")
        # Compute the index of the rear element
        last = self.index(self._front + self._size - 1)
        return self._nums[last]

    def to_array(self) -> list[int]:
        """Return a list for printing."""
        # Copy only the elements currently in the deque
        res = []
        for i in range(self._size):
            res.append(self._nums[self.index(self._front + i)])
        return res

  ### Peek at the rear element ###
  def peek_last
    raise IndexError, 'Deque is empty' if is_empty?

    # Compute the index of the rear element
    last = index(@front + size - 1)
    @nums[last]
  end

  ### Return an array for printing ###
  def to_array
    # Copy only the elements currently in the deque
    res = []
    for i in 0...size
      res << @nums[index(@front + i)]
    end
    res
  end

  private

  ### Compute the circular array index ###
  def index(i)
    # Use the remainder to wrap indices around the array
    # When i goes past the end, wrap it back to the start
    # When i goes before the start, wrap it around to the end
    (i + capacity) % capacity
  end
end

items.title: 5.3.3   Uses of deques
items.text:
A deque supports the behavior of both a stack and a queue, so it can serve all the same purposes while offering more flexibility.

Software typically uses a stack for undo: the system uses push to add each change to the stack, then uses pop to undo it. Because system resources are limited, software often caps the number of undo steps it keeps, for example at \(50\). When the stack grows beyond \(50\) steps, the software needs to remove the oldest step from the bottom of the stack (the front of the queue). A stack does not support this operation, so we need a deque in its place. Undo still follows the last-in, first-out rule. The deque gives us the flexibility to handle the additional operation.

items.title: 1.   Which element comes out first in a stack or a queue?
items.text:
Start with an empty stack S and an empty queue Q. Perform the same steps on each.

Step 1. Add A. Step 2. Add B. Step 3. Remove one element and record it. Step 4. Add C. Step 5. Keep removing elements and recording each one until the container is empty.

Write down the removal order for S and for Q. Explain the difference using “last in, first out” or “first in, first out” as appropriate.

Sample answer

The elements come off stack S in the order B, C, A. After pushing the elements A, B in that order, pop B first because it was added last. Then push C. The next two pops return C, A in that order. This is last in, first out.

The elements leave queue Q in the order A, B, C. After enqueuing the elements A, B in that order, dequeue A first because it was added first. Then enqueue C. The next two dequeues return B, C in that order. This is first in, first out.

items.title: 2.   What happens when the rear of a queue passes the end of the array?
items.text:
A queue uses a circular array of length 5 with indices in the range 0–4. Currently, front = 3 and size = 2. The queue elements A, B are at indices 3 and 4, respectively.

  1. When you enqueue C, at which index should you store C? What is the value of size afterward?
  2. Next, dequeue one element. Which element comes out, and what are the new values of front and size?
  3. What is the logical order of the elements from front to rear now? Does dequeuing require moving any other elements in the array? Why or why not?
Sample answer

  1. The index for the new element is (front + size) % 5 = (3 + 2) % 5 = 0, so C goes at index 0. After the enqueue operation, size = 3.

  2. Dequeuing removes A, the element currently at the front. The new front index is (3 + 1) % 5 = 4, so front = 4 and size = 2.

  3. The remaining elements are in the logical order B, C, with B at index 4 and C at index 0. To dequeue, you only need to advance front and update size. The modulo operation lets the index wrap back to the beginning of the array, so there is no need to shift the other elements forward.

items.title: 3.   Operations at both ends of a deque
items.text:
Here, push_first inserts at the front and push_last inserts at the rear. Likewise, pop_first removes from the front and pop_last removes from the rear.

Starting with an empty deque deq, perform the following operations in order.

  1. push_last(A)
  2. push_last(B)
  3. push_first(C)
  4. pop_last()
  5. push_last(D)
  6. pop_first()
  1. Which element does each of the two removals return?
  2. Which elements remain, from front to rear, after all the operations?
  3. Look at the six steps. Can a queue that only inserts at the rear and removes from the front perform all six? If it cannot, identify the operations it cannot perform. Then explain whether a deque can perform all six and why.
Sample answer

After the first three steps, the deque contains [C, A, B] from front to rear.

  1. pop_last() removes B. Adding D leaves the deque in the state [C, A, D]. Then pop_first() removes C.

  2. The remaining elements are [A, D].

  3. A queue that only inserts at the rear and removes from the front cannot perform all six operations. Step 3, push_first(C), requires insertion at the front. Step 4, pop_last(), requires removal from the rear. Both are outside the range of operations this queue supports. A deque supports insertion and removal at both ends, so it can perform all six steps.

items.title: 5.2   Queues
items.text:
A queue is a linear data structure that follows the first-in, first-out rule. Picture a line of people: newcomers join at the back, and people leave one at a time from the front.

The two ends of a queue are called the front and the rear, as shown below. Adding an element at the rear is called enqueueing, and removing the element at the front is called dequeueing.

Figure 5-4   The first-in, first-out rule for queues

items.title: 5.2.2   Implementing a queue
items.text: A queue needs a data structure that lets us add elements at one end and remove them from the other. Both linked lists and arrays meet this requirement.

items.title: 1.   Linked list implementation
items.text:
As shown below, we can use the head of a linked list as the front of the queue and the tail as the rear. We add nodes only at the rear and remove them only from the front.

<1><2><3>

Figure 5-5   Enqueueing and dequeueing with a linked list

The following code implements a queue with a linked list:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linkedlist_queue.py
class LinkedListQueue:
    """Queue backed by a linked list."""

    def __init__(self):
        """Initialize the queue."""
        self._front: ListNode | None = None  # Head node (_front)
        self._rear: ListNode | None = None  # Tail node (_rear)
        self._size: int = 0

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the queue size."""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the queue is empty."""
        return self._size == 0

    def push(self, num: int):
        """Enqueue an element."""
        # Add a node containing num after the tail
        node = ListNode(num)
        # If the queue is empty, point both the head and tail at the new node
        if self._front is None:
            self._front = node
            self._rear = node
        # If the queue has elements, link the new node after the tail
        else:
            self._rear.next = node
            self._rear = node
        self._size += 1

    def pop(self) -> int:
        """Remove and return the front element."""
        num = self.peek()
        # Remove the head node
        self._front = self._front.next
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def peek(self) -> int:
        """Peek at the front element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Queue is empty")
        return self._front.val

    def to_list(self) -> list[int]:
        """Convert to a list for printing."""
        queue = []
        temp = self._front
        while temp:
            queue.append(temp.val)
            temp = temp.next
        return queue

/* Queue backed by a linked list */
class LinkedListQueue {
  private:
    ListNode *front, *rear; // front points to the head node and rear to the tail node
    int queSize;

  public:
    LinkedListQueue() {
        front = nullptr;
        rear = nullptr;
        queSize = 0;
    }

    ~LinkedListQueue() {
        // Walk the list and delete each node to free its memory
        freeMemoryLinkedList(front);
    }

    /* Get the queue size */
    int size() {
        return queSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the queue is empty */
    bool isEmpty() {
        return queSize == 0;
    }

    /* Enqueue an element */
    void push(int num) {
        // Add a node containing num after the tail
        ListNode *node = new ListNode(num);
        // If the queue is empty, point both the head and tail at the new node
        if (front == nullptr) {
            front = node;
            rear = node;
        }
        // If the queue has elements, link the new node after the tail
        else {
            rear->next = node;
            rear = node;
        }
        queSize++;
    }

    /* Remove and return the front element */
    int pop() {
        int num = peek();
        // Remove the head node
        ListNode *tmp = front;
        front = front->next;
        // Free the allocated memory
        delete tmp;
        queSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Peek at the front element */
    int peek() {
        if (size() == 0)
            throw out_of_range("Queue is empty");
        return front->val;
    }

    /* Return the linked list elements as a vector */
    vector<int> toVector() {
        ListNode *node = front;
        vector<int> res(size());
        for (int i = 0; i < res.size(); i++) {
            res[i] = node->val;
            node = node->next;
        }
        return res;
    }
};

    final node = ListNode(_num);
    // If the queue is empty, point both the head and tail at the new node
    if (_front == null) {
      _front = node;
      _rear = node;
    } else {
      // If the queue has elements, link the new node after the tail
      _rear!.next = node;
      _rear = node;
    }
    _queSize++;
  }

  /* Remove and return the front element */
  int pop() {
    final int _num = peek();
    // Remove the head node
    _front = _front!.next;
    _queSize--;
    return _num;
  }

  /* Peek at the front element */

    if (_queSize == 0) {
      throw Exception('Queue is empty');
    }
    return _front!.val;
  }

    ListNode? node = _front;
    final List<int> queue = [];
    while (node != null) {

/* Queue backed by a linked list */
#[allow(dead_code)]
pub struct LinkedListQueue<T> {
    front: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, // Head node (front)
    rear: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>,  // Tail node (rear)
    que_size: usize,                         // Queue size
}

impl<T: Copy> LinkedListQueue<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            front: None,
            rear: None,
            que_size: 0,
        }
    }

    /* Get the queue size */
    pub fn size(&self) -> usize {
        return self.que_size;
    }

    /* Check whether the queue is empty */
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        return self.que_size == 0;
    }

    /* Enqueue an element */
    pub fn push(&mut self, num: T) {
        // Add a node containing num after the tail
        let new_rear = ListNode::new(num);
        match self.rear.take() {
            // If the queue has elements, link the new node after the tail
            Some(old_rear) => {
                old_rear.borrow_mut().next = Some(new_rear.clone());
                self.rear = Some(new_rear);
            }
            // If the queue is empty, point both the head and tail at the new node
            None => {
                self.front = Some(new_rear.clone());
                self.rear = Some(new_rear);
            }
        }
        self.que_size += 1;
    }

    /* Remove and return the front element */
    pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        self.front.take().map(|old_front| {
            match old_front.borrow_mut().next.take() {
                Some(new_front) => {
                    self.front = Some(new_front);
                }
                None => {
                    self.rear.take();
                }
            }
            self.que_size -= 1;
            old_front.borrow().val
        })
    }

    /* Get a reference to the front node */
    pub fn peek(&self) -> Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>> {
        self.front.as_ref()
    }

    /* Return the linked list elements as a vector */
    pub fn to_array(&self, head: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>) -> Vec<T> {
        let mut res: Vec<T> = Vec::new();

        fn recur<T: Copy>(cur: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, res: &mut Vec<T>) {
            if let Some(cur) = cur {
                res.push(cur.borrow().val);
                recur(cur.borrow().next.as_ref(), res);
            }
        }

        recur(head, &mut res);

        res
    }
}

items.title: 2.   Array implementation
items.text:
Removing the first element of an array takes \(O(n)\) time, which would make dequeueing inefficient. We can avoid this cost by changing how we keep track of the front.

Let front hold the index of the front element and size track the number of elements in the queue. With rear = front + size, the resulting index rear points one slot past the last element.

With this design, the queue elements occupy the closed interval [front, rear - 1] in the array. Figure 5-6 shows how the operations work.

  • To enqueue, store the new element at index rear and increase size by 1.
  • To dequeue, simply increase front by 1 and decrease size by 1.

Enqueueing and dequeueing each take a fixed number of steps without shifting any elements, so both run in \(O(1)\) time.

<1><2><3>

Figure 5-6   Enqueueing and dequeueing with an array

There is a catch. As we repeatedly enqueue and dequeue, front and rear move to the right. Once they reach the end of the array, they can go no farther. To solve this problem, we can treat the array as a circular array whose ends connect.

In a circular array, whenever front or rear goes past the end, it wraps around to the beginning and continues from there. The following code uses the remainder operation to implement this wraparound:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array_queue.py
class ArrayQueue:
    """Queue backed by a circular array."""

    def __init__(self, size: int):
        """Initialize the queue."""
        self._nums: list[int] = [0] * size  # Array that stores the queue elements
        self._front: int = 0  # Index of the front element
        self._size: int = 0  # Queue size

    def capacity(self) -> int:
        """Get the queue capacity."""
        return len(self._nums)

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the queue size."""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the queue is empty."""
        return self._size == 0

    def push(self, num: int):
        """Enqueue an element."""
        if self._size == self.capacity():
            raise IndexError("Queue is full")
        # Compute the index one slot past the rear element
        # Use the remainder to wrap rear back to the start of the array
        rear: int = (self._front + self._size) % self.capacity()
        # Add num at the rear
        self._nums[rear] = num
        self._size += 1

    def pop(self) -> int:
        """Remove and return the front element."""
        num: int = self.peek()
        # Advance the front index by one, wrapping to the start if it passes the end
        self._front = (self._front + 1) % self.capacity()
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def peek(self) -> int:
        """Peek at the front element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Queue is empty")
        return self._nums[self._front]

    def to_list(self) -> list[int]:
        """Return a list for printing."""
        res = [0] * self.size()
        j: int = self._front
        for i in range(self.size()):
            res[i] = self._nums[(j % self.capacity())]
            j += 1
        return res

    _queSize++;

impl<T: Copy + Default> ArrayQueue<T> {

        }

        if self.que_size == self.capacity() {

            return;
        }
        // Compute the index one slot past the rear element
        // Use the remainder to wrap rear back to the start of the array
        let rear = (self.front + self.que_size) % self.que_capacity;
        // Add num at the rear
        self.nums[rear as usize] = num;
        self.que_size += 1;
    }

    /* Remove and return the front element */
    fn pop(&mut self) -> T {
        let num = self.peek();
        // Advance the front index by one, wrapping to the start if it passes the end
        self.front = (self.front + 1) % self.que_capacity;
        self.que_size -= 1;
        num
    }

        if self.is_empty() {

            j += 1;

items.title: 5.2.3   Common uses of queues
items.text:
• Orders on Taobao. When a shopper places an order, it joins a queue. The system then processes orders in the order they arrived. During the Singles’ Day shopping festival, huge numbers of orders arrive in a short time, making high concurrency a major challenge for engineers.
  • Tasks waiting their turn. A queue keeps tasks in order wherever they need to be handled on a first-come, first-served basis. Examples include print jobs and orders waiting to be served at a restaurant.

items.title: 5.1   Stacks
items.text:
A stack is a linear data structure that follows the last-in, first-out rule.

Imagine a stack of plates on a table. If you can move only one plate at a time, to reach the bottom plate you must first remove each plate above it in turn. Replace the plates with elements such as integers, characters, or objects, and you have a stack.

As shown below, the two ends are called the top and the bottom of the stack. Adding an element to the top is called pushing, and removing the top element is called popping.

Figure 5-1   The last-in, first-out rule for stacks

items.title: 5.1.1   Common stack operations
items.text:
Table 5-1 lists common stack operations. Method names depend on the programming language. Here we use the familiar names push(), pop(), and peek().

Table 5-1   Time complexity of stack operations

Method Description Time complexity push() Push an element onto the top \(O(1)\) pop() Pop the top element \(O(1)\) peek() Access the top element \(O(1)\)

items.title: 5.1.2   Implementing a stack
items.text:
To see how a stack works, let’s implement a stack class ourselves.

The last-in, first-out rule allows us to add or remove elements only at the top. Arrays and linked lists allow insertion and removal at any position, so we can think of a stack as a restricted array or linked list. By hiding the operations a stack does not use, we can give the array or linked list the behavior of a stack.

items.title: 1.   Linked list implementation
items.text:
In a linked-list stack, we can use the head node as the top and the tail node as the bottom.

To push, insert the element at the head of the list, as shown below. This is called head insertion. To pop, simply remove the head node.

<1><2><3>

Figure 5-2   Pushing and popping with a linked list

The following code implements a stack with a linked list:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby linkedlist_stack.py
class LinkedListStack:
    """Stack backed by a linked list."""

    def __init__(self):
        """Initialize the stack."""
        self._peek: ListNode | None = None
        self._size: int = 0

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the stack size."""
        return self._size

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the stack is empty."""
        return self._size == 0

    def push(self, val: int):
        """Push an element onto the stack."""
        node = ListNode(val)
        node.next = self._peek
        self._peek = node
        self._size += 1

    def pop(self) -> int:
        """Remove and return the top element."""
        num = self.peek()
        self._peek = self._peek.next
        self._size -= 1
        return num

    def peek(self) -> int:
        """Peek at the top element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack is empty")
        return self._peek.val

    def to_list(self) -> list[int]:
        """Convert to a list for printing."""
        arr = []
        node = self._peek
        while node:
            arr.append(node.val)
            node = node.next
        arr.reverse()
        return arr

/* Stack backed by a linked list */
class LinkedListStack {
  private:
    ListNode *stackTop; // Use the head node as the top of the stack
    int stkSize;        // Stack size

  public:
    LinkedListStack() {
        stackTop = nullptr;
        stkSize = 0;
    }

    ~LinkedListStack() {
        // Walk the list and delete each node to free its memory
        freeMemoryLinkedList(stackTop);
    }

    /* Get the stack size */
    int size() {
        return stkSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the stack is empty */
    bool isEmpty() {
        return size() == 0;
    }

    /* Push an element onto the stack */
    void push(int num) {
        ListNode *node = new ListNode(num);
        node->next = stackTop;
        stackTop = node;
        stkSize++;
    }

    /* Remove and return the top element */
    int pop() {
        int num = top();
        ListNode *tmp = stackTop;
        stackTop = stackTop->next;
        // Free the allocated memory
        delete tmp;
        stkSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Peek at the top element */
    int top() {
        if (isEmpty())
            throw out_of_range("Stack is empty");
        return stackTop->val;
    }

    /* Return the linked list elements as a vector */
    vector<int> toVector() {
        ListNode *node = stackTop;
        vector<int> res(size());
        for (int i = res.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            res[i] = node->val;
            node = node->next;
        }
        return res;
    }
};

    e := s.data.Back()

class LinkedListStack {
    private var _peek: ListNode? // Use the head node as the top of the stack
    private var _size: Int // Stack size

    init() {
        _size = 0

    /* Get the stack size */
    func size() -> Int {

    func isEmpty() -> Bool {
        size() == 0

    func push(num: Int) {
        let node = ListNode(x: num)
        node.next = _peek
        _peek = node
        _size += 1

        _peek = _peek?.next
        _size -= 1

        var res = Array(repeating: 0, count: size())
        for i in res.indices.reversed() {
            res[i] = node!.val
            node = node?.next
        }
        return res
    }

        return this.#stkSize;
    }

    /* Check whether the stack is empty */
    isEmpty() {
        return this.size === 0;
    }

    /* Push an element onto the stack */
    push(num) {
        const node = new ListNode(num);
        node.next = this.#stackPeek;
        this.#stackPeek = node;
        this.#stkSize++;
    }

    /* Remove and return the top element */
    pop() {
        const num = this.peek();
        this.#stackPeek = this.#stackPeek.next;
        this.#stkSize--;
        return num;
    }

    /* Peek at the top element */
    peek() {
        if (!this.#stackPeek) throw new Error('Stack is empty');
        return this.#stackPeek.val;
    }

    /* Return the linked list elements as an array */
    toArray() {
        let node = this.#stackPeek;
        const res = new Array(this.size);
        for (let i = res.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            res[i] = node.val;
            node = node.next;
        }
        return res;
    }
}

/* Stack backed by a linked list */
#[allow(dead_code)]
pub struct LinkedListStack<T> {
    stack_peek: Option<Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>, // Use the head node as the top of the stack
    stk_size: usize,                              // Stack size
}

impl<T: Copy> LinkedListStack<T> {
    pub fn new() -> Self {
        Self {
            stack_peek: None,
            stk_size: 0,
        }
    }

    /* Get the stack size */
    pub fn size(&self) -> usize {
        return self.stk_size;
    }

    /* Check whether the stack is empty */
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
        return self.size() == 0;
    }

    /* Push an element onto the stack */
    pub fn push(&mut self, num: T) {
        let node = ListNode::new(num);
        node.borrow_mut().next = self.stack_peek.take();
        self.stack_peek = Some(node);
        self.stk_size += 1;
    }

    /* Remove and return the top element */
    pub fn pop(&mut self) -> Option<T> {
        self.stack_peek.take().map(|old_head| {
            self.stack_peek = old_head.borrow_mut().next.take();
            self.stk_size -= 1;

            old_head.borrow().val
        })
    }

    /* Get a reference to the top node */
    pub fn peek(&self) -> Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>> {
        self.stack_peek.as_ref()
    }

    /* Return the linked list elements as a vector */
    pub fn to_array(&self) -> Vec<T> {
        fn _to_array<T: Sized + Copy>(head: Option<&Rc<RefCell<ListNode<T>>>>) -> Vec<T> {
            if let Some(node) = head {
                let mut nums = _to_array(node.borrow().next.as_ref());
                nums.push(node.borrow().val);
                return nums;
            }
            return Vec::new();
        }

        _to_array(self.peek())
    }
}

/* Stack backed by a linked list */
typedef struct {

        free(s->top);
        s->top = n;
    }
    free(s);

    ListNode *node = (ListNode *)malloc(sizeof(ListNode));
    node->next = s->top; // Link the new node to the current top
    node->val = num;     // Set the value of the new node
    s->top = node;       // Update the top of the stack

items.title: 2.   Array implementation
items.text:
In an array-based stack, we can use the end of the array as the top. As shown below, a push adds an element at the end, and a pop removes the last element. Both take \(O(1)\) time.

<1><2><3>

Figure 5-3   Pushing and popping with an array

As more and more elements are pushed, the stack may outgrow its array. A dynamic array handles resizing for us, as in the following example:

class ArrayStack:
    """Array-backed stack."""

    def __init__(self):
        """Initialize the stack."""
        self._stack: list[int] = []

    def size(self) -> int:
        """Get the stack size."""
        return len(self._stack)

    def is_empty(self) -> bool:
        """Check whether the stack is empty."""
        return self.size() == 0

    def push(self, item: int):
        """Push an element onto the stack."""
        self._stack.append(item)

    def pop(self) -> int:
        """Remove and return the top element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack is empty")
        return self._stack.pop()

    def peek(self) -> int:
        """Peek at the top element."""
        if self.is_empty():
            raise IndexError("Stack is empty")
        return self._stack[-1]

    def to_list(self) -> list[int]:
        """Return the backing list for printing."""
        return self._stack

items.title: 5.1.3   Comparing the two implementations
items.text:
Supported operations

Both implementations support every operation in the definition of a stack. An array also supports random access, but that falls outside the stack interface and is generally unused here.

Time efficiency

In an array-based stack, pushes and pops use preallocated, contiguous memory. This gives them good cache locality and makes them fast. However, pushing an element beyond the array’s capacity triggers a resize, so that particular push takes \(O(n)\) time.

A linked list grows one node at a time and avoids the slowdown of resizing an array. However, a push needs to initialize a node object and update pointers, which makes it comparatively slow. If the element being pushed is already a node object, we can skip initialization and make the push faster.

For pushes and pops involving primitive types such as int or double, we can draw the following conclusions.

  • An array-based stack slows down when it resizes, but resizing is infrequent, so its operations are faster on average.
  • A linked-list stack offers more consistent operation times.

Space efficiency

When a list is initialized, the system allocates an initial capacity that may exceed what the list actually needs. Later, it typically grows by a fixed factor, for example by doubling, which can again leave capacity unused. As a result, an array-based stack may waste some space.

A linked list node, however, also needs to store a pointer, so each node takes up more space than an array element.

Which implementation uses less memory depends on the circumstances.

items.title: 5.1.4   Common uses of stacks
items.text:
• Back and forward in a browser, undo and redo in software. Whenever you open a new page, the browser pushes the previous page onto a stack. Going back pops that page off the stack so you can return to it. In this approach, supporting both back and forward requires two stacks working together.
  • Program memory management. Each time a function is called, the system pushes a stack frame that records the function’s context. In a recursive function, the system pushes a frame for each successive call and pops the frames as the calls return.

items.title: 1.   Key takeaways
items.text:
• A stack follows the last-in, first-out rule. You can implement one with an array or a linked list.
  • An array-based stack is faster on average, but a single push takes \(O(n)\) time when the array needs to grow. A linked-list stack has more consistent operation times.
  • An array-based stack may leave some memory unused. On the other hand, a linked list node takes up more memory than an array element.
  • A queue follows the first-in, first-out rule. Like a stack, it can use either an array or a linked list, with similar trade-offs in time and space.
  • A deque offers more flexibility than an ordinary queue because it allows insertion and removal at either end.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: Does a browser use a doubly linked list for back and forward navigation?

A browser’s back and forward navigation follows the logic of a stack. When you visit a new page, the browser pushes it onto the stack. When you click Back, the browser pops the current page off the stack. As the section on deques explains, using a deque makes it easy to support some additional operations.

Q: After popping a node, do I need to free its memory?

If you still need the node, keep its memory allocated. Once you no longer need it, languages such as Java and Python use automatic garbage collection, so you do not have to free the memory yourself. In C and C++, you must free it manually.

Q: A deque looks like two stacks joined together. What is it used for?

You can think of a deque as a stack and a queue combined, or as two stacks joined together. It supports both stack and queue operations, so it can serve all the same purposes and offers more flexibility.

Q: How do undo and redo work?

Use two stacks, A for undo and B for redo.

  1. Whenever the user performs a new action, push it onto stack A and clear stack B.
  2. When the user selects Undo, pop the most recent action from stack A and push it onto stack B.
  3. When the user selects Redo, pop the most recent action from stack B and push it onto stack A.

items.title: 7.3   Representing binary trees with arrays
items.text:
In the linked representation of a binary tree, each TreeNode node is a unit of storage, and pointers connect the nodes. The previous section introduced basic binary tree operations using this representation.

Can we also represent a binary tree with an array? Yes.

items.title: 7.3.1   Representing a perfect binary tree
items.text:
Start with a simple case: a perfect binary tree. If we store its nodes in an array in level order, each node has a unique array index.

Level order gives us a formula relating parent and child indices: if a node has index \(i\), its left child has index \(2i + 1\) and its right child has index \(2i + 2\). Figure 7-12 shows how the indices correspond.

Figure 7-12   Array representation of a perfect binary tree

The index formulas play the same role as node references (pointers) in the linked representation. Given any node in the array, we can use the formulas to access its left or right child.

items.title: 7.3.2   Representing an arbitrary binary tree
items.text:
A perfect binary tree is a special case. In general, a binary tree may have many None entries at intermediate levels. A level-order traversal skips these None entries, so the sequence alone tells us neither how many None entries there are nor where they belong. Several tree shapes can therefore produce the same level-order sequence.

As Figure 7-13 shows, the array representation we used above breaks down for a tree that is not perfect.

Figure 7-13   Different binary trees can have the same level-order sequence

To solve this problem, we can explicitly include every None in the level-order sequence. As Figure 7-14 shows, the sequence then identifies the tree uniquely. Here is an example in code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby 
# Array representation of a binary tree
# Use None to represent an empty slot
tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, None, 6, 7, 8, 9, None, None, 12, None, None, 15]

/* Array representation of a binary tree */
// Use INT_MAX, the largest int value, to mark an empty slot
vector<int> tree = {1, 2, 3, 4, INT_MAX, 6, 7, 8, 9, INT_MAX, INT_MAX, 12, INT_MAX, INT_MAX, 15};

/* Array representation of a binary tree */
// Use Integer, the wrapper class for int, so null can mark an empty slot
Integer[] tree = { 1, 2, 3, 4, null, 6, 7, 8, 9, null, null, 12, null, null, 15 };

/* Array representation of a binary tree */
// Use the nullable type int? so null can mark an empty slot
int?[] tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, null, 6, 7, 8, 9, null, null, 12, null, null, 15];

/* Array representation of a binary tree */

tree := []any{1, 2, 3, 4, nil, 6, 7, 8, 9, nil, nil, 12, nil, nil, 15}

/* Array representation of a binary tree */

/* Array representation of a binary tree */
// Use the largest int value to mark an empty slot, so node values must differ from INT_MAX
int tree[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, INT_MAX, 6, 7, 8, 9, INT_MAX, INT_MAX, 12, INT_MAX, INT_MAX, 15};

/* Array representation of a binary tree */
// Use null to represent an empty slot

### Array representation of a binary tree ###
# Use nil to represent an empty slot
tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, nil, 6, 7, 8, 9, nil, nil, 12, nil, nil, 15]

Figure 7-14   Array representation of an arbitrary binary tree

Complete binary trees are especially well suited to array representation. Recall that in a complete binary tree, None entries occur only at the far right of the bottom level, so all None entries come at the end of the level-order sequence.

That means we can conveniently omit all None entries when storing a complete binary tree in an array. Figure 7-15 gives an example.

Figure 7-15   Array representation of a complete binary tree

The following code implements an array-based binary tree with these operations:

  • Given a node, get its value, its left or right child, or its parent.
  • Get the preorder, inorder, postorder, and level-order traversal sequences.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby array_binary_tree.py
class ArrayBinaryTree:
    """Array-based binary tree class"""

    def __init__(self, arr: list[int | None]):
        """Constructor"""
        self._tree = list(arr)

    def size(self):
        """List capacity"""
        return len(self._tree)

    def val(self, i: int) -> int | None:
        """Get the value of the node at index i"""
        # If the index is out of bounds, return None to indicate an empty slot
        if i < 0 or i >= self.size():
            return None
        return self._tree[i]

    def left(self, i: int) -> int | None:
        """Get the index of the left child of the node at index i"""
        return 2 * i + 1

    def right(self, i: int) -> int | None:
        """Get the index of the right child of the node at index i"""
        return 2 * i + 2

    def parent(self, i: int) -> int | None:
        """Get the index of the parent of the node at index i"""
        return (i - 1) // 2

    def level_order(self) -> list[int]:
        """Level-order traversal"""
        self.res = []
        # Iterate directly over the array
        for i in range(self.size()):
            if self.val(i) is not None:
                self.res.append(self.val(i))
        return self.res

    def dfs(self, i: int, order: str):
        """Depth-first traversal"""
        if self.val(i) is None:
            return
        # Preorder traversal
        if order == "pre":
            self.res.append(self.val(i))
        self.dfs(self.left(i), order)
        # Inorder traversal
        if order == "in":
            self.res.append(self.val(i))
        self.dfs(self.right(i), order)
        # Postorder traversal
        if order == "post":
            self.res.append(self.val(i))

    def pre_order(self) -> list[int]:
        """Preorder traversal"""
        self.res = []
        self.dfs(0, order="pre")
        return self.res

    def in_order(self) -> list[int]:
        """Inorder traversal"""
        self.res = []
        self.dfs(0, order="in")
        return self.res

    def post_order(self) -> list[int]:
        """Postorder traversal"""
        self.res = []
        self.dfs(0, order="post")
        return self.res

    int size() {

    }

    /* Get the value of the node at index i */
    int val(int i) {
        // If the index is out of bounds, return INT_MAX to indicate an empty slot
        if (i < 0 || i >= size())
            return INT_MAX;
        return tree[i];

        return 2 * i + 2;
    }

    /* Get the index of the parent of the node at index i */
    int parent(int i) {
        return (i - 1) / 2;
    }

    /* Level-order traversal */
    vector<int> levelOrder() {
        vector<int> res;
        // Iterate directly over the array
        for (int i = 0; i < size(); i++) {
            if (val(i) != INT_MAX)
                res.push_back(val(i));
        }
        return res;
    }

    /* Preorder traversal */
    vector<int> preOrder() {
        vector<int> res;
        dfs(0, "pre", res);
        return res;

        dfs(0, "in", res);

        vector<int> res;
        dfs(0, "post", res);
        return res;
    }

  private:
    vector<int> tree;

    /* Depth-first traversal */
    void dfs(int i, string order, vector<int> &res) {

        if (val(i) == INT_MAX)
            return;
        // Preorder traversal
        if (order == "pre")
            res.push_back(val(i));
        dfs(left(i), order, res);
        // Inorder traversal
        if (order == "in")
            res.push_back(val(i));
        dfs(right(i), order, res);
        // Postorder traversal
        if (order == "post")
            res.push_back(val(i));
    }
};

class ArrayBinaryTree(List<int?> arr) {
    List<int?> tree = new(arr);

    /* List capacity */
    public int Size() {
        return tree.Count;
    }

    /* Get the value of the node at index i */
    public int? Val(int i) {
        // If the index is out of bounds, return null to indicate an empty slot
        if (i < 0 || i >= Size())
            return null;
        return tree[i];
    }

    /* Get the index of the left child of the node at index i */
    public int Left(int i) {
        return 2 * i + 1;
    }

    /* Get the index of the right child of the node at index i */
    public int Right(int i) {
        return 2 * i + 2;
    }

    /* Get the index of the parent of the node at index i */
    public int Parent(int i) {
        return (i - 1) / 2;
    }

    /* Level-order traversal */
    public List<int> LevelOrder() {
        List<int> res = [];
        // Iterate directly over the array
        for (int i = 0; i < Size(); i++) {
            if (Val(i).HasValue)
                res.Add(Val(i)!.Value);
        }
        return res;
    }

    /* Depth-first traversal */
    void DFS(int i, string order, List<int> res) {
        // Return if the slot is empty
        if (!Val(i).HasValue)
            return;
        // Preorder traversal
        if (order == "pre")
            res.Add(Val(i)!.Value);
        DFS(Left(i), order, res);
        // Inorder traversal
        if (order == "in")
            res.Add(Val(i)!.Value);
        DFS(Right(i), order, res);
        // Postorder traversal
        if (order == "post")
            res.Add(Val(i)!.Value);
    }

    /* Preorder traversal */
    public List<int> PreOrder() {
        List<int> res = [];
        DFS(0, "pre", res);
        return res;
    }

    /* Inorder traversal */
    public List<int> InOrder() {
        List<int> res = [];
        DFS(0, "in", res);
        return res;
    }

    /* Postorder traversal */
    public List<int> PostOrder() {
        List<int> res = [];
        DFS(0, "post", res);
        return res;
    }
}

class ArrayBinaryTree {
    private var tree: [Int?]

    /* Constructor */
    init(arr: [Int?]) {
        tree = arr
    }

    /* List capacity */
    func size() -> Int {
        tree.count
    }

    /* Get the value of the node at index i */
    func val(i: Int) -> Int? {
        // If the index is out of bounds, return null to indicate an empty slot
        if i < 0 || i >= size() {
            return nil
        }
        return tree[i]
    }

    /* Get the index of the left child of the node at index i */
    func left(i: Int) -> Int {
        2 * i + 1
    }

    /* Get the index of the right child of the node at index i */
    func right(i: Int) -> Int {
        2 * i + 2
    }

    /* Get the index of the parent of the node at index i */
    func parent(i: Int) -> Int {
        (i - 1) / 2
    }

    /* Level-order traversal */
    func levelOrder() -> [Int] {
        var res: [Int] = []
        // Iterate directly over the array
        for i in 0 ..< size() {
            if let val = val(i: i) {
                res.append(val)
            }
        }
        return res

        }
        dfs(i: left(i: i), order: order, res: &res)
        // Inorder traversal
        if order == "in" {
            res.append(val)
        }
        dfs(i: right(i: i), order: order, res: &res)
        // Postorder traversal
        if order == "post" {
            res.append(val)
        }
    }

        var res: [Int] = []
        dfs(i: 0, order: "pre", res: &res)
        return res

    /* Inorder traversal */
    func inOrder() -> [Int] {
        var res: [Int] = []
        dfs(i: 0, order: "in", res: &res)
        return res
    }

    /* Postorder traversal */
    func postOrder() -> [Int] {
        var res: [Int] = []
        dfs(i: 0, order: "post", res: &res)

    return 2 * i + 1;
  }

  /* Get the index of the right child of the node at index i */
  int? right(int i) {
    return 2 * i + 2;
  }

  /* Get the index of the parent of the node at index i */
  int? parent(int i) {
    return (i - 1) ~/ 2;
  }

  /* Level-order traversal */
  List<int> levelOrder() {
    List<int> res = [];
    for (int i = 0; i < size(); i++) {
      if (val(i) != null) {
        res.add(val(i)!);
      }
    }
    return res;
  }

  /* Depth-first traversal */
  void dfs(int i, String order, List<int?> res) {
    // Return if the slot is empty
    if (val(i) == null) {
      return;
    }
    // Preorder traversal
    if (order == 'pre') {
      res.add(val(i));
    }
    dfs(left(i)!, order, res);
    // Inorder traversal
    if (order == 'in') {
      res.add(val(i));
    }
    dfs(right(i)!, order, res);
    // Postorder traversal
    if (order == 'post') {
      res.add(val(i));
    }
  }

  /* Preorder traversal */
  List<int?> preOrder() {
    List<int?> res = [];
    dfs(0, 'pre', res);
    return res;
  }

  /* Inorder traversal */
  List<int?> inOrder() {
    List<int?> res = [];
    dfs(0, 'in', res);
    return res;
  }

  /* Postorder traversal */
  List<int?> postOrder() {
    List<int?> res = [];
    dfs(0, 'post', res);
    return res;

/* Array-based binary tree class */
struct ArrayBinaryTree {
    tree: Vec<Option<i32>>,
}

impl ArrayBinaryTree {
    /* Constructor */
    fn new(arr: Vec<Option<i32>>) -> Self {
        Self { tree: arr }
    }

    /* List capacity */
    fn size(&self) -> i32 {
        self.tree.len() as i32
    }

    /* Get the value of the node at index i */
    fn val(&self, i: i32) -> Option<i32> {
        // If the index is out of bounds, return None to indicate an empty slot
        if i < 0 || i >= self.size() {
            None
        } else {
            self.tree[i as usize]
        }
    }

    /* Get the index of the left child of the node at index i */
    fn left(&self, i: i32) -> i32 {
        2 * i + 1
    }

    /* Get the index of the right child of the node at index i */
    fn right(&self, i: i32) -> i32 {
        2 * i + 2
    }

    /* Get the index of the parent of the node at index i */
    fn parent(&self, i: i32) -> i32 {
        (i - 1) / 2
    }

    /* Level-order traversal */
    fn level_order(&self) -> Vec<i32> {
        self.tree.iter().filter_map(|&x| x).collect()
    }

    /* Depth-first traversal */
    fn dfs(&self, i: i32, order: &'static str, res: &mut Vec<i32>) {
        if self.val(i).is_none() {
            return;
        }
        let val = self.val(i).unwrap();
        // Preorder traversal
        if order == "pre" {
            res.push(val);
        }
        self.dfs(self.left(i), order, res);
        // Inorder traversal
        if order == "in" {
            res.push(val);
        }
        self.dfs(self.right(i), order, res);
        // Postorder traversal
        if order == "post" {
            res.push(val);
        }
    }

    /* Preorder traversal */
    fn pre_order(&self) -> Vec<i32> {
        let mut res = vec![];
        self.dfs(0, "pre", &mut res);
        res
    }

    /* Inorder traversal */
    fn in_order(&self) -> Vec<i32> {
        let mut res = vec![];
        self.dfs(0, "in", &mut res);
        res
    }

    /* Postorder traversal */
    fn post_order(&self) -> Vec<i32> {
        let mut res = vec![];
        self.dfs(0, "post", &mut res);
        res
    }
}

    dfs(abt, right(i), order, res, index);
