items.title: 7.3.3   Advantages and limitations
items.text:
The array representation of a binary tree has several advantages.

  • Arrays occupy contiguous memory. This makes them cache-friendly and allows fast access and traversal.
  • There are no pointers to store, which saves space.
  • Nodes support random access.

The array representation also has some limitations.

  • Arrays need contiguous memory, which makes them unsuitable for very large trees.
  • Adding and removing nodes requires array insertions and deletions, which are relatively inefficient.
  • If a binary tree contains many None entries, only a small fraction of the array holds node data, so space utilization is low.

items.title: 7.5   AVL trees *
items.text:
As we saw in the section on binary search trees, repeated insertions and deletions can turn a binary search tree into a linked list. When that happens, the time complexity of each operation worsens from \(O(\log n)\) to \(O(n)\).

In Figure 7-24, just two deletions turn the binary search tree into a linked list.

Figure 7-24   An AVL tree degenerates after node deletions

Similarly, inserting two nodes into the perfect binary tree below makes it lean heavily to the left, worsening the time complexity of search.

Figure 7-25   An AVL tree degenerates after node insertions

In 1962, G. M. Adelson-Velsky and E. M. Landis introduced the AVL tree in their paper “An algorithm for the organization of information.” They described operations that prevent the tree from degenerating under repeated insertions and deletions, keeping its operations at \(O(\log n)\) time. This makes AVL trees useful when data must be inserted, deleted, searched, and updated frequently.

items.title: 7.5.1   AVL tree terminology
items.text: An AVL tree is both a binary search tree and a balanced binary tree. It satisfies all the properties of both, making it a balanced binary search tree.

A node's height is the distance to its farthest leaf, measured in edges. A leaf has height \(0\), and a null node has height \(-1\). We will define two helper functions, one to get a node's height and one to update it:

    """Get the node height"""

    if node is not None:

    return -1

def update_height(self, node: TreeNode | None):
    """Update the node height"""
    # Node height is the height of the taller subtree plus 1
    node.height = max([self.height(node.left), self.height(node.right)]) + 1

items.title: 2.   Node balance factor
items.text:
A node's balance factor is the height of its left subtree minus the height of its right subtree. We define the balance factor of a null node to be \(0\). For convenience, we put this calculation in a function too:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def balance_factor(self, node: TreeNode | None) -> int:
    """Get the balance factor"""
    # A null node has a balance factor of 0
    if node is None:
        return 0
    # Balance factor = left subtree height - right subtree height
    return self.height(node.left) - self.height(node.right)

}

items.title: 7.5.2   AVL tree rotations
items.text:
The defining operation of an AVL tree is the rotation. It restores balance at a node without changing the inorder sequence of the tree. In other words, rotation preserves the binary search tree property while bringing the tree back into balance.

A node is unbalanced if the absolute value of its balance factor is \(> 1\). Depending on the shape of the imbalance, we use one of four rotations: right, left, right-left, or left-right. Let's look at each in turn.

items.title: 1.   Rotate right
items.text:
In Figure 7-26, each node's balance factor appears beneath it. Working from the bottom up, node 3 is the first unbalanced node. Focus on the subtree rooted there. Call that node node and its left child child, and perform a right rotation. The subtree regains balance and still satisfies the binary search tree property.

<1><2><3><4>

Figure 7-26   Steps in a right rotation

As shown below, if child has a right child (called grand_child), the right rotation needs one more step: make grand_child the left child of node.

Figure 7-27   Right rotation with grand_child

“Rotate right” describes what the movement looks like. To implement it, we update node pointers as follows:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def right_rotate(self, node: TreeNode | None) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Right rotation"""
    child = node.left
    grand_child = child.right
    # Rotate node to the right around child
    child.right = node
    node.left = grand_child
    # Update the node height
    self.update_height(node)
    self.update_height(child)
    # Return the root of the rotated subtree
    return child

items.title: 3.   Rotate left, then right
items.text:
For unbalanced node 3 in Figure 7-30, neither a single left rotation nor a single right rotation will balance the subtree. First rotate child to the left, then rotate node to the right.

Figure 7-30   Left rotation followed by right rotation

items.title: 4.   Rotate right, then left
items.text:
In the mirror image of the preceding case, shown below, first rotate child to the right, then rotate node to the left.

Figure 7-31   Right rotation followed by left rotation

items.title: 5.   Choosing a rotation
items.text:
The four imbalances below correspond to the examples above. From left to right, they require a right rotation, a left-right rotation, a right-left rotation, and a left rotation.

Figure 7-32   Four rotation cases in an AVL tree

As the table shows, we can identify the case by checking the balance factor of the unbalanced node and the sign of the balance factor of its child on the taller side.

Table 7-3   Conditions for choosing among the four rotations

Balance factor of the unbalanced node Balance factor of the child Rotation to use \(> 1\) (left-heavy tree) \(\geq 0\) Rotate right \(> 1\) (left-heavy tree) \(<0\) Rotate left, then right \(< -1\) (right-heavy tree) \(\leq 0\) Rotate left \(< -1\) (right-heavy tree) \(>0\) Rotate right, then left

For convenience, we put the rotation logic in a function. This function handles each kind of imbalance and restores balance at the affected node. Here is the code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def rotate(self, node: TreeNode | None) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Rebalance the subtree by rotating it"""
    # Get the balance factor of node
    balance_factor = self.balance_factor(node)
    # Left-heavy tree
    if balance_factor > 1:
        if self.balance_factor(node.left) >= 0:
            # Rotate right
            return self.right_rotate(node)
        else:
            # Rotate left, then right
            node.left = self.left_rotate(node.left)
            return self.right_rotate(node)
    # Right-heavy tree
    elif balance_factor < -1:
        if self.balance_factor(node.right) <= 0:
            # Rotate left
            return self.left_rotate(node)
        else:
            # Rotate right, then left
            node.right = self.right_rotate(node.right)
            return self.left_rotate(node)
    # The tree is balanced, so return without rotating
    return node

            node.borrow_mut().right = Self::right_rotate(right);

    // Get the balance factor of node
    int bf = balanceFactor(node);
    // Left-heavy tree
    if (bf > 1) {
        if (balanceFactor(node->left) >= 0) {
            // Rotate right
            return rightRotate(node);
        } else {
            // Rotate left, then right
            node->left = leftRotate(node->left);
            return rightRotate(node);
        }
    }
    // Right-heavy tree
    if (bf < -1) {
        if (balanceFactor(node->right) <= 0) {
            // Rotate left
            return leftRotate(node);
        } else {
            // Rotate right, then left
            node->right = rightRotate(node->right);
            return leftRotate(node);
        }
    }
    // The tree is balanced, so return without rotating
    return node;
}

items.title: 1.   Insert a node
items.text:
Inserting a node into an AVL tree works much like inserting one into a binary search tree. The difference is that after insertion, nodes along the path from the new node to the root may be unbalanced. Starting at the new node, we work upward and apply rotations to rebalance every affected node. Here is the code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def insert(self, val):
    """Insert a node"""
    self._root = self.insert_helper(self._root, val)

def insert_helper(self, node: TreeNode | None, val: int) -> TreeNode:
    """Insert a node recursively (helper method)"""
    if node is None:
        return TreeNode(val)
    # 1. Find the insertion position and insert the node
    if val < node.val:
        node.left = self.insert_helper(node.left, val)
    elif val > node.val:
        node.right = self.insert_helper(node.right, val)
    else:
        # Return without inserting a duplicate
        return node
    # Update the node height
    self.update_height(node)
    # 2. Rebalance the subtree by rotating it
    return self.rotate(node)

    if (val < node->val)
        node->left = insertHelper(node->left, val);
    else if (val > node->val)
        node->right = insertHelper(node->right, val);
    else
        return node;    // Return without inserting a duplicate
    updateHeight(node); // Update the node height
    /* 2. Rebalance the subtree by rotating it */
    node = rotate(node);
    // Return the root of the subtree
    return node;
}

items.title: 2.   Delete a node
items.text:
Similarly, we extend binary search tree deletion by applying rotations from the bottom up to rebalance every affected node. Here is the code:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby avl_tree.py
def remove(self, val: int):
    """Delete a node"""
    self._root = self.remove_helper(self._root, val)

def remove_helper(self, node: TreeNode | None, val: int) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Delete a node recursively (helper method)"""
    if node is None:
        return None
    # 1. Find the node and delete it
    if val < node.val:
        node.left = self.remove_helper(node.left, val)
    elif val > node.val:
        node.right = self.remove_helper(node.right, val)
    else:
        if node.left is None or node.right is None:
            child = node.left or node.right
            # No children: delete node and return
            if child is None:
                return None
            # One child: delete node
            else:
                node = child
        else:
            # Two children: delete the inorder successor and use it to replace the current node
            temp = node.right
            while temp.left is not None:
                temp = temp.left
            node.right = self.remove_helper(node.right, temp.val)
            node.val = temp.val
    # Update the node height
    self.update_height(node)
    # 2. Rebalance the subtree by rotating it
    return self.rotate(node)

    /* 1. Find the node and delete it */
    if (val < node->val)
        node->left = removeHelper(node->left, val);
    else if (val > node->val)
        node->right = removeHelper(node->right, val);
    else {
        if (node->left == nullptr || node->right == nullptr) {
            TreeNode *child = node->left != nullptr ? node->left : node->right;
            // No children: delete node and return
            if (child == nullptr) {
                delete node;
                return nullptr;
            }
            // One child: delete node
            else {
                delete node;
                node = child;
            }
        } else {
            // Two children: delete the inorder successor and use it to replace the current node
            TreeNode *temp = node->right;
            while (temp->left != nullptr) {
                temp = temp->left;
            }
            int tempVal = temp->val;
            node->right = removeHelper(node->right, temp->val);
            node->val = tempVal;
        }
    }
    updateHeight(node); // Update the node height
    /* 2. Rebalance the subtree by rotating it */
    node = rotate(node);
    // Return the root of the subtree
    return node;
}

                node.borrow_mut().right = Self::remove_helper(right, val);
            } else if node.borrow().left.is_none() || node.borrow().right.is_none() {
                let child = if node.borrow().left.is_some() {
                    node.borrow().left.clone()
                } else {
                    node.borrow().right.clone()
                };
                match child {
                    // No children: delete node and return
                    None => {
                        return None;
                    }
                    // One child: delete node
                    Some(child) => node = child,
                }
            } else {
                // Two children: delete the inorder successor and use it to replace the current node
                let mut temp = node.borrow().right.clone().unwrap();
                loop {
                    let temp_left = temp.borrow().left.clone();
                    if temp_left.is_none() {
                        break;
                    }
                    temp = temp_left.unwrap();
                }
                let right = node.borrow().right.clone();
                node.borrow_mut().right = Self::remove_helper(right, temp.borrow().val);
                node.borrow_mut().val = temp.borrow().val;
            }
            Self::update_height(Some(node.clone())); // Update the node height

            /* 2. Rebalance the subtree by rotating it */
            node = Self::rotate(Some(node)).unwrap();
            // Return the root of the subtree
            Some(node)
        }
        None => None,
    }
}

/* Delete a node recursively (helper function) */
TreeNode *removeHelper(TreeNode *node, int val) {
    TreeNode *child, *grandChild;
    if (node == NULL) {
        return NULL;
    }
    /* 1. Find the node and delete it */
    if (val < node->val) {
        node->left = removeHelper(node->left, val);
    } else if (val > node->val) {
        node->right = removeHelper(node->right, val);
    } else {
        if (node->left == NULL || node->right == NULL) {
            child = node->left;
            if (node->right != NULL) {
                child = node->right;
            }
            // No children: delete node and return
            if (child == NULL) {
                return NULL;
            } else {
                // One child: delete node
                node = child;
            }
        } else {
            // Two children: delete the inorder successor and use it to replace the current node
            TreeNode *temp = node->right;
            while (temp->left != NULL) {
                temp = temp->left;
            }
            int tempVal = temp->val;
            node->right = removeHelper(node->right, temp->val);
            node->val = tempVal;
        }
    }
    // Update the node height
    updateHeight(node);
    /* 2. Rebalance the subtree by rotating it */
    node = rotate(node);
    // Return the root of the subtree
    return node;
}

items.title: 3.   Search for a node
items.text: Searching an AVL tree works exactly like searching a binary search tree.

items.title: 7.5.4   Typical applications of AVL trees
items.text:
• Organizing and storing large amounts of data when searches are frequent and insertions and deletions are infrequent.
  • Building database indexes.
  • A red-black tree is another common balanced binary search tree. It has looser balance requirements than an AVL tree, needs fewer rotations for insertions and deletions, and on average performs those operations more efficiently.

items.title: 7.4   Binary search tree
items.text:
As Figure 7-16 shows, a binary search tree satisfies the following conditions.

  1. At the root, every value in the left subtree \(<\) the root value \(<\) every value in the right subtree.
  2. The left and right subtrees of every node are themselves binary search trees, so they too satisfy condition 1..

Figure 7-16   Binary search tree

items.title: 7.4.1   Binary search tree operations
items.text: We implement the tree as a BinarySearchTree class with a member variable root that points to the root.

items.title: 1.   Search for a node
items.text:
Given a target value num, we can use the search tree property to find it. As shown below, start a node reference cur at the root root and repeatedly compare the current value cur.val with num.

  • If cur.val < num, the target belongs in the right subtree of cur, so set cur = cur.right.
  • If cur.val > num, the target belongs in the left subtree of cur, so set cur = cur.left.
  • If cur.val = num, we have found the target. Exit the loop and return the node.
<1><2><3><4>

Figure 7-17   Searching for a node in a binary search tree

Searching a binary search tree uses the same principle as binary search: each round eliminates half the possibilities. The tree height bounds the number of iterations, and a balanced tree takes \(O(\log n)\) time. Here is an implementation:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_search_tree.py
def search(self, num: int) -> TreeNode | None:
    """Search for a node"""
    cur = self._root
    # Stop the search after passing a leaf
    while cur is not None:
        # The target is in the right subtree of cur
        if cur.val < num:
            cur = cur.right
        # The target is in the left subtree of cur
        elif cur.val > num:
            cur = cur.left
        # The target was found, so exit the loop
        else:
            break
    return cur

items.title: 2.   Insert a node
items.text:
To insert a value num while preserving the ordering “left subtree < root < right subtree,” follow the steps shown below.

  1. Find the insertion position. As in a search, start at the root and compare each node's value with num to decide which way to go. Stop when you pass a leaf and reach None.
  2. Insert the node at that position. Create a node with value num and put it in the position occupied by None.

Figure 7-18   Inserting a node into a binary search tree

Keep two points in mind when implementing insertion.

  • Duplicate values would violate our definition of a binary search tree. If the value is already in the tree, return without inserting a node.
  • Use pre to remember the node from the previous iteration. When you reach None, you will still have the parent reference you need to attach the new node.
PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_search_tree.py
def insert(self, num: int):
    """Insert a node"""
    # If the tree is empty, initialize the root
    if self._root is None:
        self._root = TreeNode(num)
        return
    # Stop the search after passing a leaf
    cur, pre = self._root, None
    while cur is not None:
        # Return if a duplicate is found
        if cur.val == num:
            return
        pre = cur
        # The insertion position is in the right subtree of cur
        if cur.val < num:
            cur = cur.right
        # The insertion position is in the left subtree of cur
        else:
            cur = cur.left
    # Insert a node
    node = TreeNode(num)
    if pre.val < num:
        pre.right = node
    else:
        pre.left = node

pub fn insert(&mut self, num: i32) {
    // If the tree is empty, initialize the root
    if self.root.is_none() {
        self.root = Some(TreeNode::new(num));
        return;
    }
    let mut cur = self.root.clone();
    let mut pre = None;
    // Stop the search after passing a leaf
    while let Some(node) = cur.clone() {
        match num.cmp(&node.borrow().val) {
            // Return if a duplicate is found
            Ordering::Equal => return,
            // The insertion position is in the right subtree of cur
            Ordering::Greater => {
                pre = cur.clone();
                cur = node.borrow().right.clone();
            }
            // The insertion position is in the left subtree of cur
            Ordering::Less => {
                pre = cur.clone();
                cur = node.borrow().left.clone();
            }
        }
    }
    // Insert a node
    let pre = pre.unwrap();
    let node = Some(TreeNode::new(num));
    if num > pre.borrow().val {
        pre.borrow_mut().right = node;
    } else {
        pre.borrow_mut().left = node;
    }

items.title: 3.   Delete a node
items.text:
First find the target in the binary tree, then delete it. As with insertion, deletion must preserve the ordering “left subtree < root < right subtree.” How we delete the target depends on whether it has zero, one, or two children.

As shown below, a node of degree \(0\) is a leaf and can be deleted directly.

Figure 7-19   Deleting a node of degree 0 from a binary search tree

As shown below, a node of degree \(1\) can simply be replaced by its only child.

Figure 7-20   Deleting a node of degree 1 from a binary search tree

We cannot simply remove a node of degree \(2\). We need a replacement. To preserve the ordering “left subtree \(<\) root \(<\) right subtree,” we can use either the smallest node in the right subtree or the largest node in the left subtree.

Suppose we choose the smallest node in the right subtree, which comes next in inorder traversal. Figure 7-21 shows the deletion.

  1. Find the node immediately after the target in the inorder sequence and call it tmp.
  2. Use the value of tmp to overwrite the target's value, and recursively delete node tmp from the tree.
<1><2><3><4>

Figure 7-21   Deleting a node of degree 2 from a binary search tree

Deletion also takes \(O(\log n)\) time. Finding the target takes \(O(\log n)\) time, and finding its inorder successor takes \(O(\log n)\) time. Here is an implementation:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_search_tree.py
def remove(self, num: int):
    """Delete a node"""
    # Return immediately if the tree is empty
    if self._root is None:
        return
    # Stop the search after passing a leaf
    cur, pre = self._root, None
    while cur is not None:
        # The node to delete was found, so exit the loop
        if cur.val == num:
            break
        pre = cur
        # The node to delete is in the right subtree of cur
        if cur.val < num:
            cur = cur.right
        # The node to delete is in the left subtree of cur
        else:
            cur = cur.left
    # Return if the node to delete does not exist
    if cur is None:
        return

    # Number of children = 0 or 1
    if cur.left is None or cur.right is None:
        # With no children, child = null. With one child, child is that child.
        child = cur.left or cur.right
        # Delete node cur
        if cur != self._root:
            if pre.left == cur:
                pre.left = child
            else:
                pre.right = child
        else:
            # If deleting the root, assign a new root
            self._root = child
    # Number of children = 2
    else:
        # Get the inorder successor of cur
        tmp: TreeNode = cur.right
        while tmp.left is not None:
            tmp = tmp.left
        # Recursively delete node tmp
        self.remove(tmp.val)
        # Replace the value of cur with that of tmp
        cur.val = tmp.val

/* Delete a node */
void remove(int num) {
    // Return immediately if the tree is empty
    if (root == nullptr)
        return;
    TreeNode *cur = root, *pre = nullptr;
    // Stop the search after passing a leaf
    while (cur != nullptr) {
        // The node to delete was found, so exit the loop
        if (cur->val == num)
            break;
        pre = cur;
        // The node to delete is in the right subtree of cur
        if (cur->val < num)
            cur = cur->right;
        // The node to delete is in the left subtree of cur
        else
            cur = cur->left;
    }
    // Return if the node to delete does not exist
    if (cur == nullptr)
        return;
    // Number of children = 0 or 1
    if (cur->left == nullptr || cur->right == nullptr) {
        // With no children, child = nullptr. With one child, child is that child.
        TreeNode *child = cur->left != nullptr ? cur->left : cur->right;
        // Delete node cur
        if (cur != root) {
            if (pre->left == cur)
                pre->left = child;
            else
                pre->right = child;
        } else {
            // If deleting the root, assign a new root
            root = child;
        }
        // Free memory
        delete cur;
    }
    // Number of children = 2
    else {
        // Get the inorder successor of cur
        TreeNode *tmp = cur->right;
        while (tmp->left != nullptr) {
            tmp = tmp->left;
        }
        int tmpVal = tmp->val;
        // Recursively delete node tmp
        remove(tmp->val);
        // Replace the value of cur with that of tmp
        cur->val = tmpVal;
    }
}

binary_search_tree.go
/* Delete a node */
func (bst *binarySearchTree) remove(num int) {
    cur := bst.root
    // Return immediately if the tree is empty
    if cur == nil {
        return
    }
    // Track the parent of the node to delete
    var pre *TreeNode = nil
    // Stop the search after passing a leaf
    for cur != nil {
        if cur.Val == num {
            break
        }
        pre = cur
        if cur.Val.(int) < num {
            // The node to delete is in the right subtree
            cur = cur.Right
        } else {
            // The node to delete is in the left subtree
            cur = cur.Left
        }
    }
    // Return if the node to delete does not exist
    if cur == nil {
        return
    }
    // Zero or one child
    if cur.Left == nil || cur.Right == nil {
        var child *TreeNode = nil
        // Get the child of the node to delete
        if cur.Left != nil {
            child = cur.Left
        } else {
            child = cur.Right
        }
        // Delete node cur
        if cur != bst.root {
            if pre.Left == cur {
                pre.Left = child
            } else {
                pre.Right = child
            }
        } else {
            // If deleting the root, assign a new root
            bst.root = child
        }
        // Two children
    } else {
        // Get the inorder successor of the node cur to be deleted
        tmp := cur.Right
        for tmp.Left != nil {
            tmp = tmp.Left
        }
        // Recursively delete node tmp
        bst.remove(tmp.Val.(int))
        // Replace the value of cur with that of tmp
        cur.Val = tmp.Val
    }
}

/* Delete a node */
pub fn remove(&mut self, num: i32) {
    // Return immediately if the tree is empty
    if self.root.is_none() {
        return;
    }
    let mut cur = self.root.clone();
    let mut pre = None;
    // Stop the search after passing a leaf
    while let Some(node) = cur.clone() {
        match num.cmp(&node.borrow().val) {
            // The node to delete was found, so exit the loop
            Ordering::Equal => break,
            // The node to delete is in the right subtree of cur
            Ordering::Greater => {
                pre = cur.clone();
                cur = node.borrow().right.clone();
            }
            // The node to delete is in the left subtree of cur
            Ordering::Less => {
                pre = cur.clone();
                cur = node.borrow().left.clone();
            }
        }
    }
    // Return if the node to delete does not exist
    if cur.is_none() {
        return;
    }
    let cur = cur.unwrap();
    let (left_child, right_child) = (cur.borrow().left.clone(), cur.borrow().right.clone());
    match (left_child.clone(), right_child.clone()) {
        // Number of children = 0 or 1
        (None, None) | (Some(_), None) | (None, Some(_)) => {
            // With no children, child = nullptr. With one child, child is that child.
            let child = left_child.or(right_child);
            // Delete node cur
            if !Rc::ptr_eq(&cur, self.root.as_ref().unwrap()) {
                let pre = pre.unwrap();
                let left = pre.borrow().left.clone();
                if left.is_some() && Rc::ptr_eq(left.as_ref().unwrap(), &cur) {
                    pre.borrow_mut().left = child;
                } else {
                    pre.borrow_mut().right = child;
                }
            } else {
                // If deleting the root, assign a new root
                self.root = child;
            }
        }
        // Number of children = 2
        (Some(_), Some(_)) => {
            // Get the inorder successor of cur
            let mut tmp = cur.borrow().right.clone();
            while let Some(node) = tmp.clone() {
                if node.borrow().left.is_some() {
                    tmp = node.borrow().left.clone();
                } else {
                    break;
                }
            }
            let tmp_val = tmp.unwrap().borrow().val;
            // Recursively delete node tmp
            self.remove(tmp_val);
            // Replace the value of cur with that of tmp
            cur.borrow_mut().val = tmp_val;
        }
    }
}

/* Delete a node */
// Including stdio.h prevents us from using the name remove here
void removeItem(BinarySearchTree *bst, int num) {
    // Return immediately if the tree is empty
    if (bst->root == NULL)
        return;
    TreeNode *cur = bst->root, *pre = NULL;
    // Stop the search after passing a leaf
    while (cur != NULL) {
        // The node to delete was found, so exit the loop
        if (cur->val == num)
            break;
        pre = cur;
        if (cur->val < num) {
            // The node to delete is in the right subtree of root
            cur = cur->right;
        } else {
            // The node to delete is in the left subtree of root
            cur = cur->left;
        }
    }
    // Return if the node to delete does not exist
    if (cur == NULL)
        return;
    // Check whether the node to delete has children
    if (cur->left == NULL || cur->right == NULL) {
        /* Number of children = 0 or 1 */
        // With no children, child = nullptr. With one child, child is that child.
        TreeNode *child = cur->left != NULL ? cur->left : cur->right;
        // Delete node cur
        if (pre == NULL) {
            bst->root = child;
        } else if (pre->left == cur) {
            pre->left = child;
        } else {
            pre->right = child;
        }
        // Free memory
        free(cur);
    } else {
        /* Number of children = 2 */
        // Get the inorder successor of cur
        TreeNode *tmp = cur->right;
        while (tmp->left != NULL) {
            tmp = tmp->left;
        }
        int tmpVal = tmp->val;
        // Recursively delete node tmp
        removeItem(bst, tmp->val);
        // Replace the value of cur with that of tmp
        cur->val = tmpVal;
    }
}

def remove(num)
  # Return immediately if the tree is empty
  return if @root.nil?

  # Stop the search after passing a leaf
  cur, pre = @root, nil
  while !cur.nil?
    # The node to delete was found, so exit the loop
    break if cur.val == num

    pre = cur
    # The node to delete is in the right subtree of cur
    if cur.val < num
      cur = cur.right
    # The node to delete is in the left subtree of cur
    else
      cur = cur.left
    end
  end
  # Return if the node to delete does not exist
  return if cur.nil?

  # Number of children = 0 or 1
  if cur.left.nil? || cur.right.nil?
    # With no children, child = null. With one child, child is that child.
    child = cur.left || cur.right

    if cur != @root
      if pre.left == cur
        pre.left = child
      else
        pre.right = child
      end
    else
      # If deleting the root, assign a new root
      @root = child

    # Get the inorder successor of cur
    tmp = cur.right
    while !tmp.left.nil?
      tmp = tmp.left
    end
    # Recursively delete node tmp
    remove(tmp.val)
    # Replace the value of cur with that of tmp
    cur.val = tmp.val
  end
end

items.title: 4.   Inorder traversal yields sorted values
items.text:
As Figure 7-22 shows, inorder traversal visits a binary tree in the order “left \(\rightarrow\) root \(\rightarrow\) right,” while a binary search tree satisfies “left child \(<\) root \(<\) right child.”

An inorder traversal of a binary search tree therefore always visits the next smallest node. This gives us an important property: the inorder sequence of a binary search tree is in ascending order.

This property lets us obtain sorted data from a binary search tree in just \(O(n)\) time, without a separate sorting step.

Figure 7-22   Inorder sequence of a binary search tree

items.title: 7.4.2   Efficiency of binary search trees
items.text:
Suppose we want to store a collection of values in either an array or a binary search tree. In Table 7-2, the search tree operations all take logarithmic time, giving consistent, efficient performance. An array is more efficient only when additions are frequent and searches and deletions are infrequent.

Table 7-2   Efficiency of arrays and search trees

Unsorted array Binary search tree Find an element \(O(n)\) \(O(\log n)\) Insert an element \(O(1)\) \(O(\log n)\) Delete an element \(O(n)\) \(O(\log n)\)

Ideally, a binary search tree is balanced, so we can find any node within \(\log n\) iterations.

Repeated insertions and deletions, however, can turn a binary search tree into a linked list, as shown below. The time complexity of its operations then worsens to \(O(n)\).

Figure 7-23   A binary search tree degenerates into a chain

items.title: 7.4.3   Common applications of binary search trees
items.text:
• Multilevel indexes that support efficient searches, insertions, and deletions.
  • The underlying data structure for certain search algorithms.
  • Storing streaming data in sorted order.

items.title: 7.1   Binary tree
items.text:
A binary tree is a nonlinear data structure that represents relationships between ancestors and descendants. Its two branches reflect the divide-and-conquer idea of splitting a problem in two. As with a linked list, the basic unit is a node. Each node contains a value and references to its left and right children.

    left: TreeNode | null;
    right: TreeNode | null;

    constructor(val?: number, left?: TreeNode | null, right?: TreeNode | null) {
        this.val = val === undefined ? 0 : val; // Node value
        this.left = left === undefined ? null : left; // Left child reference
        this.right = right === undefined ? null : right; // Right child reference
    }
}

/* Binary tree node class */
class TreeNode {
  int val;         // Node value
  TreeNode? left;  // Left child reference
  TreeNode? right; // Right child reference
  TreeNode(this.val, [this.left, this.right]);
}

use std::rc::Rc;
use std::cell::RefCell;

/* Binary tree node structure */
struct TreeNode {
    val: i32,                               // Node value
    left: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,    // Left child reference
    right: Option<Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>,   // Right child reference
}

impl TreeNode {
    /* Constructor */
    fn new(val: i32) -> Rc<RefCell<Self>> {
        Rc::new(RefCell::new(Self {
            val,
            left: None,
            right: None
        }))
    }
}

/* Binary tree node structure */
typedef struct TreeNode {
    int val;                // Node value
    struct TreeNode *left;  // Left child pointer
    struct TreeNode *right; // Right child pointer
} TreeNode;

/* Constructor */
TreeNode *newTreeNode(int val) {
    TreeNode *node;

    node = (TreeNode *)malloc(sizeof(TreeNode));
    node->val = val;
    node->left = NULL;
    node->right = NULL;
    return node;
}

/* Binary tree node class */
class TreeNode(val _val: Int) {  // Node value
    var left: TreeNode? = null   // Left child reference
    var right: TreeNode? = null  // Right child reference
}

### Binary tree node class ###
class TreeNode
  attr_accessor :val    # Node value
  attr_accessor :left   # Left child reference
  attr_accessor :right  # Right child reference

  def initialize(val)
    @val = val
  end
end

Each node has two references (pointers), one to its left child and one to its right child. The node is the parent of these children. For a given node, the tree consisting of its left child and all that child's descendants is its left subtree. Its right subtree is defined in the same way.

Every node in a binary tree except a leaf has at least one child and a nonempty subtree. For example, take node 2 as the parent in Figure 7-1. Its left and right children are nodes 4 and 5. Its left subtree consists of node 4 and all its descendants, and its right subtree consists of node 5 and all its descendants.

Figure 7-1   Parent, children, and subtrees

items.title: 7.1.1   Binary tree terminology
items.text:
Figure 7-2 illustrates common binary tree terms.

  • The root is the node at the top of a binary tree. It has no parent.
  • A leaf has no children. Both its pointers refer to None.
  • An edge is a line connecting two nodes. It represents a node reference (pointer).
  • A node's level increases from top to bottom. The root is at level 1.
  • A node's degree is its number of children. In a binary tree, the possible degrees are 0, 1, and 2.
  • The height of a binary tree is the number of edges from the root to the farthest leaf.
  • A node's depth is the number of edges from the root to that node.
  • A node's height is the number of edges between it and its farthest descendant leaf.

Figure 7-2   Common binary tree terms

Tip

We usually define height and depth by counting edges. Some problems and textbooks count nodes instead. Under that convention, add 1 to both height and depth.

items.title: 1.   Perfect binary tree
items.text:
In a perfect binary tree, every level is completely filled, as shown below. Leaves have degree \(0\), and every other node has degree \(2\). A tree of height \(h\) has \(2^{h+1} - 1\) nodes. This exponential relationship mirrors the familiar pattern of cell division in nature.

Tip

In Chinese usage, a perfect binary tree is often called a mǎn èrchāshù.

Figure 7-4   Perfect binary tree

items.title: 2.   Complete binary tree
items.text:
In a complete binary tree, only the bottom level may be partially filled, and its nodes must occupy consecutive positions from left to right, as shown below. Every perfect binary tree is also complete.

Figure 7-5   Complete binary tree

items.title: 3.   Full binary tree
items.text:
In a full binary tree, every node except a leaf has two children, as shown below.

Figure 7-6   Full binary tree

items.title: 4.   Balanced binary tree
items.text:
In a balanced binary tree, the absolute difference between the heights of the left and right subtrees at every node is at most 1, as shown below.

Figure 7-7   Balanced binary tree

items.title: 7.1.4   How a binary tree degenerates
items.text:
Figure 7-8 shows the ideal and degenerate forms of a binary tree. When every level is full, the tree is perfect. When all nodes lean to one side, the tree degenerates into a linked list.

  • A perfect binary tree is the ideal case. It takes full advantage of a binary tree's divide-and-conquer structure.
  • A linked list is the other extreme. Operations become linear, with time complexity \(O(n)\).

Figure 7-8   Best- and worst-case binary tree shapes

As Table 7-1 shows, quantities such as the number of leaves, total node count, and height reach their maximum or minimum values in the best- and worst-case shapes.

Table 7-1   Best- and worst-case binary tree shapes

Perfect binary tree Linked list Number of nodes at level \(i\) \(2^{i-1}\) \(1\) Number of leaves in a tree of height \(h\) \(2^h\) \(1\) Total number of nodes in a tree of height \(h\) \(2^{h+1} - 1\) \(h + 1\) Height of a tree with \(n\) nodes \(\log_2 (n+1) - 1\) \(n - 1\)

items.title: 7.2   Binary tree traversal
items.text:
In its linked representation, a tree is built from nodes connected by pointers, much like a linked list. We follow those pointers to visit the nodes one by one. A tree is nonlinear, however, so traversing it is more involved than following a list and calls for a search algorithm.

Common ways to traverse a binary tree include level-order, preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal.

items.title: 7.2.1   Level-order traversal
items.text:
As shown below, level-order traversal visits a binary tree one level at a time from top to bottom, moving from left to right within each level.

Level-order traversal is a breadth-first traversal, also called breadth-first search (BFS). It expands outward one level at a time.

Figure 7-9   Level-order traversal of a binary tree

items.title: 1.   Implementation
items.text:
Breadth-first traversal usually uses a queue. Its first-in, first-out rule fits the level-by-level progression of the traversal. Here is an implementation:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_tree_bfs.py
def level_order(root: TreeNode | None) -> list[int]:
    """Level-order traversal"""
    # Initialize the queue with the root
    queue: deque[TreeNode] = deque()
    queue.append(root)
    # Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    res = []
    while queue:
        node: TreeNode = queue.popleft()  # Dequeue a node
        res.append(node.val)  # Save the node value
        if node.left is not None:
            queue.append(node.left)  # Enqueue the left child
        if node.right is not None:
            queue.append(node.right)  # Enqueue the right child
    return res
binary_tree_bfs.cpp
/* Level-order traversal */
vector<int> levelOrder(TreeNode *root) {
    // Initialize the queue with the root
    queue<TreeNode *> queue;
    queue.push(root);
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    vector<int> vec;
    while (!queue.empty()) {
        TreeNode *node = queue.front();
        queue.pop();              // Dequeue a node
        vec.push_back(node->val); // Save the node value
        if (node->left != nullptr)
            queue.push(node->left); // Enqueue the left child
        if (node->right != nullptr)
            queue.push(node->right); // Enqueue the right child
    }
    return vec;
}

    queue.add(root);
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
    while (!queue.isEmpty()) {
        TreeNode node = queue.poll(); // Dequeue a node
        list.add(node.val);           // Save the node value
        if (node.left != null)
            queue.offer(node.left);   // Enqueue the left child
        if (node.right != null)
            queue.offer(node.right);  // Enqueue the right child
    }
    return list;
}

    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    List<int> list = [];
    while (queue.Count != 0) {
        TreeNode node = queue.Dequeue(); // Dequeue a node
        list.Add(node.val!.Value);       // Save the node value
        if (node.left != null)
            queue.Enqueue(node.left);    // Enqueue the left child
        if (node.right != null)
            queue.Enqueue(node.right);   // Enqueue the right child
    }
    return list;
}

func levelOrder(root *TreeNode) []any {
    // Initialize the queue with the root
    queue := list.New()
    queue.PushBack(root)
    // Initialize a slice to store the traversal sequence
    nums := make([]any, 0)
    for queue.Len() > 0 {
        // Dequeue a node
        node := queue.Remove(queue.Front()).(*TreeNode)
        // Save the node value
        nums = append(nums, node.Val)
        if node.Left != nil {
            // Enqueue the left child
            queue.PushBack(node.Left)
        }
        if node.Right != nil {
            // Enqueue the right child
            queue.PushBack(node.Right)
        }
    }
    return nums
}

/* Level-order traversal */
fn level_order(root: &Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>) -> Vec<i32> {
    // Initialize the queue with the root
    let mut que = VecDeque::new();
    que.push_back(root.clone());
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    let mut vec = Vec::new();

    while let Some(node) = que.pop_front() {
        // Dequeue a node
        vec.push(node.borrow().val); // Save the node value
        if let Some(left) = node.borrow().left.as_ref() {
            que.push_back(left.clone()); // Enqueue the left child
        }
        if let Some(right) = node.borrow().right.as_ref() {
            que.push_back(right.clone()); // Enqueue the right child
        };
    }
    vec
}
binary_tree_bfs.c
/* Level-order traversal */
int *levelOrder(TreeNode *root, int *size) {
    /* Auxiliary queue */
    int front, rear;
    int index, *arr;
    TreeNode *node;
    TreeNode **queue;

    /* Auxiliary queue */
    queue = (TreeNode **)malloc(sizeof(TreeNode *) * MAX_SIZE);
    // Queue pointers
    front = 0, rear = 0;
    // Enqueue the root
    queue[rear++] = root;
    // Initialize a list to store the traversal sequence
    /* Auxiliary array */
    arr = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int) * MAX_SIZE);
    // Array pointer
    index = 0;
    while (front < rear) {
        // Dequeue a node
        node = queue[front++];
        // Save the node value
        arr[index++] = node->val;
        if (node->left != NULL) {
            // Enqueue the left child
            queue[rear++] = node->left;
        }
        if (node->right != NULL) {
            // Enqueue the right child
            queue[rear++] = node->right;
        }
    }
    // Update the array length
    *size = index;
    arr = realloc(arr, sizeof(int) * (*size));

    // Free the auxiliary array
    free(queue);
    return arr;
}

    }

items.title: 2.   Complexity analysis
items.text:
• Time complexity: \(O(n)\). Each node is visited once, taking \(O(n)\) time, where \(n\) is the number of nodes.
  • Space complexity: \(O(n)\). In the worst case, a perfect binary tree, the queue holds up to \((n + 1) / 2\) nodes at once just before the bottom level is visited, using \(O(n)\) space.

items.title: 7.2.2   Preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal
items.text:
Preorder, inorder, and postorder are all forms of depth-first traversal, also called depth-first search (DFS). Each follows a branch to its end before backtracking to continue.

Figure 7-10 illustrates depth-first traversal of a binary tree. Imagine walking around the entire outline of the tree. You pass each node at three points, corresponding to preorder, inorder, and postorder.

Figure 7-10   Preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal of a binary search tree

items.title: 1.   Implementation
items.text:
Depth-first search is usually implemented recursively:

PythonC++JavaC#GoSwiftJSTSDartRustCKotlinRuby binary_tree_dfs.py
def pre_order(root: TreeNode | None):
    """Preorder traversal"""
    if root is None:
        return
    # Visit order: root -> left subtree -> right subtree
    res.append(root.val)
    pre_order(root=root.left)
    pre_order(root=root.right)

def in_order(root: TreeNode | None):
    """Inorder traversal"""
    if root is None:
        return

/* Preorder traversal */
fn pre_order(root: Option<&Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>) -> Vec<i32> {
    let mut result = vec![];

    fn dfs(root: Option<&Rc<RefCell<TreeNode>>>, res: &mut Vec<i32>) {
        if let Some(node) = root {
            // Visit order: root -> left subtree -> right subtree
            let node = node.borrow();
            res.push(node.val);
            dfs(node.left.as_ref(), res);
            dfs(node.right.as_ref(), res);
        }
    }
    dfs(root, &mut result);

    result
}

items.title: 2.   Complexity analysis
items.text:
• Time complexity: \(O(n)\). Each node is visited once, taking \(O(n)\) time.
  • Space complexity: \(O(n)\). In the worst case, the tree degenerates into a linked list. Recursion reaches depth \(n\), and the system uses \(O(n)\) space for stack frames.

items.title: 1.   Complete, full, and perfect binary trees
items.text:
The two arrays below represent binary trees in level order. An None entry marks an empty position.

  • Tree A: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
  • Tree B: [1, 2, 3, None, None, 6, 7]
  1. Which tree is complete?
  2. Which tree is full, meaning that every non-leaf node has two children?
  3. Is either tree perfect? Explain your reasoning for each tree.
Sample answer

  1. Tree A is complete. Only its bottom level is partially filled, and the nodes occupy consecutive positions starting on the left. Tree B is not complete because there are empty positions on the left of the bottom level with nodes farther to the right.

  2. Tree B is full. Nodes 1 and 3 each have two children, and all the other nodes are leaves. Tree A is not full because node 3 has only a left child, 6.

  3. Neither tree is perfect because neither has a full bottom level.

items.title: 2.   Three traversal orders for the same tree
items.text:
Use the array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] to fill a complete binary tree in level order.

  1. Draw the tree.
  2. Write down its preorder, inorder, and postorder traversal sequences.
  3. In the inorder sequence, which parts of the tree correspond to the values before and after the root, 1?
Sample answer

  1. The tree looks like this:

          1
    /   \
   2     3
  / \   / \
 4   5 6   7

  2. Preorder: 1, 2, 4, 5, 3, 6, 7. Inorder: 4, 2, 5, 1, 6, 3, 7. Postorder: 4, 5, 2, 6, 7, 3, 1.

  3. The sequence 4, 2, 5 before the root, 1, is the inorder traversal of the left subtree. The sequence 6, 3, 7 after the root is the inorder traversal of the right subtree.

items.title: 3.   Compare two binary search trees
items.text:
For each sequence below, start with an empty binary search tree and insert the values from left to right.

  • Sequence A: [4, 2, 6, 1, 3, 5, 7]
  • Sequence B: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
  1. For each tree, list the nodes visited when searching for 7.
  2. If height is measured in edges from the root to the farthest leaf, what is the height of each tree?
  3. Based on your previous two answers, is searching for 7 equally efficient in both trees? Explain using the tree shapes and search paths.
Sample answer

  1. In the tree built from sequence A, the search path is 4 → 6 → 7. In the tree built from sequence B, the search path is 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7.

  2. Every level of the first tree is full, so its height is 2. The second tree has only right children, so its height is 6.

  3. Searching for 7 takes different amounts of work in the two trees. The insertion order changes the shape and height of a binary search tree. The search for 7 visits just 3 nodes in the first tree, but it visits all 7 nodes in order in the second tree. The taller the tree, the more nodes a search must compare along a path in the worst case.

items.title: 1.   Maximum depth of a binary tree
items.text:
You are given the root root of a binary tree. Each node holds an integer and references to its left and right children.

The maximum depth of a binary tree is the number of nodes on the path from the root to the farthest leaf. Return the maximum depth of the tree. An empty tree has a maximum depth of 0. Use recursion.

  2. Have the recursive function return the maximum depth of the subtree rooted at the current node.
  3. For a null node, return 0. Otherwise, return max(depth(left), depth(right)) + 1.

items.title: 1.   Key points
items.text:
• A binary tree is a nonlinear data structure that embodies the divide-and-conquer idea of splitting in two. Each node holds a value and two pointers, one to its left child and one to its right.
  • For any node in a binary tree, its left subtree consists of its left child and all that child's descendants. Its right subtree is defined in the same way.
  • Binary tree terminology includes root, leaf, level, degree, edge, height, and depth.
  • Initializing a binary tree and inserting or deleting a node are similar to the corresponding linked list operations.
  • Common types include perfect, complete, full, and balanced binary trees. A perfect binary tree is the ideal shape. A tree that degenerates into a linked list has the worst shape.
  • To represent a binary tree in an array, arrange node values and empty slots in level order. Formulas relating parent and child indices take the place of pointers.
  • Level-order traversal of a binary tree is a breadth-first search. It expands outward one level at a time and usually uses a queue.
  • Preorder, inorder, and postorder are depth-first searches. They follow a branch to its end before backtracking to continue and are usually implemented recursively.
  • A binary search tree supports efficient lookup. Search, insertion, and deletion take \(O(\log n)\) time. When the tree degenerates into a linked list, these operations worsen to \(O(n)\) time.
  • An AVL tree is a balanced binary search tree that uses rotations to maintain balance through repeated insertions and deletions.
  • AVL rotations include right, left, right-left, and left-right rotations. After insertion or deletion, an AVL tree works upward from the bottom, applying rotations to restore balance.

items.title: 2.   Q & A
items.text:
Q: In a binary tree with just one node, are the tree height and the root's depth both \(0\)?

Yes. Height and depth usually count the edges on a path.

Q: Inserting or deleting a node in a binary tree generally requires several coordinated operations. What are those operations? Does this mean freeing the resources held by child nodes?

Consider deletion in a binary search tree. There are three cases, and each takes several steps involving nodes.

Q: Why does depth-first traversal of a binary tree have three orders, and what is each one used for?

Much as an array can be traversed forward or backward, a binary tree can be traversed in preorder, inorder, or postorder to obtain a particular ordering. For example, values in a binary search tree satisfy left child value < root value < right child value. Visiting the tree in the order “left \(\rightarrow\) root \(\rightarrow\) right” therefore yields a sorted sequence.

Q: A right rotation handles the relationships among the unbalanced node node, child, and grand_child. What about the original connection between the parent of node and node? Doesn't the rotation break it?

Think of the recursive calls. The right rotation right_rotate(root) receives a subtree root, and return child returns the root of the rotated subtree. The new subtree root is connected to its parent after the function returns, outside the right rotation itself.

Q: In C++, how do we decide which functions belong in private and which in public? Why are height() and updateHeight() placed in public and private, respectively?

It mainly depends on where a method is used. A method used only within the class should be private. For example, there is no reason for a user to call updateHeight() on its own. It is just one step in insertion or deletion. In contrast, height() accesses a node's height, much like vector.size() accesses a size, so it is public for convenient access.

Q: How can we build a binary search tree from a collection of input values? Does the choice of root matter?

Yes. The build_tree() method in the binary search tree code shows how to build the tree. To choose the root, we usually sort the input, take the middle element as the root, and recursively build the left and right subtrees. This keeps the tree as balanced as possible.

Q: In Java, do we always need the equals() method to compare strings?

For Java primitive types, == compares the values of two variables. For reference types, the two forms of comparison work differently.

  • == checks whether the variables refer to the same object, that is, the same location in memory.
  • equals() checks whether two objects have equal values.

To compare values, use equals(). However, strings initialized by String a = "hi"; String b = "hi"; are stored in the string pool and refer to the same object, so a == b can also be used to compare the contents of these two strings.

Q: Just before breadth-first traversal visits the bottom level, does the queue contain \(2^h\) nodes?

Yes. For example, a perfect binary tree of height \(h = 2\) has \(n = 7\) nodes in total and \(4 = 2^h = (n + 1) / 2\) nodes on its bottom level.
